1979.  And some of the alleged connections are not persuasive -- for 
example,  in connection with an April 24, 1996 bombing, the authors note 
that Kaczynski stayed at a Helena, Montana hotel on March 13.  So?

The authors of both books apparently were looking to beef up their 
length.  Mad Genius includes an essay written by computer scientist 
David Gelertner, who was severely injured by a bomb in 1993.   Unabomber 
includes a chapter titled "A Second Opinion," which quotes a behavioral 
analysis based, in part, on an examination of handwriting that is 
assumed to be the bomber's.  The note read:  "Call Nathan R -- Wed 7 
p.m."  The curious aspect of the "Second Opinion" is that the authors 
nowhere allude to whether they view the "Nathan R" note as being in 
Kaczynski's handwriting.  

Importantly, both books contain the manifesto and many people will buy 
the books just to have a copy of the manifesto. 

For those who have already been following the press on the Unabom 
matter, the  greatest strength of Douglas' book is his apt comments on 
the manifesto.   After noting the Unabomber's insistence that all modern 
technology be eliminated, Douglas writes:

"Let's be real, here, folks.  He knows that isn't going to happen.  ... 
He's got a personal ax to grind based on his own deep problems and 
inadequacies."  

As "true crime" books,  the books without a doubt prove that the man 
living in the shed was Theodore John Kaczynski.   Moreover, it appears 
clear that he had bomb-making materials in his possession.   They may 
even provide ample evidence that he was a clever and careful mailbomber.  
As for enlightening the public on the question whether the Kaczynski is 
the Unabomber, however, the books suffer the same drawback as the press 
reports.  We still do not know which of the press leaks are accurate.  
Mad Genius has this odd statement:  "From the day of the raid on, there 
was little doubt in the public mind that he and the Unabomber were one 
and the same."  This is an ironic statement for these influential 
journalists to make.  Only passing mention is made of the many grossly 
inaccurate headlines that pummelled readers in early and mid April.   
For example, just three days after Kaczynski's arrest, the  headline in 
New York Daily News of a story about the two typewriters found headline 
screamed "Typewriter bombshell."   The reports were proved wrong when 
the lab tests did not confirm the agents' initial reported impressions 
that one of the two typewriters matched the one used to type the 
manifesto.   At about the same time that the disappointing lab tests 
came back on the first two typewriters, agents found a third typewriter, 
for which the final lab tests have not been announced.  

It would have been preferable if both books had more expressly taken 
into account the possibility that some more of the unconfirmed reports 
by unnamed sources are flat out wrong.   

The Unabomber book actually repeats a number of apparently mistaken news 
items. For example, the Unabomber book repeats the story mistakenly 
first reported by the Washington Post and then nationwide concerning a 
list of names of approximately 25 University of California-Berkeley 
mathematics professors allegedly found in the cabin.  Douglas and author 
Olshaker repeated the report even though the Post, along with most other 
major newspapers, had long since forthrightly explained that the report 
was wrong.  A campus policeman had mistakenly assumed that a handwritten 
list written by an FBI agent for his own purposes had been by the mad 
bomber. Similarly, he authors repeated the apparently unconfirmed 
reports that Kaczynski's family had purchased tickets to California (as 
opposed to have given Kaczynski money).  Finally, unlike Mad Genius, the 
Unabomber authors appear to accept the widely-reported account by the 
proprietors of Royal Hotel in Sacramento that he had stayed at their 
hotel in Sacramento, even though the New York Times has persuasively 
reported that the owner has backed off the statement and had told the 
FBI that he did not know the man in the pictures he had been shown.

It is also disappointing that someone knowledgeable about 
psycholinguistic techniques would place so much stock in the use by both 
the Unabomber and Kaczynski of the phrase "You can't eat your cake and 
have it too."   Douglas describes the phrasing as "twisted" and "too odd 
and too striking to be coincidence."  The bomber's phrasing, and 
Kaczynksi's phrasing, however, is the variation used, for example, by 
James Joyce in Ulysses in the 1920's.  Although the more conventional 
phrasing of the saying is five centuries old, the version used by both 
the Unabomber and Kacyznski is hardly a mistake -- it is simply a 
variation used by many literate and educated folks.  And it is the more 
logical phrasing -- it is only remarkable if you think you can still 
have your cake after you eat it.  By definition, you need to have it 
before you can eat it.

Relatedly, Douglas' reliance on the analysis done by psycholinguistic 
types enlisted by his former colleague, Clint Van Zandt, is also 
disappointing.  Those experts relied upon only five pages of writing 
selectively provided from among hundreds written by Ted to his mother 
and brother.  We could make authors Douglas and Olshaker look like any 
number of characters --ranging from Elmer Fudd to Frank Delano Roosevelt 
-- depending on the particular five pages we chose.  Although we do not 
yet know the exact contents of the  five pages were provided,  an expert 
might have demanded all available copies before rendering an opinion.  
Certainly, an opinion that a one of several hundred million people in 
this country was 60-80 percent likely to be a serial murderer should not 
have been given without seeing all available letters.  There are several 
authors on the usnet group "alt.fan.unabomber" ("Bandit" and "Ric 
Ricardo" to name two) who sound more like the Unabomber than Ted likely 
did in the five pages provided Van Zandt's  experts). 

Such factual errors, even though minor, threaten the integrity of some 
of the conclusions reached.  For example, the  authors in Unabomber 
conclude that the note "Wu, I told you it would work . R.V." was a 
reference to two Berkeley math professors.   The conclusion (whether 
true or not)  is far less likely once one realizes that the handwritten 
list of math professors was, in fact, not found in the cabin.  Mad 
Genius is not without its curious statements and conclusions.  For 
example, the authors in Mad Genius summarily conclude that the same note 
attached to a 1982 bomb was "probably inadvertently" left by the bomber.  
The more natural inference would be that it was left as a red herring, 
and was intended to mislead the Task Force. 

Both books make the same error that press reports have been making since 
April of last year -- the bomber, according to the conventional wisdom, 
was jealous of the attention paid to the Oklahoma City bombings.  The 
Oklahoma City bombing was April 19.  The Unabomber sent a sophisticated 
bomb on April 20 along with some fairly lengthy letters.  One of those 
letters announced that he had a lengthy manifesto (and he gave the 
approximate word count) that he would be forwarding.  It is unlikely 
that the bomber woke up on April 19 and after hearing of the explosion 
in Oklahoma said: "Boy, I'm glad I brought this typewriter to California 
with me on the bus so I could send out these letters and type these 
labels." 
        
Mad Genius shows a greater willingness to state the facts in ways that 
depart from the previous accounts.  For example, the journalist-authors 
boldly (and probably correctly) report that 22 people were injured 
rather than the 23 usually recited in the UNABOM folklore.  It was 
probably the psychology professor in 1985 that they didn't count.  He 
was merely standing by as his teaching assistant who opened the package, 
and was not, in fact, injured.  More significantly, Mad Genius casts a 
healthy dose of skepticism on a report by a man in Salt Lake City that 
he stayed at the same hotel as Kaczynski in 1978.  The fellow, now a 
karate instructor, is still waiting to keep the pompous bomber in a dark 
alley.  And to the author's credit, they raise a collective eyebrow at 
the report by the owner of the Sacramento hotel who, they note, "was 
less sure of himself when talking to investigators." 

Unabomber, however, is not without its advantages.  Not only are any 
errors of minor significance in the overall story, but the chronology 
and letters section (both of which bear an uncanny resemblance to the 
sections on a certain webpage),  serve as very useful guides in 
understanding the facts of the matter.  Moreover, Unabomber but not Mad 
Genius  includes the recent description by Professor Saari concerning 
his recollection that he had met Kaczynski, and that Kaczynski had vowed 
to get even after being treated rudely by engineering professors to whom 
Saari had referred him.  Finally, Unabomber, can easily lay claim to the 
best line: "Throughout the 1967 Summer of Love, Ted Kaczynski didn't 
have a single date."

Unabomber ends with a plea in favor of the significance of the type of 
psychological profiling done by the principal author.  One question, 
however, arises that has never been addressed by the authors or the 
press:  each week the public views the homicides presented in shows like  
NYPD Blue and Homicide.  Was the $50 million plus spent on this case 
worth it?  He hadn't made an attempt on an airline in nearly 15 years.  
It is not uncommon for several people to  die  on a given night in 
certain parts of our major urban centers.  Why, again, should we care 
about this particular murderer?

Any provable mistakes -- and there are factual inaccuracies in both 
books -- are truly minor given the wealth of detail that was summarized 
in such a short period.   On the most important issue of whether the 
manuscript was found, we can only wait to see if the leaks prove true.   

The conflicting accounts provided by these two books of the alleged 
discovery  demonstrate that such confidence may rest on a shaky 
foundation.  Mad Genius describes it as a carbon copy while Unabomber 
describes it as a "master" copy from which the Post and Time copies were 
typed.   A third view -- offered by a number of California papers -- is 
that the document appears to be an early draft -- and that it is neither 
a carbon copy or a master draft.  Four other copies were mailed, and so 
it seems unlikely to have been a carbon copy.  And the draft sent to the 
Post and NY Times  apparently was identical even in its typographical 
mistakes, and so it seems unlikely to have been a "master" copy from 
which the others were typed.  The intriguing question, then, if the 
books and the press reports are wrong on this  point, might they be 
wrong altogether?  Might the draft have merely been a writing with an 
anti-technological theme?  Might the report in both books that a carbon 
copy of the letter to the New York Times was found also be mistaken?  
Finally, might the dramatic report of a handwritten "hit list" -- 
airline industry", "computer industry" and "genetecists" -- recounted 
only in Mad Genius be mistaken?  None of these critical pieces of 
evidence were detailed on the inventory of items taken from the cabin, 
even though it is quite detailed in other respects.

We will have to wait and see whether the evidence leaked by "sources 
close to the investigation"  bears up to scrutiny.  In the meantime, 
those interested in the UNABOM matter should go out and buy one or other 
of the books, and then be sure not to serve on the jury in any 
prosecution.

by the need for power, and the

   the permission of the author. It may be reproduced in any form
   provided that no money is being charged.
   
Index

   1. What is the purpose of this newsgroup?
   
   2. What does FC stand for?
   
   3. You are a strong supporter of FC. Are you a fed?
   
   4. If you are so against technology then why do you use the Internet?
   
   5. You seem to like nature, protecting the environment, and supporting
   free speech while disliking pollution, domination of society by
   business interests, and conformity to arbitrary societal values. Are
   the fans and supporters of FC really leftists?
   
   6. You seem to like rationality, fairly obtained success, and fighting
   for justice while disliking weakness, inferiority, and collectivism.
   Are the fans and supporters of FC really conservatives?
   
   7. If you're not left-wing or right-wing then what is your political
   position? Don't you have to be one or the other?
   
   8. Dr. Ted Kaczynski wasn't a productive citizen of society. So why
   listen to him?
   
   9. What is the connection between FC and environmental groups like
   Earth First?
   
   10. Where can I find the Manifesto?
   
   11. Don't you think FC should be ignored for resorting to violence to
   make themselves heard?
   
   12. What do you revolutionaries plan to do exactly?
   
   Online Resources

---BEGIN FAQ---

  1. What is the purpose of this newsgroup?
   
   The newsgroup alt.fan.unabomber exists for "fans of the mystical and
   awe-inspiring UNABOMBER" to discuss matters related to topics
   mentioned in its charter, including FC, their Manifesto, and
   revolution.
   
   This newsgroup name reflects the media mangling of a single FBI
   suspect who has eluded them for over 17 years and is possibly a member
   of the revolutionary group FC, which has an unknown number of members.
   The FBI suspect known as UNABOM was dubbed "The Unabomber" by the
   media because the media can sell more advertising for their newspapers
   and television programs when they inflate a story, introduce fictional
   elements, and provide a oversimplified one-dimensional perspective
   that misses the meaning of the event entirely. Since they are
   interested in providing entertainment for ratings and care little
   about provoking thought or seeking truth, the media will do everything
   possible to increase their ratings and persuade audiences to depend on
   their viewpoints.
   
   For the remainder of this FAQ, we will refer to "The Unabomber" as FC,
   for the group that he belongs to. This group authored the Manifesto
   entitled Industrial_Society_and_its_Future that will be referred to
   throughout this FAQ. While the suspect is unknown, the group has
   claimed responsibility for the actions that the FBI has attributed to
   this single individual.
   
   This group does not exist to:
   
       a) Condemn the actions of FC because of their supposed lack of
       contributions to society. Their Manifesto is a work of sheer
       genius that may prove to be the force that will save humanity from
       its devolution.
       
       b) Condemn the actions of FC because they did not conform to the
       arbitrary values of a passive society.
       
       c) Spread media propaganda about "Unabomber suspects," though the
       method of propaganda used by the media can be discussed and
       exposed.
  

  2. What does FC stand for?
  
   FBI officials for a long while suspected that the initials FC that
   were carved on FC's bombs stood for "Fuck Computers" but this is
   incorrect. The FBI later realized that FC has explained that the
   initials stood for "Freedom Club" in one of many letters that they had
   sent.
   
   It is unknown how many people are members of FC, but some have
   suggested that thousands of people individually share the basic ideas
   expressed in the Manifesto and are working towards similar goals. Some
   people have suggested that revolutionaries working toward the same
   goals as FC should consider themselves part of the organization.
   
   
  3. You are a strong supporter of FC. Are you a fed?
   
   I am not a fed. I am an interested ex-scholar who believes in the
   right to free speech, and in exercising my constitutional right I
   often side with the ideas of FC and defend FC against foolish
   criticisms. However, the threat of feds tying to entrap people is very
   real, so I suggest several guidelines for the safety of FC fans,
   members, and others who are disgusted by recent social trends and wish
   to spread new, more intelligent values. This information is intended
   mostly for audiences in the United States because so far there has
   been less interest in FC and their Manifesto from other areas of the
   world.
   
       a) Do not openly organize revolutionary efforts on the Internet. All
       Internet traffic is monitored at the major hubs by the government
       (mae-east, mae-west, fixed-east, and fixed-west have been
       confirmed as fully monitored and logged and newer net hubs are
       likely the same way. Assume that all email is intercepted and
       logged forever.
       
       b) Public posts are also logged, and not only by the government
       (search for your name on USENET archives kept at
       http://www.dejanews.com and http://altavista.digital.com if
       you've posted articles previously). If a current or potential
       employer runs your name through one of these services and doesn't
       like your opinions, you might run into problems.
       
       c) PGP is ok for exchanging basic information, but the computing
       power of the future will allow brute force attacks in a decade or
       two. If you use it, assume that your message will be read by
       others at some point in the future. Also make sure to use a
       2048-bit key or larger if you have a hacked version of the PGP
       software.
       
       d) To further the revolution, it is best that you work alone or
       with people that you have known a long time and can trust with
       your life. Do not work with someone you found on the Internet
       because they could be feds trying to entrap you, no matter how
       much you think you could trust them. Even exchanging ideas with
       another person could lead to implicating you in crimes that you
       are innocent of, so be careful even when discussing ideas with
       others.
       
       e) "Anonymous" remailers aren't necessarily anonymous and can't
       always be trusted. Since the feds can monitor all major network
       connections, they can see when you use a service like the one at
       anon.penet.fi because your message goes through at least one of
       their hubs on its way to Finland and it is trivial for them to see
       your message with full headers before it reached the anonymous
       service. Better methods are one-way chains of remailers if you
       want to post to USENET or send a fellow revolutionary advice.
       
   For more information on anonymity and cryptography you can read the
   Cypherpunks page at
   
   http://nic.funet.fi/pub/unix/security/crypt/cypherpunks/Home.html
   
   You may also want to read newsgroups such as alt.privacy,
   alt.privacy.anon-server, alt.privacy.clipper, and
   comp.society.privacy.
   
   If you are comfortable with the feds monitoring you and feel that this
   cause is important enough that you should participate in the
   discussion, then it is ok to use your name, but be warned of the
   possible dangers. Just be sure to refrain from offering information
   which is too specific or could implicate you in anything.
   
   
  4. If you are so against technology then why do you use the Internet?
   
   This question appears almost every week and seems to come only from
   people who have not read the Manifesto and understand it only
   superficially from what the media has told them about it. The short
   answer is that we are using the Internet to communicate with other
   revolutionaries and to spread the message of FC to others who are
   disenfranchised with the strangle hold of the system. We agree that
   technology is powerful, especially methods of communication, and we
   are using these powerful technologies solely as weapons to weaken and
   ultimately destroy the system.
   
   As FC wrote in the Manifesto:
   
   202. It would be hopeless for revolutionaries to try to attack the
       system without using SOME modern technology. If nothing else they
       must use the communications media to spread their message. But
       they should use modern technology for ONE purpose: to attack the
       technological system.
       
   
  5. You seem to like nature, protecting the environment, and supporting free
  speech while disliking pollution, domination of society by business
  interests, and conformity to arbitrary societal values. Are the fans and
  supporters of FC really leftists?
   
   Fans and supporters of FC rarely identify with one of the two
   mainstream parties. Most of us dislike the leftists and see them as
   harmful for many reasons, including their "feelings of inferiority"
   and "oversocialization." Paragraphs 6 - 32 and 213 - 230 discuss FC's
   position on this in detail.
   
   "Political correctness" has been a disaster for society because it has
   eliminated certain ideas from being acceptable for discussion. The
   left has decided that it didn't want people to think and communicate
   about things it doesn't like and declared that these ideas were
   improper. The left is only for free speech when it is not dominant and
   is rapidly fascist when it is dominant. This alone makes the leftist
   movement unacceptable to anyone who supports freedom.
   
   The leftist of old had several appealing ideas when they were not
   dominant, but they turned out to be worse than their opponents when
   they gain power.
   
   It is safe to assume that the vast majority of FC fans and supporters
   are not leftists.
   
   
  6. You seem to like rationality, fairly obtained success, and fighting for
  justice while disliking weakness, inferiority, and collectivism. Are the fans
  and supporters of FC really conservatives?
   
   Fans and supporters of FC rarely identify with one of the two
   mainstream parties. Most of us dislike modern conservatives and see
   them as harmful for many reasons, including their forced submission of
   individual rights to business rights, blind support of "progress" and
   the technoindustrial system, and dogma towards old, antiquated methods
   for dealing with new problems they have inflicted on society. While
   these topics are addressed throughout the Manifesto, there is a
   paragraph directed at the conservatives.
   
   50. The conservatives are fools: They whine about the decay of
       traditional values, yet they enthusiastically support
       technological progress and economic growth. Apparently it never
       occurs to them that you can't make rapid, drastic changes in the
       technology and the economy of a society without causing rapid
       changes in all other aspects of the society as well, and that such
       rapid changes inevitably break down traditional values.
       
   We note that conservatism used to mean individual freedom and limited
   government control over people's lives. While modern conservatism in
   the United States includes a good deal of government control over
   freedoms, including the prohibition of "consensual crimes" and forced
   acceptance of governmental morals (both of which are largely based on
   Christian roots), it also creates an environment where business
   dictates how government is run. This means that the proletariat are
   merely cogs in the machine who can have their freedoms removed if it
   would serve business better. For example, look at the hysteria of the
   drug war. While educated people understand the parallels with the
   first Prohibition (when was the last time you heard of someone killed
   over alcohol - when it was illegal) and that most drug users keep to
   themselves, the great fear from business is that people will use drugs
   and will lose interest in their mindless jobs and not be as productive
   as possible.
   
   Conservatives claim to be for less government control and less
   interference with people's private affairs but these claims are only
   true as long as people are doing things that are in accordance with
   the conservative's values. As soon as people start wanting these
   freedoms for their individual rights instead of as business rights (or
   as human machines for business), they find that this great
   conservative promise of freedom does not apply to them.
   
   It is safe to assume that the vast majority of FC fans and supporters
   are not conservatives.
   
   
  7. If you're not left-wing or right-wing then what is your political
  position? Don't you have to be one or the other?
   
   Most of the fans of FC don't buy the idea of a two-party dictatorship
   wherein all citizens are supposed to believe in the ideas of one of
   the two parties. We find this concept to be far too limiting. We also
   find both parties to be in error in most of their decisions. However,
   the political process of appealing to herd values is largely to blame
   for this. Politicians are generally not interested in addressing
   legitimate problems and prefer instead to do whatever will gain them
   the most public support. There are few politicians who have genuine
   concern over the problems they face and for that reason and their
   general ineptness and stupidity, we oppose the two-party system they
   have created.
   
   Some supporters of FC are libertarians, though because of their pledge
   to never impose force on other people, they oppose FC's occasionally
   violent methods. Apparently is never occurs to them that revolution is
   often accompanied by violence because the oppressors who are the root
   causes of social stresses will not relinquish their positions of power
   without being violently overthrown by the proletariat. But because
   these people are interested in similar reforms to gain autonomy we
   gladly work with them, though some of the supporters of FC are not at
   all interested in political positions beyond reducing the amount of
   government control in our lives.
   
   Some supporters of FC are members of the Green party, which is most
   active in environmental issues. While the danger of dealing with
   leftist is possible, the benefit of being involved with this sort of
   party is that you can meet many enlightened individuals who are
   interested in achieving the same goals. The position on technology
   also varies with some believing that technology is the only way to fix
   the damage inflicted by the technoindustrial system and others
   thinking that widespread support for Green issues will allow nature to
   heal itself.
   
   
  8. Dr. Ted Kaczynski wasn't a productive citizen of society. So why listen to
  him?
  
   [Dr. Kaczynski is the latest FBI suspect in the "Unabomber crimes" but
   this in no way means that he was the Unabomber, a member of FC, or the
   author of the Manifesto.]
   
   This question most frequently is asked by people who have been
   oversocialized and believe that everyone must serve society in some
   way. These people believe that everyone should perform their 40-hour
   work weeks involved in a surrogate activity so that workers can earn
   money to provide for their nuclear family while making the company
   owner more wealthy in the process. People who make this argument do
   not seem to have great tolerance for others who aren't eager to
   conform to this model of societal behavior.
   
   The most obvious response is that there is no law that someone must be
   a "productive" citizen and spend the majority of their waking hours
   working. Wouldn't it make more sense to do what you wanted to do all
   day instead of what your boss wanted? The relevance of Dr. Kaczynski
   to this discussion is that he was a hermit who lived on very little
   money and spent his time expanding his intellect instead of doing
   pointless work for a company. This was his choice for a lifestyle,
   which he adopted after resigning from being a Berkeley professor.
   Since there is no reason to expect others to work for your society,
   there is no basis for disliking someone for their lack of contribution
   to it in the manner that you would prefer.
   
   Historically, many authors and artists have dropped out from the
   working world so they can dedicate themselves to developing their
   skills and producing work which often pays little or nothing and is
   not recognized as genius until after their deaths. People today who
   have great spirits often find themselves beaten down by the stress of
   modern work environments and society and are forced to make a
   difficult decision between letting their natural abilities fade or
   quitting their jobs to tap the energies and talents of their
   abilities.
   
   If Dr. Kaczynski is the author of the Manifesto, it could be said that
   he was much more productive than most citizens because of his ability
   to start a dialog about important topics and inspire revolutionaries
   to wage war against a broken system that is held together with
   delusions and empty promises. If he is the author, then we owe him a
   great deal of gratitude and respect for his work.
   
   
  9. What is the connection between FC and environmental groups like Earth
  First?
   
   While FC has strong environmental concerns, they have no link to
   groups like Earth First. While many fans and supporters of FC support
   the efforts of environmental groups such as Earth First, these groups
   are largely composed of leftist collectivists and are opposed for this
   reason.
   
   214. [...] A movement that exalts nature and opposes technology must
       take a resolutely anti-leftist stance and must avoid all
       collaborations with leftists. Leftism is in the long run
       inconsistent with wild nature, with human freedom and with the
       elimination of modern technology. Leftism is collectivist: it
       seeks to bind together the entire world (both nature and the human
       race) into a unified whole. But this implies management of nature
       and of human life by organized society, and it requires advanced
       technology. You can't have a united world without rapid
       transportation and communication, you can't make all people love
       one another without sophisticated psychological techniques, you
       can't have a "planned society" without the necessary technological
       base. Above all, leftism is drive by the need for power, and the
       leftist seeks power on a collective basis, through identification
       with a mass movement or an organization. Leftism is unlikely to
       ever give up technology, because technology is too valuable a
       source of collective power.
   
   For this reason, Earth First is an organization to avoid though on the
   surface it appears to share a few positions with FC.
   
   
  10. Where can I find the Manifesto?
  
   The Manifesto is online in several locations, including the UNAPACK
   page at http://www.paranoia.com/unapack/
   
   Serious fans may want to purchase a softcover version of the Manifesto
   from Jolly Roger Press, a Berkeley publisher. This is available at
   Tower Records or directly from the publisher.
   
   Jolly Roger Press
   P.O. Box 295
   Berkeley, CA 94701
   
   
  11. Don't you think FC should be ignored for resorting to violence to make
  themselves heard?
  
   The answer to this question requires the discussion of several related
   topics. For the first section we will quote FC from the Manifesto.
   
   96. [...] Anyone who has a little money can have something printed, or
       can distribute it on the Internet or in some such way, but what he
       has to say will be swamped by the vast volume of material put out
       by the media, hence it will have no practical effect. To make an
       impression on society with words is therefore almost impossible
       for most individuals and small groups. Take us (FC) for example.
       If we had never done anything violent and had submitted the
       present writings to a publisher, they probably would not have been
       accepted. If they had been accepted and published, they probably
       would not have attracted many readers, because it's more fun to
       watch the entertainment put out by the media than to read a sober
       essay. Even if these writings had had many readers, most of these
       readers would soon have forgotten what they had read as their
       minds were flooded by the mass of material to which the media
       expose them. In order to get our message before the public with
       some chance of making a lasting impression, we've had to kill
       people.
       
   Some oversocialized people will say that violence is wrong and that
   using freedom of speech is the best way to change problems in our
   society. However, this is flawed because few people today are willing
   to listen to intelligent, reasoned conversation and either hold
   tightly to their own preconceived notions about the way society should
   function and what individual rights are deserved. Others are
   uninterested in discussion of a rational nature because thinking is
   either difficult for them or causes boredom because of withdrawal from
   the entertainment media stimulus they are accustomed to. While people
   can certainly freely discuss their views, others rarely listen or
   respond to them, so freedom of speech is often of no use. In the
   spirit of being "open-minded" others simply disregard opinions with
   which they do not already agree.
   
   Since authority has traditionally used violence to keep others down,
   it seems fair that violence can be used against them to gain back
   freedom and autonomy.
   
   FC's dedication to their beliefs is certainly admirable in a time when
   few people stand for anything consistently. This is especially true
   when our society is exerting continuous pressure to conform, be
   passive, and refrain from confronting threats to one's lifestyle or
   freedom. While we are forced to walk the plank a step away from pure
   apathy, groups like FC who stand up for freedom are should be
   supported. FC's reasoning can be summarized in the following
   approximation: actions produce change, talk produces no change.
  

  12. What do you revolutionaries plan to do exactly?
  
   Most of us who are committed to changing the harm we see in society
   are not going to disclose our plans, but our intentions are fairly
   obvious. You might read about our work in newspapers and maybe your
   grandchildren will read about them in history books, but you'll
   probably see little offered in the newsgroup about our plans because
   that would be harmful to the revolution. A basic overview of some
   methods we will use is available in paragraphs 180 - 206.
   
     _________________________________________________________________
   
Online Resources

   UNAPACK
   http://www.paranoia.com/unapack/
   
   The Definitive Unabomber Homepage
   http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom/
   
   Though the media supported propaganda would be ignored in a perfect
   world, we live among idiots and sheep. We have to inform them and
   correct the lies they so eagerly repeat. It is our duty to either shun
   these people completely and let them die out from the consequences of
   their delusion or to correct the stupidities they accept as truth. For
   this reason media sites are included:
   
   Time Warner
   http://www.pathfinder.com
   
   CNN
   http://www.cnn.com/

>some would argue that technology is what destabilizes society,

>technology and the economy of a society without causing rapid changes
>in all other aspects of the society as well, and that such rapid

>

You make an excellent point and one with much merrit. Let us assume that 
a society is very conservative in it's values and closed to new ideas. 
Perhaps it has a political power structure similar to the War Lords of 
Japan. Would not such a society be more fragile and susceptible to 
destablizing factors than a pragmatic and dyamic society that is vibrant 
and open to opportunity? I offer Japan in the early 1900's as only one 
example. Perhaps you can think of others, more recent or current. 

One might be led to determine that societies, not unlike people cannot be 
generalized when considering the effects of drastic change. I would offer 
that it is not so much technology which alters society, but technologies 
effect on the quality of life of a society. To the extent that technology 
alters nature, one might contend that it alters society. To the extent 
that it destroys nature, it destroys the quality of life for all mankind. 
To the extent that it enhances nature, it enhances the quality of life of 
all mankind.

   It is unknown how many people are members of FC, but some have
   suggested that thousands of people individually share the basic ideas
   expressed in the Manifesto and are working towards similar goals. Some
   people have suggested that revolutionaries working toward the same
   goals as FC should consider themselves part of the organization.
   
   
  3. You are a strong supporter of FC. Are you a fed?
   
   I am not a fed. I am an interested ex-scholar who believes in the
   right to free speech, and in exercising my constitutional right I
   often side with the ideas of FC and defend FC against foolish
   criticisms. However, the threat of feds tying to entrap people is very
   real, so I suggest several guidelines for the safety of FC fans,
   members, and others who are disgusted by recent social trends and wish
   to spread new, more intelligent values. This information is intended
   mostly for audiences in the United States because so far there has
   been less interest in FC and their Manifesto from other areas of the
   world.
   
       a) Do not openly organize revolutionary efforts on the Internet. All
       Internet traffic is monitored at the major hubs by the government
       (mae-east, mae-west, fixed-east, and fixed-west have been
       confirmed as fully monitored and logged and newer net hubs are
       likely the same way. Assume that all email is intercepted and
       logged forever.
       
       b) Public posts are also logged, and not only by the government
       (search for your name on USENET archives kept at
       http://www.dejanews.com and http://altavista.digital.com if
       you've posted articles previously). If a current or potential
       employer runs your name through one of these services and doesn't
       like your opinions, you might run into problems.
       
       c) PGP is ok for exchanging basic information, but the computing
       power of the future will allow brute force attacks in a decade or
       two. If you use it, assume that your message will be read by
       others at some point in the future. Also make sure to use a
       2048-bit key or larger if you have a hacked version of the PGP
       software.
       
       d) To further the revolution, it is best that you work alone or
       with people that you have known a long time and can trust with
       your life. Do not work with someone you found on the Internet
       because they could be feds trying to entrap you, no matter how
       much you think you could trust them. Even exchanging ideas with
       another person could lead to implicating you in crimes that you
       are innocent of, so be careful even when discussing ideas with
       others.
       
       e) "Anonymous" remailers aren't necessarily anonymous and can't
       always be trusted. Since the feds can monitor all major network
       connections, they can see when you use a service like the one at
       anon.penet.fi because your message goes through at least one of
       their hubs on its way to Finland and it is trivial for them to see
       your message with full headers before it reached the anonymous
       service. Better methods are one-way chains of remailers if you
       want to post to USENET or send a fellow revolutionary advice.
       
   For more information on anonymity and cryptography you can read the
   Cypherpunks page at
   
   http://nic.funet.fi/pub/unix/security/crypt/cypherpunks/Home.html
   
   You may also want to read newsgroups such as alt.privacy,
   alt.privacy.anon-server, alt.privacy.clipper, and
   comp.society.privacy.
   
   If you are comfortable with the feds monitoring you and feel that this
   cause is important enough that you should participate in the
   discussion, then it is ok to use your name, but be warned of the
   possible dangers. Just be sure to refrain from offering information
   which is too specific or could implicate you in anything.
   
   
  4. If you are so against technology then why do you use the Internet?
   
   This question appears almost every week and seems to come only from
   people who have not read the Manifesto and understand it only
   superficially from what the media has told them about it. The short
   answer is that we are using the Internet to communicate with other
   revolutionaries and to spread the message of FC to others who are
   disenfranchised with the strangle hold of the system. We agree that
   technology is powerful, especially methods of communication, and we
   are using these powerful technologies solely as weapons to weaken and
   ultimately destroy the system.
   
   As FC wrote in the Manifesto:
   
   202. It would be hopeless for revolutionaries to try to attack the
       system without using SOME modern technology. If nothing else they
       must use the communications media to spread their message. But
       they should use modern technology for ONE purpose: to attack the
       technological system.
       
   
  5. You seem to like nature, protecting the environment, and supporting free
  speech while disliking pollution, domination of society by business
  interests, and conformity to arbitrary societal values. Are the fans and
  supporters of FC really leftists?
   
   Fans and supporters of FC rarely identify with one of the two
   mainstream parties. Most of us dislike the leftists and see them as
   harmful for many reasons, including their "feelings of inferiority"
   and "oversocialization." Paragraphs 6 - 32 and 213 - 230 discuss FC's
   position on this in detail.
   
   "Political correctness" has been a disaster for society because it has
   eliminated certain ideas from being acceptable for discussion. The
   left has decided that it didn't want people to think and communicate
   about things it doesn't like and declared that these ideas were
   improper. The left is only for free speech when it is not dominant and
   is rapidly fascist when it is dominant. This alone makes the leftist
   movement unacceptable to anyone who supports freedom.
   
   The leftist of old had several appealing ideas when they were not
   dominant, but they turned out to be worse than their opponents when
   they gain power.
   
   It is safe to assume that the vast majority of FC fans and supporters
   are not leftists.
   
   
  6. You seem to like rationality, fairly obtained success, and fighting for
  justice while disliking weakness, inferiority, and collectivism. Are the fans
  and supporters of FC really conservatives?
   
   Fans and supporters of FC rarely identify with one of the two
   mainstream parties. Most of us dislike modern conservatives and see
   them as harmful for many reasons, including their forced submission of
   individual rights to business rights, blind support of "progress" and
   the technoindustrial system, and dogma towards old, antiquated methods
   for dealing with new problems they have inflicted on society. While
   these topics are addressed throughout the Manifesto, there is a
   paragraph directed at the conservatives.
   
   50. The conservatives are fools: They whine about the decay of
       traditional values, yet they enthusiastically support
       technological progress and economic growth. Apparently it never
       occurs to them that you can't make rapid, drastic changes in the
       technology and the economy of a society without causing rapid
       changes in all other aspects of the society as well, and that such
       rapid changes inevitably break down traditional values.
       
   We note that conservatism used to mean individual freedom and limited
   government control over people's lives. While modern conservatism in
   the United States includes a good deal of government control over
   freedoms, including the prohibition of "consensual crimes" and forced
   acceptance of governmental morals (both of which are largely based on
   Christian roots), it also creates an environment where business
   dictates how government is run. This means that the proletariat are
   merely cogs in the machine who can have their freedoms removed if it
   would serve business better. For example, look at the hysteria of the
   drug war. While educated people understand the parallels with the
   first Prohibition (when was the last time you heard of someone killed
   over alcohol - when it was illegal) and that most drug users keep to
   themselves, the great fear from business is that people will use drugs
   and will lose interest in their mindless jobs and not be as productive
   as possible.
   
   Conservatives claim to be for less government control and less
   interference with people's private affairs but these claims are only
   true as long as people are doing things that are in accordance with
   the conservative's values. As soon as people start wanting these
   freedoms for their individual rights instead of as business rights (or
   as human machines for business), they find that this great
   conservative promise of freedom does not apply to them.
   
   It is safe to assume that the vast majority of FC fans and supporters
   are not conservatives.
   
   
  7. If you're not left-wing or right-wing then what is your political
  position? Don't you have to be one or the other?
   
   Most of the fans of FC don't buy the idea of a two-party dictatorship
   wherein all citizens are supposed to believe in the ideas of one of
   the two parties. We find this concept to be far too limiting. We also
   find both parties to be in error in most of their decisions. However,
   the political process of appealing to herd values is largely to blame
   for this. Politicians are generally not interested in addressing
   legitimate problems and prefer instead to do whatever will gain them
   the most public support. There are few politicians who have genuine
   concern over the problems they face and for that reason and their
   general ineptness and stupidity, we oppose the two-party system they
   have created.
   
   Some supporters of FC are libertarians, though because of their pledge
   to never impose force on other people, they oppose FC's occasionally
   violent methods. Apparently is never occurs to them that revolution is
   often accompanied by violence because the oppressors who are the root
   causes of social stresses will not relinquish their positions of power
   without being violently overthrown by the proletariat. But because
   these people are interested in similar reforms to gain autonomy we
   gladly work with them, though some of the supporters of FC are not at
   all interested in political positions beyond reducing the amount of
   government control in our lives.
   
   Some supporters of FC are members of the Green party, which is most
   active in environmental issues. While the danger of dealing with
   leftist is possible, the benefit of being involved with this sort of
   party is that you can meet many enlightened individuals who are
   interested in achieving the same goals. The position on technology
   also varies with some believing that technology is the only way to fix
   the damage inflicted by the technoindustrial system and others
   thinking that widespread support for Green issues will allow nature to
   heal itself.
   
   
  8. Dr. Ted Kaczynski wasn't a productive citizen of society. So why listen to
  him?
  
   [Dr. Kaczynski is the latest FBI suspect in the "Unabomber crimes" but
   this in no way means that he was the Unabomber, a member of FC, or the
   author of the Manifesto.]
   
   This question most frequently is asked by people who have been
   oversocialized and believe that everyone must serve society in some
   way. These people believe that everyone should perform their 40-hour
   work weeks involved in a surrogate activity so that workers can earn
   money to provide for their nuclear family while making the company
   owner more wealthy in the process. People who make this argument do
   not seem to have great tolerance for others who aren't eager to
   conform to this model of societal behavior.
   
   The most obvious response is that there is no law that someone must be
   a "productive" citizen and spend the majority of their waking hours
   working. Wouldn't it make more sense to do what you wanted to do all
   day instead of what your boss wanted? The relevance of Dr. Kaczynski
   to this discussion is that he was a hermit who lived on very little
   money and spent his time expanding his intellect instead of doing
   pointless work for a company. This was his choice for a lifestyle,
   which he adopted after resigning from being a Berkeley professor.
   Since there is no reason to expect others to work for your society,
   there is no basis for disliking someone for their lack of contribution
   to it in the manner that you would prefer.
   
   Historically, many authors and artists have dropped out from the
   working world so they can dedicate themselves to developing their
   skills and producing work which often pays little or nothing and is
   not recognized as genius until after their deaths. People today who
   have great spirits often find themselves beaten down by the stress of
   modern work environments and society and are forced to make a
   difficult decision between letting their natural abilities fade or
   quitting their jobs to tap the energies and talents of their
   abilities.
   
   If Dr. Kaczynski is the author of the Manifesto, it could be said that
   he was much more productive than most citizens because of his ability
   to start a dialog about important topics and inspire revolutionaries
   to wage war against a broken system that is held together with
   delusions and empty promises. If he is the author, then we owe him a
   great deal of gratitude and respect for his work.
   
   
  9. What is the connection between FC and environmental groups like Earth
  First?
   
   While FC has strong environmental concerns, they have no link to
   groups like Earth First. While many fans and supporters of FC support
   the efforts of environmental groups such as Earth First, these groups
   are largely composed of leftist collectivists and are opposed for this
   reason.
   
   214. [...] A movement that exalts nature and opposes technology must
       take a resolutely anti-leftist stance and must avoid all
       collaborations with leftists. Leftism is in the long run
       inconsistent with wild nature, with human freedom and with the
       elimination of modern technology. Leftism is collectivist: it
       seeks to bind together the entire world (both nature and the human
       race) into a unified whole. But this implies management of nature
       and of human life by organized society, and it requires advanced
       technology. You can't have a united world without rapid
       transportation and communication, you can't make all people love
       one another without sophisticated psychological techniques, you
       can't have a "planned society" without the necessary technological
       base. Above all, leftism is drive by the need for power, and the
       leftist seeks power on a collective basis, through identification
       with a mass movement or an organization. Leftism is unlikely to
       ever give up technology, because technology is too valuable a
       source of collective power.
   
   For this reason, Earth First is an organization to avoid though on the
   surface it appears to share a few positions with FC.
   
   
  10. Where can I find the Manifesto?
  
   The Manifesto is online in several locations, including the UNAPACK
   page at http://www.paranoia.com/unapack/
   
   Serious fans may want to purchase a softcover version of the Manifesto
   from Jolly Roger Press, a Berkeley publisher. This is available at
   Tower Records or directly from the publisher.
   
   Jolly Roger Press
   P.O. Box 295
   Berkeley, CA 94701
   
   
  11. Don't you think FC should be ignored for resorting to violence to make
  themselves heard?
  
   The answer to this question requires the discussion of several related
   topics. For the first section we will quote FC from the Manifesto.
   
   96. [...] Anyone who has a little money can have something printed, or
       can distribute it on the Internet or in some such way, but what he
       has to say will be swamped by the vast volume of material put out
       by the media, hence it will have no practical effect. To make an
       impression on society with words is therefore almost impossible
       for most individuals and small groups. Take us (FC) for example.
       If we had never done anything violent and had submitted the
       present writings to a publisher, they probably would not have been
       accepted. If they had been accepted and published, they probably
       would not have attracted many readers, because it's more fun to
       watch the entertainment put out by the media than to read a sober
       essay. Even if these writings had had many readers, most of these
       readers would soon have forgotten what they had read as their
       minds were flooded by the mass of material to which the media
       expose them. In order to get our message before the public with
       some chance of making a lasting impression, we've had to kill
       people.
       
   Some oversocialized people will say that violence is wrong and that
   using freedom of speech is the best way to change problems in our
   society. However, this is flawed because few people today are willing
   to listen to intelligent, reasoned conversation and either hold
   tightly to their own preconceived notions about the way society should
   function and what individual rights are deserved. Others are
   uninterested in discussion of a rational nature because thinking is
   either difficult for them or causes boredom because of withdrawal from
   the entertainment media stimulus they are accustomed to. While people
   can certainly freely discuss their views, others rarely listen or
   respond to them, so freedom of speech is often of no use. In the
   spirit of being "open-minded" others simply disregard opinions with
   which they do not already agree.
   
   Since authority has traditionally used violence to keep others down,
   it seems fair that violence can be used against them to gain back
   freedom and autonomy.
   
   FC's dedication to their beliefs is certainly admirable in a time when
   few people stand for anything consistently. This is especially true
   when our society is exerting continuous pressure to conform, be
   passive, and refrain from confronting threats to one's lifestyle or
   freedom. While we are forced to walk the plank a step away from pure
   apathy, groups like FC who stand up for freedom are should be
   supported. FC's reasoning can be summarized in the following
   approximation: actions produce change, talk produces no change.
  

  12. What do you revolutionaries plan to do exactly?
  
   Most of us who are committed to changing the harm we see in society
   are not going to disclose our plans, but our intentions are fairly
   obvious. You might read about our work in newspapers and maybe your
   grandchildren will read about them in history books, but you'll
   probably see little offered in the newsgroup about our plans because
   that would be harmful to the revolution. A basic overview of some
   methods we will use is available in paragraphs 180 - 206.
   
     _________________________________________________________________
   
Online Resources

   UNAPACK
   http://www.paranoia.com/unapack/
   
   The Definitive Unabomber Homepage
   http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom/
   
   Though the media supported propaganda would be ignored in a perfect
   world, we live among idiots and sheep. We have to inform them and
   correct the lies they so eagerly repeat. It is our duty to either shun
   these people completely and let them die out from the consequences of
   their delusion or to correct the stupidities they accept as truth. For
   this reason media sites are included:
   
   Time Warner
   http://www.pathfinder.com
   
   CNN
   http://www.cnn.com/

   ---END OF FAQ---

	Extracts from 13 may 1996 edition of 'The New Yorker'

	Article: 'A reporter at large: The Unlamented West'
	     by: Jonathan Raban

	Subject:  Historical, sociological, geographical pastiche
		  of Montana.

	Extracts: Where Ted Kaczynski gets a mention.

	Comment: This whole article is well worth reading. I suggest
		 that you try and obtain a copy of the magazine.


	p.76


	The town of Lincoln, the capital of this happy valley was a mile-long avenue of motels ("Hunters Welcome!"), R.V. courts, bars, eateries, craft-shops, and sporting goods stores. My attention must have been failing, for I did not notice an unkempt bearded man, just three weeks older than I am, pedalling away from the Lincoln Community Library with a sackful of books on sociology and Chinese philosophy. I would like to have spotted Theodore Kaczynski, the Unabomber suspect, a full five months before his arrest by the F.B.I., but, as I later found, it would have been nearly impossible to single him out from all
the other bearded loners on bicycles, with self-inflicted haircuts, who are part of the Lincoln landscape.
p.. 79
Shortly after Ted Kaczynski was seized at his cabin, on the afternoon of April 3rd this year, I drove back to Lincoln, to find out why this taciturn refugee from big-city life in Salt Lake, Berkeley, Ann Arbor, Cambridge, and Chicago had chosen the high valley as his sanctuary from the urban industrial world. Newspaper reports had described Lincoln as the heart of the
heart of the backwoods - which didn't chime with any my fleeting memory. Journalists from the world's press were still quartered in the town's half-dozen lodgings, so I packed my fly rod and went to Lincoln as an uncredentialled fisherman, scoping out the Blackfoot River.

I stayed at the Lincoln Lodge Hotel, a fine log pile, built as a dude ranch in the 1920's, when Lincoln was beginning to make 	itself known as a hunting-and-fishing resort. It was now owned 	by Diana Holliday and a partner. Diana turned out to be far from Ismay and we traded gossip from the far east of the state. She'd never gone back to the homestead on which she grew up. Her memories of Ismay were penury, dust, and bitter cold. She had
	longed to escape to a greener world. She'd lived in Great Falls "and that was so green to me - after Ismay," she said. Last  summer, she and a partner had bought the old hotel in Lincoln, and they were in love with the town - its wateriness, its woods, 
its air of unpretentious prosperity.

"When I heard on the TV that they'd caught the Unabomber in a 'remote' part of Montana, I thought they must mean some place like Jordan. I couldn't believe it when they said Lincoln. This isn't 'remote'!"

"To a reporter from New York, I suppose, Lincoln might look like the wilderness. Maybe that's how it looked to Ted Kaczynski, too."

I took an evening stroll through town. Novelty windmills creaked in front yards. Antique wagon wheels were propped against the walls of houses. Most of the year-rounders had some cottage-industry to support them; they were taxidermists, 	woodcarvers, flytiers, or the makers of wooden painted butterflies. I peered through the window of the Lost Woodsman
Gallery - Sculptures by Rowley. His rough-cut bears, Indians, and frontiersman, hewn from pine logs, were masterpieces of Easter Island kitsch . The ornamental wagon wheels came, Iguessed, from Roly-Poly Land Antiques.

Deer wandered from cabin to cabin, scrounging for leftovers. People put out bowls of oats, and restaurants fed them on the wilted remains of their salad bars.

Kaczynski, mooning around Montana in '71, had lit on this idyllic family vacation spot with it's friendly animals and tinkling streams. To the Chicagoan, the docile student, raised on the highschool American classics, Lincoln must have looked like Thoreau's pond, Twain's river, and Cooper's forest conveniently rolled into one.

I sent myself to sleep reading the Unabomber's tangled thesis, "Industrial Society and Its Future." The author, who identified himself only as "FC",: was a very urban nature lover. "The
positive ideal that we propose is Nature," he wrote, but his idea of nature was infuriatingly hazy and sentimental. He doted	on the early settlers of the West for eating "wild meat" and
living in such isolation that "they belonged to no community at all." With characteristic bathos, he opined that "Nature makes a perfect counter-ideal to technology for several reasons" and 	that "most people will agree that nature is beautiful." The word "natural" cropped up in sentence after sentence as a synonym for "good."
p.80
In the dead center of the thesis - paragraph 115 out of two hundred and thirty two paragraphs - was a fragment of miserable autobiography, an unmistakable cry from the Unabombers heart.
     The system HAS TO force people to behave in ways that are increasingly remote from the natural pattern of human  mathematicians and engineers. It can't function without  them. So heavy pressure is put on children to excel in  these fields. It isn't natural for  adolescent human  being to spend the bulk of his time sitting at a desk  absorbed in study. A normal adolescent wants to spend his time in active contact with the real world. Among primitive peoples the things that children are trained to do tend to be in reasonable harmony with natural human impulses. Among the American Indians, for example, boys were trained in active outdoor pursuits - just the sort of things that boys like.
I never camped in the woods! I never went fishing! I never had an air-gun! They never let me be a boy!
Ted Kaczynski was nearing 30 when he arrived in Lincoln. Was it his lost boyhood of "active outdoor pursuits" that he found 	here?
The next morning, Bill Holliday, Diana's husband, said, "He
wasn't too different from a lot of folks round here. Vets
mostly. They make do without electricity. They hunt and fish -
live off the fat of the land. They keep themselves to
themselves."
"They ride bicycles?"
"A lot of people get around on bicycles,"Mrs. Holliday said."It's so flat." I went out to the river. The Blackfoot swirled greenly under the road bridge, but was too swollen with snowmelt to be fishable. As it was, I followed Stemple Pass Road over toward the Kaczynski place, with Humbug and Poorman Creeks chattering within earshot.  It was a pleasant 40 minute walk, past summer homes and pastureland, to the schoolbus stop beside Gehrig's Lumber, where the F.B.I. had pinned its search warrant to a post and officiously blocked the logging trail that led to Kaczynskis cabin. The cabin was just out of sight, but I could see the satellite dish of its immediate neighbour, like a creamy giant mushroom in an aspen glade.
It was woodsy, but it was not "the woods." When the spirit of Emersonian self-reliance failed him, Kaczynski could ride his bike to the Blackfoot market and pick up Del Monte food, whose cans meticulously labelled, figure prominently in the F.B.I. inventory. But this proximity to town must have had its disadvantages. Snowmobiling is Lincoln's economic mainstay in the winter months, and when Kaczynski was labouring on his life story (Item MB28 in the inventory is a "Brown Clasp Envelope Marked 'Autobiography'") he must have been plagued by the din of the rainbow striped machines whizzing past the cabin, for the
logging road, which takes a zigzag path through a shallow canyon, is perfect for snowmobilers. FC was similarly troubled. His thesis complains of "noise-making devices" intruding on his autonomy.
Yet here were deer, elk, bears, rabbits, and fish. The F.B.I. inventory, with its fishhooks, bows and arrows, and guns (one of them home made) alongside the chemistry set, the peanut butter jars, the hersheys cocoa cans, the raspberry Super Sip bottles, suggests the life not of a man but of a dangerous boy.
Item L9 interested me: "A Plastic Bottle Labelled 'Strychnine Oats.'" I mentioned it to Diana Holliday, "You feed oats to the deer, don't you?"
"Oh," she said, "that makes me really angry at him. he hated the deer, they used to eat his garden."
The positive ideal that we propose is Nature.
Lambkin's bar and Casino , at the center of Lincoln, was loud with talk, and welcoming.
"You're from Seattle?" the bartender said. "That's where all the serial murderers come from. Ted Bundy. The Green River Killer.... This guy is our first. We're kind of inexperienced."
She was down to her last 6 "Lincoln, Home of the Unabomber - The last best place to hide" Tshirts. The first edition had arrived at nine the previous evening; 15 hours later, I bought the last tshirt but one. A rush reorder had been sent out to the factory.
Profits on the tshirt sales were going to Lincoln's volunteer fire department, which had set its sights on a defibrillator. By Saturday morning, the defibrillator was in the bag and the volunteers were looking at the next item on the shopping list - compressor for filling air cylinders. After that, they needed new jackets.
"It's split this town right down the middle," according to Jay Verdi, a bearded firefighter who is also the fire departments PR man.  "Some folks are mad as hell at us for doing it."
I thought of the fire hall in Ismay, stacked from floor to ceiling with Joe, Montana, tshirts. Lincoln's sudden blaze of notoriety and fortune seemed more securely rooted.
"Did you pay any attention to Kaczynski before he became famous?" I asked Jay Verdi.
"I rode with him to Helena once. In 1978. I was buying a new Blazer. Sat with Ted on the stage."
"What did you talk about?"
"He said,'Hello.'"
"And that was all he said, all the way to Helena?"
"At the end, he said, 'I wont be riding back with you.' That was a long sentence for Ted."
As I was leaving, Verdi said, "The two guys who made the arrest - I heard that when they grabbed him, he didn't struggle, or anything like that. 'The wind just went right out of him. Total relief."

	Extracts from 13 may 1996 edition of 'The New Yorker'

	Article: 'A reporter at large: The Unlamented West'
	     by: Jonathan Raban

	Subject:  Historical, sociological, geographical pastiche
		  of Montana.

	Extracts: Where Ted Kaczynski gets a mention.

	Comment: This whole article is well worth reading. I suggest
		 that you try and obtain a copy of the magazine.


	p.76


	The town of Lincoln, the capital of this happy valley was a mile-long avenue of motels ("Hunters Welcome!"), R.V. courts, bars, eateries, craft-shops, and sporting goods stores. My attention must have been failing, for I did not notice an unkempt bearded man, just three weeks older than I am, pedalling away from the Lincoln Community Library with a sackful of books on sociology and Chinese philosophy. I would like to have spotted Theodore Kaczynski, the Unabomber suspect, a full five months before his arrest by the F.B.I., but, as I later found, it would have been nearly impossible to single him out from all
the other bearded loners on bicycles, with self-inflicted haircuts, who are part of the Lincoln landscape.
p.. 79
Shortly after Ted Kaczynski was seized at his cabin, on the afternoon of April 3rd this year, I drove back to Lincoln, to find out why this taciturn refugee from big-city life in Salt Lake, Berkeley, Ann Arbor, Cambridge, and Chicago had chosen the high valley as his sanctuary from the urban industrial world. Newspaper reports had described Lincoln as the heart of the
heart of the backwoods - which didn't chime with any my fleeting memory. Journalists from the world's press were still quartered in the town's half-dozen lodgings, so I packed my fly rod and went to Lincoln as an uncredentialled fisherman, scoping out the Blackfoot River.

I stayed at the Lincoln Lodge Hotel, a fine log pile, built as a dude ranch in the 1920's, when Lincoln was beginning to make 	itself known as a hunting-and-fishing resort. It was now owned 	by Diana Holliday and a partner. Diana turned out to be far from Ismay and we traded gossip from the far east of the state. She'd never gone back to the homestead on which she grew up. Her memories of Ismay were penury, dust, and bitter cold. She had
	longed to escape to a greener world. She'd lived in Great Falls "and that was so green to me - after Ismay," she said. Last  summer, she and a partner had bought the old hotel in Lincoln, and they were in love with the town - its wateriness, its woods, 
its air of unpretentious prosperity.

"When I heard on the TV that they'd caught the Unabomber in a 'remote' part of Montana, I thought they must mean some place like Jordan. I couldn't believe it when they said Lincoln. This isn't 'remote'!"

"To a reporter from New York, I suppose, Lincoln might look like the wilderness. Maybe that's how it looked to Ted Kaczynski, too."

I took an evening stroll through town. Novelty windmills creaked in front yards. Antique wagon wheels were propped against the walls of houses. Most of the year-rounders had some cottage-industry to support them; they were taxidermists, 	woodcarvers, flytiers, or the makers of wooden painted butterflies. I peered through the window of the Lost Woodsman
Gallery - Sculptures by Rowley. His rough-cut bears, Indians, and frontiersman, hewn from pine logs, were masterpieces of Easter Island kitsch . The ornamental wagon wheels came, Iguessed, from Roly-Poly Land Antiques.

Deer wandered from cabin to cabin, scrounging for leftovers. People put out bowls of oats, and restaurants fed them on the wilted remains of their salad bars.

Kaczynski, mooning around Montana in '71, had lit on this idyllic family vacation spot with it's friendly animals and tinkling streams. To the Chicagoan, the docile student, raised on the highschool American classics, Lincoln must have looked like Thoreau's pond, Twain's river, and Cooper's forest conveniently rolled into one.

I sent myself to sleep reading the Unabomber's tangled thesis, "Industrial Society and Its Future." The author, who identified himself only as "FC",: was a very urban nature lover. "The
positive ideal that we propose is Nature," he wrote, but his idea of nature was infuriatingly hazy and sentimental. He doted	on the early settlers of the West for eating "wild meat" and
living in such isolation that "they belonged to no community at all." With characteristic bathos, he opined that "Nature makes a perfect counter-ideal to technology for several reasons" and 	that "most people will agree that nature is beautiful." The word "natural" cropped up in sentence after sentence as a synonym for "good."
p.80
In the dead center of the thesis - paragraph 115 out of two hundred and thirty two paragraphs - was a fragment of miserable autobiography, an unmistakable cry from the Unabombers heart.
     The system HAS TO force people to behave in ways that are increasingly remote from the natural pattern of human  mathematicians and engineers. It can't function without  them. So heavy pressure is put on children to excel in  these fields. It isn't natural for  adolescent human  being to spend the bulk of his time sitting at a desk  absorbed in study. A normal adolescent wants to spend his time in active contact with the real world. Among primitive peoples the things that children are trained to do tend to be in reasonable harmony with natural human impulses. Among the American Indians, for example, boys were trained in active outdoor pursuits - just the sort of things that boys like.
I never camped in the woods! I never went fishing! I never had an air-gun! They never let me be a boy!
Ted Kaczynski was nearing 30 when he arrived in Lincoln. Was it his lost boyhood of "active outdoor pursuits" that he found 	here?
The next morning, Bill Holliday, Diana's husband, said, "He
wasn't too different from a lot of folks round here. Vets
mostly. They make do without electricity. They hunt and fish -
live off the fat of the land. They keep themselves to
themselves."
"They ride bicycles?"
"A lot of people get around on bicycles,"Mrs. Holliday said."It's so flat." I went out to the river. The Blackfoot swirled greenly under the road bridge, but was too swollen with snowmelt to be fishable. As it was, I followed Stemple Pass Road over toward the Kaczynski place, with Humbug and Poorman Creeks chattering within earshot.  It was a pleasant 40 minute walk, past summer homes and pastureland, to the schoolbus stop beside Gehrig's Lumber, where the F.B.I. had pinned its search warrant to a post and officiously blocked the logging trail that led to Kaczynskis cabin. The cabin was just out of sight, but I could see the satellite dish of its immediate neighbour, like a creamy giant mushroom in an aspen glade.
It was woodsy, but it was not "the woods." When the spirit of Emersonian self-reliance failed him, Kaczynski could ride his bike to the Blackfoot market and pick up Del Monte food, whose cans meticulously labelled, figure prominently in the F.B.I. inventory. But this proximity to town must have had its disadvantages. Snowmobiling is Lincoln's economic mainstay in the winter months, and when Kaczynski was labouring on his life story (Item MB28 in the inventory is a "Brown Clasp Envelope Marked 'Autobiography'") he must have been plagued by the din of the rainbow striped machines whizzing past the cabin, for the
logging road, which takes a zigzag path through a shallow canyon, is perfect for snowmobilers. FC was similarly troubled. His thesis complains of "noise-making devices" intruding on his autonomy.
Yet here were deer, elk, bears, rabbits, and fish. The F.B.I. inventory, with its fishhooks, bows and arrows, and guns (one of them home made) alongside the chemistry set, the peanut butter jars, the hersheys cocoa cans, the raspberry Super Sip bottles, suggests the life not of a man but of a dangerous boy.
Item L9 interested me: "A Plastic Bottle Labelled 'Strychnine Oats.'" I mentioned it to Diana Holliday, "You feed oats to the deer, don't you?"
"Oh," she said, "that makes me really angry at him. he hated the deer, they used to eat his garden."
The positive ideal that we propose is Nature.
Lambkin's bar and Casino , at the center of Lincoln, was loud with talk, and welcoming.
"You're from Seattle?" the bartender said. "That's where all the serial murderers come from. Ted Bundy. The Green River Killer.... This guy is our first. We're kind of inexperienced."
She was down to her last 6 "Lincoln, Home of the Unabomber - The last best place to hide" Tshirts. The first edition had arrived at nine the previous evening; 15 hours later, I bought the last tshirt but one. A rush reorder had been sent out to the factory.
Profits on the tshirt sales were going to Lincoln's volunteer fire department, which had set its sights on a defibrillator. By Saturday morning, the defibrillator was in the bag and the volunteers were looking at the next item on the shopping list - compressor for filling air cylinders. After that, they needed new jackets.
"It's split this town right down the middle," according to Jay Verdi, a bearded firefighter who is also the fire departments PR man.  "Some folks are mad as hell at us for doing it."
I thought of the fire hall in Ismay, stacked from floor to ceiling with Joe, Montana, tshirts. Lincoln's sudden blaze of notoriety and fortune seemed more securely rooted.
"Did you pay any attention to Kaczynski before he became famous?" I asked Jay Verdi.
"I rode with him to Helena once. In 1978. I was buying a new Blazer. Sat with Ted on the stage."
"What did you talk about?"
"He said,'Hello.'"
"And that was all he said, all the way to Helena?"
"At the end, he said, 'I wont be riding back with you.' That was a long sentence for Ted."
As I was leaving, Verdi said, "The two guys who made the arrest - I heard that when they grabbed him, he didn't struggle, or anything like that. 'The wind just went right out of him. Total relief."
