body:
found on the Sac Bee page:

Role in capture haunts Kaczynski's brother 

     By Cynthia Hubert
     Bee Staff Writer 
     (Published Jan. 19, 1997) 

       One is a "cool-headed logician," a brilliant but unemotional
scientist who seems never
     to have known true intimacy.

     The other is a social worker, a sensitive counselor of troubled
youths who has steeped
     himself in the lives of others.

     Today, Theodore and David Kaczynski, who grew up together but
remain strangers in
     many ways, live in their unique versions of hell.

     Theodore, 54, who bonded with nature in ways he never did with
people, is locked in
     a stark jail cell in Sacramento, accused of being the calculating
and murderous
     Unabomber.

     David, 47, lives with the horrifying reality that he helped put his
older brother behind
     bars, and that a conviction could lead to his only sibling's
execution.

     "I deeply love Ted, and that love has been made more poignant, more
real in some
     ways by the tragedy of this whole situation," David Kaczynski told
The Bee last week.

     In one of his first lengthy interviews since his brother's arrest
in April, David Kaczynski
     talked about his complex relationship with his brother, his
conflicted feelings about his
     role in the Unabomber case and his vision of justice. He spoke
softly, between long
     pauses, clearly uncomfortable with the glare of publicity that has
been cast upon him.

     At times, he smiled warmly as he recounted happy times with his
brother, whose genius
     IQ led him to Harvard at 16 and a brief stint as a mathematics
professor at Berkeley
     before he retreated to the life of a hermit.

     They played friendly but competitive games of Monopoly and chess,
David recalled,
     and performed duets, with Ted on the trombone and his little
brother on the trumpet.
     They loved word games, and Ted punned incessantly.

     While other young people listened to rock 'n' roll, Ted preferred
classical music by
     Vivaldi and Bach that "had mathematical perfection and symmetry,"
his brother said. "I
     can't ever recall him singing songs or listening to lyrics."

     The brothers grew up in a middle-class, Midwestern home led by
Wanda and Ted
     Kaczynski, strong Democrats and "talkers" who spoke often of the
value of education
     and of the need to do what is right. "They weren't rigid
disciplinarians and by and large
     I don't think they needed to be," said David. "Neither of their
children ever created
     problems in the community or problems in school." Both parents were
warm and
     nurturing, he said.

     As a young boy and adolescent, Ted was often "moody" and would
retreat to his attic
     bedroom for long stretches, rebuffing attempts by his parents to
find out what was
     wrong, David said. 

     Yet Ted was capable of small acts of kindness, his brother said.
One of his earliest
     memories of Ted was when David was a toddler and his brother
fashioned a special
     knob on the family's screen door that the younger boy could reach.

     One summer day when Ted was home from college, the brothers took a
long walk with
     their father in the woods near their home in Iowa, picked wild
blackberries and
     gooseberries and later excitedly baked pies.

     "We said later that those were the best pies we ever tasted," said
David.

     But those tender moments were rare, he said, and he described Ted
as isolated,
     withdrawn and "terribly disturbed" for most of his life. He rarely
"acted out" or showed
     violent tendencies as a child, his brother said. But he seemed to
become angrier and
     more alienated as he grew older. For most of the past three
decades, he lived as a
     recluse in Montana.

     "I have always had an uneasy feeling that for all his development
as a mind, as a
     thinker, something was wrong with Ted's emotional development,"
said David,
     speaking in the Washington, D.C., office of his lawyer Anthony
Bisceglie. "He has
     always had a lack of connection to others, an inability to
understand others." 

     He said his brother never had an intimate friend, and retreated
deeper into his shell
     when family members expressed concern about his emotional state or
his isolation.
     Nearly 10 years ago, Ted wrote his brother a venomous letter
stating, in capital letters,
     that he never wanted to see or hear from David "or any other member
of our family"
     again. He was angry because his brother was getting married.

     Ted did not attend the funeral of his father when he committed
suicide five years later,
     though he "expressed condolences" to his mother over the telephone,
David said.

     "Ted is an extraordinarily complex person," he said. "His mind is
like a building with
     many rooms, many doors. It's as if all the parts of a full human
being are there, but they
     are not integrated into a whole personality."

     Theodore John Kaczynski has pleaded not guilty to charges that he
is responsible for
     bombings that killed computer store operator Hugh Scrutton in 1985
and timber
     lobbyist Gilbert Murray in 1995, both in Sacramento, and seriously
injured academics
     in San Francisco and in Connecticut in 1993. Trial is scheduled for
next November in
     Sacramento. He also is charged in a separate case with killing New
Jersey advertising
     executive Thomas Mosser with a package bomb that was mailed to his
home. 

     Devices placed or mailed by the Unabomber injured 21 other people
between 1978
     and 1995, but Ted Kaczynski has not been charged with those crimes.

     Since his arrest in April, Ted has refused any contact with his
brother or their mother,
     Wanda, 79, David said. He wondered aloud how the man who lived as a
hermit for 30
     years in the wilds of Montana is coping with his new environment at
the Sacramento
     County Jail.

     "Ted has always hated noise," he said. "Noise is something that is
terribly, terribly
     disturbing to him. I know how tormented Ted could be by noise in a
normal human
     environment, and in jail all of that is intensified. So I'm afraid
it's much worse for him." 

     In the woods, Ted hunted and gathered much of his food, rode a
bicycle for
     transportation, and had no electricity or indoor plumbing. He kept
records of every
     penny he spent and once calculated his cost of living at about 30
cents per day, his
     brother said. 

     "He was very proud of that," he said.

     "I think that Ted sensed in the wilderness a connection with
something good, something
     larger, that many of us get from our interactions with other
people," David said. "It was
     something benign and free and good, and to be cut off from that
resource for him
     would be extremely painful."

     Nine months after government agents arrested Kaczynski at his
ramshackle cabin near
     Lincoln, Mont., ending one of the costliest and most intriguing
manhunts in history, his
     brother said he has some regrets about his role in the case. But he
has not wavered in
     his conviction that he "did the right thing" in reporting his
strong suspicions of Ted to
     authorities.

     "I regret what I did every moment, every time I think about it," he
said. "I regret Ted's
     suffering. On the other hand, I don't think there is anything I
could have done
     differently."

     He went to authorities because "I could not have lived with myself"
if another person
     were hurt and killed by a bomb that he might have prevented.

     David's inner torment, he said, has been made worse by the belief
that he and his wife,
     Linda Patrik, may have unwittingly helped fund some of the bombings
with loans to
     Ted. And the invasive media coverage of the once private family has
"made it all even
     more surreal."

     "It has been very, very painful," David said, acknowledging that he
has had bouts of
     depression in recent months. "At times I wondered how I could
function."

     But with the support of his family and friends, he said, "I have
bounced back."

     An assistant director of a program for homeless children in
Schenectady, N.Y.,
     Kaczynski took some time off this fall to process his feelings
about what had happened,
     he said.

     "I needed some space that was purely mine," he said. He also wanted
to take some
     time to assist lawyers in the case, to respond to an avalanche of
letters that he had
     received from supporters, and to write letters to family members of
the Unabomber's
     victims.

     "I thought about what the victims may have suffered, and it sunk
into me. It felt so sad
     and so tragic that I wanted to reach out to them in some way. I
wanted to express
     sorrow for what had happened."

     David Kaczynski, while stopping short of saying that he is
convinced that his brother is
     the Unabomber, discussed his suspicions and the evidence that he
took to authorities.

     He recalled a discussion that he had with Ted in 1969, when the two
went to Canada
     to look for land to purchase. "He talked a good deal about his
sense that our culture,
     basically through technology, had taken a wrong direction," he
said. "That was the first
     time that I had any sense that he had given any thought to a social
or cultural agenda."

     A year later, he wrote a 23-page paper calling for an end to
scientific progress, and
     proposed that he and David launch "an organization dedicated to
stopping federal aid"
     to such research.

     The paper, which is certain to be a centerpiece of the case against
Ted Kaczynski, said
     that people's interactions "in relation to technology" are a threat
to human freedom.

     David recognized a strikingly similar theme 25 years later in the
Unabomber's widely
     published anarchist manifesto. The document criticized the
industrial revolution as "a
     disaster for the human race" and said scientific progress had to be
stopped at all costs. 

     The author of the densely worded treatise expressed disdain for
loud noises and said
     society must revert back to "wild nature." 

     The ideas were startlingly familiar, David thought with increasing
horror. "I saw a lot of
     the same desperation that I sensed in some of the letters that he
had written to us," he
     said.

     But it was not only the theme, but some of the specific words and
turns of phrase that
     led him to believe that his brother might be the author, he said.
"It just sounded like his
     words, it sounded like his rigid, methodical intellectualizing of
things."

     Three words, in particular, caught his eye: cool-headed logicians.

     "But it is obvious that modern leftist philosophers are not simply
cool-headed logicians
     systematically analyzing the foundations of knowledge," reads an
excerpt from the
     35,000-word manifesto's introduction. "They are deeply involved
emotionally in their
     attack on truth and reality." 

     A chill went through David when he read that paragraph. He
remembered how Ted
     had chided him in the past for inserting emotions into decisions.
"You are no
     cool-headed logician," he had told him. 

     "I thought, 'Who else have I ever heard use that phrase but Ted?'
No one."

     "It's got to be him."

     But he "went back and forth" with his suspicions, in part because
he did not feel Ted
     capable of inflicting violence on another person.

     "We are not talking about someone who took pleasure in hurting
people," said David.
     "He certainly is not a person who could have taken a knife and
slashed someone. That
     would have been impossible for Ted."

     Finally, after reading the document several more times, he was
convinced enough to
     pursue the matter further. He didn't tell his mother about his
suspicions, even though she
     had previously told him that "the thought has crossed my mind" that
Ted might be the
     bomber.

     "My reasoning was that I was still hopeful that Ted could be ruled
out," David said. "I
     didn't want her to worry and I knew it would be agonizing for her
if I approached her. I
     didn't want her to be involved in the decision. How awful to be
responsible for your
     brother being arrested, spending his life in prison or, God forbid,
executed? How much
     more terrible for a mother to be in that position."

     He consulted a handwriting expert, who concluded that his
suspicions were well
     founded. Only then did he approach Bisceglie, a friend of a family
friend, who advised
     him to contact authorities.

     Some members of the task force investigating the serial bomber were
doubtful that
     Kaczynski was a credible suspect, his brother said. Authorities
agreed to monitor him
     clandestinely, which they did for weeks before apprehending him in
his hand-built
     shack. Among the items they discovered inside: a completed bomb.

     In the days leading up to and following his brother's arrest, David
said, he was anxious
     and sorrowful. 

     "I recall dreaming about it. I recall having lots of dreams about
Ted," he said. "I recall
     waking up many mornings with that awful feeling of doom and saying
to myself, 'It's not
     a bad dream. It's real. It's real.' "

     Seeing television images of the disheveled hermit being led out of
his cabin was a
     shock, he said. "The images of his tattered clothes, of his
appearance, gave me this
     awful sense of woe that this person I do love and have been close
to has really
     deteriorated. He looked so isolated, so disconnected. I felt
terrible, just terrible."

     Now it is David Kaczynski's goal to do everything he can to prevent
his brother from
     being put to death if he is convicted, he said. 

     Bisceglie said the family will address a federal team reviewing the
case and will argue
     that it would "not be fair or just" to execute Theodore Kaczynski.

     First, David Kaczynski's pivotal role in the case should be
strongly considered,
     Bisceglie said. 

     Second, the family will argue that Ted is mentally unstable, a
"mitigating factor" in
     federal death penalty cases, Bisceglie said.

     Third, the government would discourage others from coming forward
with information
     about crimes committed by loved ones by demonstrating that doing so
would result in
     the execution of their loved one, he argued.

     "I don't think that anyone wants to believe that justice is a cold,
ruthless engine," David
     Kaczynski said. "I did what I did because there was hope that there
would be some
     consideration of my brother's mental fragility and emotional
disturbances."

     David, for his part, said he would "suffer in the extreme" if his
brother were given the
     death penalty.

     "I would be plunged into hell for the rest of my life," he said,
"and I don't think I
     deserve that."

>

>

>

> as either get rid of the car or don't.  Bicycles are good for short
> trips, which are hard on cars' engines.  You'll have much fewer car

> carrying really large loads.
> 
>

> hell smashing anyone in their way out of this world.  Bicycling is
> better because it's at peace with the world.  It's soothing to bicycle,
> it puts one in touch with the world and it's good for your body.
> One is unlikely to seriously hurt anyone on a bicycle.
> 
> I suggest that people ask themselves before getting in the car
> whether they really need to drive, or whether they can take a
> bicycle instead or get what they're looking for in some other way.
> 
> I like to think when I'm going along on my bicycle smiling, shopping on my
> bicycle, that I'm giving people seditious thoughts like "do I really

>

Very well spoken. Except that some of us find ourselves stuck in the
sort of community where it's very difficult to ride your bike anywyere
without risking being sideswiped by maniacal cars. Or having water
splashed on you, or having the drivers shout things at you... unless you
live in a nice civilized town with quiet streets, you are taking your
life in your hands by riding a bike or walking. Plus, it's not very
pleasant. And in many cases, when the nearest store is several miles
away and you are shopping for a family, it is nearly impossible to get
the job done by riding a bike.

Once our car broke down & we had no transportation for a week. I learned
how much physical energy the "primitive" folks expend, just getting from
place to place. Only, today it is worse for the carless.. because
automobiles have totally altered the environment to the benefit of the
drivers & the detriment of everyone else. 

I have heard that in the 30's or so, the auto manufacturers made a
secret agreement with the government to encourage the building of roads
at the detriment of railroads. Had this not happened, perhaps our cities
would never have evolved into the auto-dependent suburban sprawl they
have become.

". In many cases the new technology changes society so that eventually

In article <199706081420211480229@remote4-line36.cis.yale.edu>,
Peter Bell <bell@pantheon.yale.edu> wrote:
>
> categorize his parents as True Believers) and people in academic
> circles.  There's a certain formalism to the construction of the
> manifesto that seems like some sort of an attempt at a nod to
> academics.

Well, he does say in his manifesto that he intends to convince the
academics first, and leave the conversion of the masses until later.
He seems to approach it like a marxist might: convince the
discontented amoung the middle or upper class, and let them convince
the lower class.  However, I don't see that this approach would
necessarily work in America.

>> It the manifesto had been more articulate and convincing, I believe
>> he would have generated tenfold more interest in his beliefs.
>
> I'm actually not sure that I agree; you're assuming people would
> have read it.  Americans, his chosen group, simply do not read.

Look at the nonfiction on the New York Times bestseller list. :) We
*do* read, just not things like Aristotle or Thomas Aquiness. As to
the literary types, I'm not so sure you are correct there. Of course,
I could imagine that it is true since there is so *much* material out
there, for each field, that it must be impossible to keep fully up to
date.

I'm interested in this subject myself.  How different would society be
if we all were brought up to believe that a broad education and the
desire to learn and develop our minds was an essential component of
life? 


> [television] can be used to convince Americans of *anything,* if
> used properly.

Humph, you mean like presidential elections? :)

>> I certainly wouldn't have taken any notice of his
>> manifesto he had gone about getting it published in a normal way.
>
> Do you think you might have run across similar strains of thought
> later on in your life? 

I had run across stuff, but I never paid any attention to it.  My area
in college was political science, so I did look at some things
regarding the effects of technology on society, but never modern
technology in the here and now.

>      Section 1.  Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a
>      punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly
>      convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place
>      subject to their jurisdiction.  
>
> Prisoners are now being employed to make a popular line of blue
> jeans in Oregon, to take reservations by a number of hotel chains,
> and for an ever-growing variety of tasks as more and more states see
> self-sufficiency for prisons by hiring out the inmates as a
> necessity.

Other then "human rights" abuses, there is the whole question of
politcal prisoners who are being "reeducated through labor."  I don't
think there is a valid comparison between China and the US. the US, in
general, isn't in the habit of picking up every political dissenter
and throwing him in prison until his will is broken.  This isn't to
say that individuals aren't above doing that (as you seem to know very
well, we only have to look at the civil rights movements for
examples), but that it isn't a recognized national policy.


> The problem I have with terrorists/freedom fighters/revolutions/wars
> as a whole is this: assume one side just, and one is not.  The side
> which is in the wrong is there because of policy which has been
> authored by its leaders.  Rarely are the killers for justice in a
> position to kill the authors of injustice; rather, they are killing
> others who are acting lawfully.  So, in the best possible case we
> have just warriors and lawful warriors killing one another.  Not
> just warriors and the authors of the unjust laws.  And it's very,
> very rarely close to that clean-cut.

Well, I sort of agree with this.  It isn't clear cut, but don't you
think that this is the easy way out?  To essentially say that, since
they operated within a legal framework, they can't be punished?  Say
you have people who have been picked up off the street and tortured.
A year later, a new government is in place. These people see their
torturers walking around free as a bird. There is likely to be a lot
of anger in that society...

But in any case, my point essentially matches with yours.  I'm not
sure if you saw that I was being very sarcastic when I wrote:

  acceptable as long as they don't turn around and start slaughtering
  everyone from the other group when they get the chance (which slims
  the group down a touch).


>> One example is the Vietnam conflict.  Lots of people say that the
>> North Vietnamese were liberating their fellows from the capitalist
>> pigs.
>
> Wow, where do you hang out?  I haven't heard this argument in years, and
> rarely heard it even in Berkeley during the 80's.  

You are very lucky. I heard it all the time for a whole semester when
I took a class that examined the 60s and 70s in America.  Thena gain,
my college was weird: freshmen are usually 15 or 16 years old.  Since
this was a junior level class, my classmates were around 18 years old.
Perhaps they didn't have a very broad perspective on the matter. :) In
any case, that crap is what I had to argue against all the time.

But, back to my point: I wasn't writing about the cause of the war,
but was making the argument that there were people who couldn't give a
damn about which side wanted what government, as long as they were
left in peace.  Some hated Diem's government, others hated the Viet
Minh, probably many hated both.


> I'd be interested in asking whether that soldier knew there'd been
> elections which the nationalists won in the mid-50's.  Not many
> folks do; I didn't learn about until 1989 or so, as for some odd
> reason, it's not mentioned much by the media.  Also, what I've read

This isn't what I've read. From what I'd heard, the elections never
occurred in the South.  Not to say that the south wouldn't have voted
nationalist, Diem was doing a wonderful job of pissing off almost
everyone...

From what I've read:

Japan essentially took control of Vietnam over from France (who were
under German control at this point) during World War II.  At that time
the Viet Minh was organized from the nationalist movements that had
sprung up because of massive discontent during French rule
("protection" is what the French called it). The nationalists were
prepared to seize power when Japan was defeated by America.  The Viet
Minh took over North Vietnam, and also invaded South Vietnam (there
has already been a North and South for a long, long time).  The French
fought them, drove them out of the South, and both parties tried to
negotiate a settlement.  This attempt failed, and war broke out.

The French had US aid, and were powerful enough to to force the Viet
Minh into adopting guerrilla warfare tactics.  Dien Bien Phu was a
turning point, and France finally agreed to negotiations.  This was in
1954.  Both sides were to have elections in 1956. Diem came into power
in the South, and never held elections.

So where did you read about elections being held in the South?


>> It is simply this: to admire a group fighting for its principles is
>> never black and white.  The wrongs and rights of both sides can be
>> examined and found to contain "truth."
>
> I'd be interested in your comments on Ghandi's wrongs and on the
> wrongs committed by the Southern Christian Leadership Council in
> Mississippi.

You over-interpreted me here.  The context was two groups who are
being physically unpleasant to each other (that is, both sides are
violent).


>> Were the Unabomber victims evil people who were destroying the
>> world? [Not really. Were they part of the system that could be seen
>> as destroying the world? Yes. Does that make it right to kill them?
>> Nope, nor does it come across as a valiant freedom fighter's
>> methods.]
>
> How much sympathy do you have for the fellow who was a lead lobbyist
> for the timber industry?  If he'd been a lead lobbyist for the
> tobacco industry?  I ask, because my reading of the coverage is that
> a lot more emphasis is being put on the advertising executive who
> was both apparently wrongly targeted and at more of a remove from
> the industry in question even had he been rightly targeted, and on
> the "harmless academic" victims than on the timber lobbyist.

Why did you just quote the first sentence of my paragraph?  To answer
your question, I have a lot of sympathy for *all* the victims and the
family and friends of those victims. I don't think it was justifiable
to make *any* of those attacks.  Why in the world would I feel it was
more justifiable to kill a lobbyist as opposed to a scientist?
Neither one, as far as I know, were sitting around plotting world
domination and the destruction of all things green.

As to what the media puts out, I can't answer for them.  Perhaps they
see this as a Greenpeace movement, and aren't looking any further then
that.


>> I'm just making the point that killing people for a "righteous
>> cause" doesn't mean we can or should hold hold a terrorist up for
>> admiration.
>
> [List of people/companies who have been involved with death and not
> condemned as criminal madmen removed]
>
> Terrorists in suits, and all of them far more lethal and far less
> selective than F.C.  While you may or may not agree with FC's target
> selection, the bombs were not indiscriminate, which puts them a rung
> ahead on people who are insulated by complicated command structures
> from their actions.

I can only assume that you are trying to make the point that, if
society looks the other way when the US goes to war with someone, they
are hypocrites for thinking that the Unabomber is a criminal.  Well,
welcome to the world of nations, national policy, and the law. The
world certainly isn't a fair place, you get no argument from me
there. Strength seems to do a lot more then make "right" -- it also
seems to make morals for most of society. Sad, but true.

Hmm, let me see... Ah, here in the manifesto I find the following:

   135. In paragraph 125 we used an analogy of a weak neighbor who is
   left destitute by a strong neighbor who takes all his land by forcing
   on him a series of compromises. But suppose now that the strong
   neighbor gets sick, so that he is unable to defend himself. The weak
   neighbor can force the strong one to give him his land back, or he can
   kill him. If he lets the strong man survive and only forces him to
   give his land back, he is a fool, because when the strong man gets
   well he will again take all the land for himself. The only sensible
   alternative for the weaker man is to kill the strong one while he has
   the chance. [...]

By his own logic, the stronger neighbor should kill the weaker one
before any chance for retaliation occurs.  I think the Unabomber is
trapped in his own logic here.  If TK is the Unabomber, how many
people here think he will be sentenced to death?

>> Well, the only thing I can say is that you need to examine why it is
>> that you need an immediate, live, "hero figure" in order to feel that
>> there is a reason to see worthiness (empowerment) in your beliefs.
>> (Dr. Spock: "So, tell me about your childhood.")
>
> I don't think this is fair.  Criticizing people for wanting heroic
> figures is like criticizing people for breathing.  On the other hand,
> there are people who are heroic figures in my mind who've come to my
> attention only because of what they've written.  Camus would be one.
> For many, Marx would be another - and in both cases, really, all either
> of them did was write.  

I think it is perfectly fair. I'm not criticizing her for wanting one,
but for needing one to feel "psychologically empower[ed]" about her
beliefs.  Personally, the trite phrase "I believe in what I believe."
sums it up.  I have reasons to back up most of those beliefs (and am
working on the others...), but I don't see how meeting someone who
agrees with me should make me feel so much better about my beliefs.

> Absolutely.  An alternate path would - and hopefully will - work
> better.  I think though, that there is an inconsistency inherent to
> our society about when we will and will not kill, and a desperate
> eagerness to be blinded by what our leaders tell us about why
> they've made the decisions they've made.

I can't see applying the term "consistent" to a society.  It is like
saying you can rationalize with a mob.  What makes you think that the
majority of Americans are immune from feeling the urge to either
dominate or to feel like they are doing a good deed?

For example, I believe many people got a kick out of the Gulf War:
seeing US troops in successful action, and seeing themselves as a
nation helping Kuwait. I don't think they were "eager to be blinded"
into believing this, I think they already believed it.  National
policy is expressed by what the people want. The seed is there, the PR
people just take advantage of it.

> Does Kennan -- and his list of unreal ojectives -- read to anyone
> else as applying more broadly than to foreign policy?  Whether it
> does or doesn't, what does it say about any moral authority our
> government has to take life in war?  If it does apply at home, as it
> seems to me it must, what does it say about the authority our
> government has to take life under any circumstances?

The moral authority for our government to take life comes from the
democratic majority of course. Each member of the majority of society
is willing to give the government certain powers and authorities in
order in ensure a relatively pleasant life for himself or herself.  If
the society becomes too large, government becomes unwieldy. It is
unable to give the people a sense of control over their lives.  People
become apathetic about their ability to make a difference.  The
political powers become an entity unto itself. Politicians grab for
votes by saying "yes" to all the concerns voters have. The population
begins to think it is too much trouble to get up and vote because "it
is all the same anyway." And on and on and on...

Sad, isn't it?


Jim
-- 
Jim Robinson <jim.robinson@stanford.edu> - http://highwire.stanford.edu/~jimr/

matches.quote: The average man's fate is no longer in his own hands

The technophiles are taking us all on an utterly reckless ride into the
unknown

body:
Here is a copy of my propaganda page, pasted from the Web
(http://www.geocities.com/SoHo/Lofts/2532/quotes.html)

"Don't Snuff the Prof"

"The average man's fate is no longer in his own hands...but in those of
politicians, corporations, executives and remote, anonymous
technicians." (128)

"Man in the future will be no longer a creation of Nature... but a
manufactured
product." (122)

"The technophiles are taking us all on an utterly reckless ride into the
unknown."(180) 


                        "There's a little bit of 
                              The
                       Unabomber
                            in all of us."
                        - Robert Wright, TIME Magazine



The Unabomber killed people, and that was wrong. I am very sorry that
innocent
people were hurt and killed. Nevertheless, there is widespread sympathy
for the
ideas expressed in his Manifesto and for the suspect, Dr. Theodore
Kaczynski, as a
person. Many people, including myself, view progress and technology as a
threat
and have admitted to a certain respect for the Unabomber for saying so,
even if
they do not agree with his violent tactics. The Federal Justice system
has already
determined they will seek the death penalty for Dr. Kaczynski if he is
convicted.
Many people, including myself, do not wish to see this happen. This page
is a
collection of quotes from such people, collected as a protest against
such a
possibility. Let us tell the authorities: Please don't "snuff" the Prof!

Sources: Unless otherwise stated, these comments came from a year's
worth of
posts on the alt.fan.unabomber newsgroup. All names have been omitted.
Some
messages have been edited for clarity.

Who we are:

These quotes are from people all over the US, as well as Canada, England
and
Germany. We are: college students in biology and history, anthropology
professors,
computer programmers and systems analysts, moms with children, desktop
publishers and working stiffs of various kinds. Many, of course, have
not wished to
divulge personal information about themselves.



"I'm very pleased that someone intelligent is addressing the problems of
our
society...the Unabomber was brave enough to discuss the current state of
humanity
when no one else could. He had the vision to see the error in blind
pursuit of
technology..."

"People call him a killer, but he was defending our planet. People will
kill to defend their country, what about the planet?"

"If the Unabomber was just a killer not many people would be a fan of
him. It is his brilliant interpretations of our society that we're fans
of."

"He dared to say what most people are too afraid, oversocialized, or
blind to say. He confronted our social problems with a thoughtful
analysis which is rare in a time when media stupidity is the main source
of most people's "information" about the world around them."

"He is ... a symbol that the human spirit has not yet been killed... he
has started a dialog on the most forbidden subject in our society: the
meaning of our existance, behavior, values and future."

"The Unabomber may have killed people but he has many redeeming
qualities."

"The Unabomber was right: technology is a raging monster that has made
us all
feebleminded drones, and eventually it is going to kill us."

"If one condemns the violence one also has to condemn any institutional
violence, say capital punishment or killing in war. Otherwise it just
means that ethics lines  neatly with the purposes of the state...a group
of people who are in power...and it's not real ethics, just the
self-justification of power."

"Sometimes drastic social situations call for drastic actions to remedy
them."

"While WE (the techno savvy) sit on our asses & stare at our screens to
rant about the power the government and large businesses have over us,
HE's the man who's trying to change things and ENLIGHTEN people to our
own self destruction."

"Look at the world today, is it a peaceful place? Do you think it will
ever be? What do you think made the world such a shit hole to live in in
the first place? If you haven't read the manifesto yet, DO so. You will
find the answers to these questions in it."

"In truth if his tinkerings had come at a different time in history, if
his thinking had gained more adherents, if his one man "movement" had
gained momentum, he might have been called a visionary, or at least a
revolutionary."

"Based on the Manifesto, I think he's in vastly better shape than
99.999% of
humanity."

"FC's greatest fear was genetic engineering and other technologies that
will control our minds and irreversibly enslave us. This... is so
frightening and inevitable to him that he regards any means as aceptable
to fight against it."

"I don't agree with his killings, but I do agree with his points. He is
not a serial killer, he is a revolutionary."

"The unabomber is a man who stands in the face of the evil powers that
will
eventually lead to the downfall of society."

"Almost all countries have achieved their independence by terrorism.
Whoever
wrote the manifesto was deeply concerned with the future freedom of
humanity..."

"[the unabomber] kills for a noble cause and he's a "murderer",
capitalists kill millions and obliterate Nature, and it's called
"business".

"When humans do screw up the planet... perhaps society will collapse and
the
Unabomber will have the last laugh from his grave or whatever."

"The Unabomber's Manifesto is a very honest and enlightening work. I
agree with
many of the views expressed... I think it's a shame that holders of
minority
opinions..have to resort to such drastic measures to get the attention
they deserve."

"The Unabomber, whoever he is, is "right on" about society." 

"The manifesto makes a lot of sense." 

"IMHO, the people who go around imposing themselves and their idea of
progress
on everyone else, often at a fatal cost to members of their own species,
other
species and the environment in general are more psychopathic than the
Unabomber. At least the Unabomber thought out his actions morally. I see
no
indications that the progress crowd even thinks about what they do."

Supporters' Descriptions of Selves

"I work in a research lab in biology at Yale, and hence I and most of my
social
circle are potentially on the hit list. We, too, are fascinated by the
Unabomber, and sympathtic to much of his message. "

"I'd like to throw my minor in comparative history, ideas and culture
behind me
when I say TK has made an important intellectual contribution to our
society. "

"An interviewer with the Sacramento Bee said that 'a lot of the sympathy
expressed for the Unabomber was from computer people...the very people
he was against.' "

"My father...has been a business executive since college...he agreed
with [una's] basic conclusions and told me of some of his business
acquaintances who agreed with a lot of [Una's beliefs]."

"I have a job and a girlfriend, two dogs and my own home, and still
admire the
Unabomber." [from an article in a British zine, name not available at
present.]

"Computer users are often intelligent and creative and these are the
people who
realize the direction in which our society is going. Some of them, such
as myself, may identify with Kaczynski because, like him, they may have
suffered rejection and loneliness because they were 'nerds' or different
from the norm."

Personal Sympathy for Theodore Kaczynski

"I think Kaczynski is an interesting character, and one whom people are
sadly
mislabling and misjudging." 

"TK/FC/Unabomb is inspiring to me simply because he/she/they/it is one
of those
very rare people with a passion for something other than money."

"I ...sympathize with TK. This is a man with a special gift that he was
unable to use, because of a disability that he could not find a way to
overcome... TK's life, in one sense, is a tragedy and a cry for help. In
another sense, it is a blow struck against inhumanity, ...the
destruction of nature and people by technology and corporate and
government greed." 

"I think Kaczynski is a deep thinker...and he may turn out to have been
quite
right." 

"TK is a sort of hero to me ... he's a fascinating character...an
accomplished person who thumbs his nose at bourgeous culture and does
things that... go beyond plain old love of self... it's epic stuff to
me."

"I felt that despite his [alleged] crimes, he had a lot of potential for
growth and change."

"He...strikes me as a vulnerable person who protected himself with
isolation...and he also seems fundamentally good, fundamentally
idealistic, and someone of much personal power."

"Ted is a misunderstood boy genius, with more intellect than that of the
[whole] US government combined. His ideas for the ceasing of technology
prove he was a great man, who took the wrong way about handling things."

"Ted K. is visibly not a monster. He's a brilliant, sensitive man who
let us know what he felt and did what he did for reasons that many of us
relate to. Many of us might even feel that in the ultimate...maybe,
history will prove him right." 

The Death Penalty

"It would be particularly horrible to see [TK executed]. He is alienated
from society for reasons that many of us can relate to: the wholesale
destruction of nature and runaway technology whose development is driven
by dollars, not by humanity's long-term best interest. He was apparently
conducting a one-man war against evils that many of us oppose. If he
were part of an army, he would be considered a prisoner of war and
executing him would be a war crime. 
Ted Kaczynski has a lot to offer the world. His (?) manifesto was
brilliant and
thought provoking. If you killed him off, you would be killing a radical
and
perceptive social critic."

"I will die a little more if he is executed. Maybe our society and all
the people will die a little more."

"You should [not] have to look hard to find many parallels of people
with multiple motives for killing, from discussions of the death penalty
to ditties sung celebrating enemy deaths in war."

"There presently is widespread sentiment against imposition of the death
penalty in this case. ( in the NY Times forum, sentiment was running
10-0 against it.)...some of the Unabomber's victims see no reason to
kill Kaczynski if he's convicted."



In conclusion:

For more information or to add your support, write to:

(Unabomber Political Action Committee)

unapack@paranoia.com

Your comments. Please note if you do not want them added to the
collection. (abusive comments will
not be printed.)

Or write to: shadow42@geocities.com.

I plan to forward a copy of these quotes to Kaczynski's lawyer, Mr. Quin
Denvir. If you agree, free to copy and print out this page and send a
signed copy to him yourself. If enough of us express our opinions,
perhaps they can be considered a "mitigating factor"?

matches.quote:
The conservatives are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional 
 values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and 
 economic growth

body:
: A Libertarian would probably say; "Sure, never trust _anyone_, always
: rely on yourself, and screw them over before they screw you over."
:
: I pity Libertarians.  What a pathetic way to go through life, always
: seeking to increase their own materialistic urges at the expense of
: others.  How many televisions you need, Mr. Libertarian? How many
: cable t.v. channels can you watch at once?  Just because Ayn Rand
: despises emotion doesn't mean you shouldn't give it a try...
:
: Along with the lose of emotions such as compassion, pity,  and guilt,
: you lose emotions such as love. empathy, and romance.
 
I think you're right about a lot of the Rand-clones but those are
just sheep looking for another master to give them orders.  They need
a dogma to define themselves with and "Objectivism" or Libertarianism
fits the bill conveniently.

There's something to their anti-emotional perspective though.  When
you look around at the predatory nature of all business, how can you
have compassion, pity, guilt, love, empathy, or romance for anything
related to capitalism.  It's all a show for your money.  In a
capitalistic society, we can have any plastic junk good for a "low"
price, but we pay the higher cost in our brutally inhumane relationships
with each other that are irreconcilably tainted by the same capitalistic
psychology.

"Is she only being nice to me because she wants my money like the salesmen?"
"Is he only being nice to me because he wants sex and then he'll skip out?"
"If I do x, she'll have to do y!"

The strategy for taking advantage of others is all that matters.  We see
each other as consumable products just like everything else in society,
so why not take advantage?  If we royally screw someone over, then we'll
just go to the store and get another.  Capitalistic society has taught
us to approach things that way, so we're "just following orders".

"I need a friend who likes x."
"One of my friends can get me y."
"I like her because she's z and my last friend was z."

Still, whatever you say about the Libertarians, they always seem to be  
nice and help me find the right book from their complex shelving system.
I need to buy one of those...
    
-Ric G.
"The conservatives are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional 
 values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and 
 economic growth." -FC, Industrial_Society_and_its_Future [50]

body:
Sorry for the cryptic post last time.
	On Jacques Ellul, he is a very interesting, but also frustrating
author.  He can completely contradict himself withing a single
sentence.  However, when he writes on something, he shows himself to
have thoroughly mastered the literature that has gone before, and always
has a unique view of his own.  He seems to have been a chronic rebel. 
Briefly a Communist, he became a devotee of the Reformed Church of
France while still a student.  Under Vichy rule, he criticized the
Nazis, and was fired from his academic job.  Joining the underground, he
became one of the movement's most prominent figures, and is credited
with smuggling 200 Jews out of the country.
	After the war, he did not join fellow Resistance leaders in positions
of national prominence, but criticized some of them (especially Sartre)
for engaging in fashionable, profitable forms of social rebellion.  It
took him four years to find a publisher for his classic attack, "The
Technological Society" which was (and is) often assigned reading in
courses about the subject.  It is still in print.
He also wrote "The Technological System," expanding on the earlier book,
and "The Political Illusion," criticizing leftist utopians.  Popular
with the American New Left, he rebelled against his own popularity by
insisting (in "The Ethics of Freedom") that technology was merely the
modern form of evil and sin, and that only salvation through Christ
could free the individual.  A couple of clear paraphrases of Ellul by
FC:

	Ellul --- "In a given civilization, technical progress is
irreversible." (Tech. Soc. p.89; originally in italics)
	FC --- "But technological advances are permanent withing the context of
a given civilization." (Ind. Soc. ���133)

	Ellul --- "The technical phenomenon cannot be broken down in such a way
as to retain the good and reject the bad." (Tech Soc, p.111)
	FC --- "The 'Bad' Parts of Technology Cannot Be Separated From the
'Good' Parts" (Ind. Soc. section title for ���121-4)

	Perhaps more importantly, FC appears to be using the word "technology"
the way Ellul did, which is to mean "all forms of technique."  That is
why FC can include forms of psychology and bureaucracy as part of the
system.  They are "techniques."
	Without going on forever, I will mention two other points of interest. 
First, FC may have started this whole project as a rejection of Ellul's
Christian perspective.  "The Ethics of Freedom" is basically a book on
theology, but it often digresses to criticize a position that is rather
similar to the one that FC later endorses.  For instance, Ellul insists
that power and freedom cannot be reconciled with one another, FC defines
freedom as the opportunity to go through the power process.  Ellul
connects anarchists to his earlier criticism of leftists by calling them
utopian.  FC is at pains to show that their anarchism is not utopian.
	Second, "The Technological Society" was translated into English at the
suggestion of Aldous Huxley, and there is a special note in the
bibliography citing the influence of fiction writers, including Huxley
and Orwell.  The "Translator's Introduction" points out that the logical
opposite of Ellul is B.F. Skinner (author of "Walden Two" and "Beyond
Freedom and Dignity").  One of FC's targets was an avid Skinnerian
psychologist, and "Industrial Society" defends "freedom and dignity" and
"freedom and autonomy."  Ellul was a long-standing analyst and critic of
science fiction (he despised 2001, Fahrenheit 451, and Alphaville
because they were too optomistic for him).  Note that the phrase "Brave
New World" is in "Industrial Society" and capitalized just as is the
phrase "True Believer" which is also the title of a book.  Ellul treated
all sorts of technical control, with long sections on economics and the
state.  FC's treatment of control is narrower, I suspect, because FC has
focussed on forms of control that appear in "1984," "Brave New World,"
and "Walden Two."
	On another topic.  I think FC's mention of Nazis is just a case of
including them as symptoms of social breakdown.  The left is seen as a
special threat, not because they are the primary enemy, but because they
are revolutionary competitors.
	As for my suggestion that an SDS veteran might be involved with FC, the
point is that SDS was considered part of the New Left, but it was built
around the ideas of C. Wright Mill, and was run as a decentralized,
small-group, participatory democracy, which means it was semi-anarchist
in practice.  It was destroyed by a battle over whether to purge a
Maoist group that had systematically infiltrated SDS.  Anyone strongly
on the pro-purge side would have an ax to grind against leftists, but
would be wise to cite foreign examples of leftist subversion rather than
one that might be self-identifying.
	On the subject of possible multiple authors for "Industrial Society,"
read the cautionary passages of ���8, 23, 31, 223-4, 227-8, and 231-2, in
that sequence.  Most of the passages on leftism are decisive analysis,
or sharp condemnation, such as "If our society had no social problems at
all, the leftists would have to INVENT problems in order to provide
thenmselves with an excuse of making a fuss," (���22) and "Leftism is a
totalitarian force." (���219)  Why does FC also insert increasingly
cautious qualifications of this denunciation?  Why, if the introduction
is so well crafted, do FC write such a bad conclusion?  Instead of
summarizing their argument as a whole, they tell us that what they said
about leftists may be "flatly false" and that they "might possibly be
wrong about this."  Doesn't it sound as if someone is decisively against
leftists, but someone is not so sure?

	Having been too brief last time, I have been too long this time.  I
guess I am trying to get a lot out because it is exciting to discuss all
this, and I will have to be off the net for about two weeks.

		Take care,

				Scott

        Experts prepare for 'an electronic Pearl Harbor'

  'The average American should be concerned'
  
November 7, 1997
From Correspondent Pierre Thomas

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- While the possible sabotage of a San Francisco
power grid two weeks ago was an inconvenience for the 126,000
people left without power, what bothers others is that it merely
hints at what could happen in the future.

Imagine, for example, phone service cut off because someone used
computers to shut down the area's telecommunications system.

Or subway cars stopped in their tracks because a saboteur has
monkeyed with a transit system's controls. Or the money of hundreds
of thousands of people frozen in banks and ATMs because someone
planted a virus in a bank's central computer.

It's not as far-fetched as it seems, at least not to the United
States government. A presidential commission has already identified
power systems, water supplies and gas and oil distribution systems
as needing added protection. The recommendations are not being
taken lightly.

"We're facing the possibility of an electronic Pearl Harbor,"
Deputy Secretary of Defense John Hamre told a congressional
hearing. "There is going to be an electronic attack on this country
some time in the future."

  Task force includes 11 U.S. agencies
  
"This may be the most difficult and important national security and
public safety concern our nation's leadership will face in the
months and years to come," says Sen. John Kyl, an Arizona
Republican.

The government has already begun preparing for scenarios that could
be nightmares to those accustomed to an infrastructure that
functions in a reasonably orderly way.

A task force of 11 federal agencies -- including the military, the
FBI, the CIA, the Treasury Department, the Transportation
Department and the Department of Energy -- is in the process of
assessing the nation's vulnerabilities.

FBI agent David Keyes, who chairs the Infrastructure Protection
Task Force, says his job is to figure out "what vulnerabilities the
cyber dimension introduces into the terrorism arena. What kinds of
ways can the United States be hurt through electronic attack,
rather than bombs?"

  'The average American should be concerned'
  
In recent months, the Pentagon conducted a secret training exercise
dubbed "Eligible Receiver" in which technicians jousted with
"villains" targeting databases and communications systems.

"The average American should be concerned," says Ray Kelly,
Undersecretary for Enforcement at the Treasury Department, "because
virtually every aspect of their daily lives is now involved in
infrastructure and, increasingly, the cyber infrastructure --
information.

"The airline control system, passenger reservations, air traffic
control; all of those are controlled by information networks," says
Buck Revell of the Institute for the Study of Terrorism and
Political Violence. "These networks extend on a global basis. And
they can be interceded and intercepted."

For those who say the federal government is crying wolf,
authorities point to the World Trade Center bombing and Oklahoma
City. And, with the incident in San Francisco, which the FBI is
investigating, they have another to add to the list.

turned out to be 2.5 milligrams three times a day.  It is
interesting to note that at the time the smallest dosage that
could be purchased was 5 mg, so I had to break the tabs in half.

The effect of that 2.5 mg dose on me was profound.  I spent a
full year on Ritalin, and made some interesting observations
during that time.  I could dedicate myself to the most petty
task with ease, and could remain attentive to the most dull and
boring material for indeterminate periods of time.
Simultaneously, I found my creativity to be nearly nill, and I
couldn't play racquetball while I was on it!

After a year on Ritalin, I found myself developing a violent
temper - something that I hadn't experienced before.  This in
itself was more than enough reason for me to end my experiment.

Overall, I found Ritalin to be an incredibly powerful drug.  The
"buzz" is distinctive and not uncomfortable, but it is
definitely a "buzz."  The main effect of the drug was to wipe
out my ability to simultaneously handle multiple stimuli, a
result that wasn't always desirable.  The irritability and
temper enhancement that developed after a while were the only
noticeable side effects.  I learned a great deal about how my own
brain works during that year.  I have no regrets, but I do not
use the drug any more and I would not permit my own children to
use it.

The best book I have read on the subject was written by Thom
Hartmann, "ADD, Another Perspective," subtitled "The Hunter In
The Farmer's World."

I would be pleased to correspond individually with anybody who
wants to learn more about my experiences.  Please contact me at
<celano@ic.net>.
--

body:
"QUOTED"

Mr. Quin Denvir & Ms. Judith Clarke
Office of the Federal Defender
Eastern District of CA
801 K Street 10th Floor
Sacramento CA 95814

Re: The Unabomber Case

Dear Mr. Denvir and Ms. Clarke,

I have been following the Unabomber case since Theodore Kaczynski was
arrested. I hope you will not mind if I offer some unsolicited advice.

Presently the defense seeks to highlight Mr. K.'s mental problems. This
is a good approach as far as it goes, but I believe there are other
factors which could help the jury understand and empathize with Mr. K.

If Kaczynski fears technological society as "an omnipotent
organization"... then his fears are only a few degrees more intense than
those of many other people in this society. Are there not many people
who fear rampant destruction of the ecosystem, genetic engineering, the
dehumanization of a mass society, and artificial intelligence? 

You may or may not be aware that the Unabomber has many supporters.
There is an internet newsgroup, alt.fan.unabomber, on which we have been
discussing the issues for a year and a half. By and large these are not
"kooks" who advocate bombing and killing... these are thoughtful,
intelligent people who are concerned about the future of this planet. We
empathize with the Unabomber's concern, even if we don't support his
methods.

I believe that this support factor is something the defense team should
tap into. My advice is to use passages of the Manifesto as testimony
that "he may have been mentally disturbed... but his fears are, to some
extent, legitimate." Would this not help to gain jury sympathy? I
certainly think it preferable to the tactic of citing the nasty things
Mr. K. said to his parents as a way of trying to prove that he is
"sick". (which,  by the way, does not make the jury like him.)

Ask the jury whether they could not agree with statements such as these
quotes from the Manifesto:

"Modern man is strapped down by a network of rules and regulations, and
his fate depends on the actions of persons remote from him whose
decisions he cannot influence." (para.114)

"Freedom and technological progress are incompatible." (p.113)

"Man in the future will be no longer a creation of Nature..but a
manufactured product."(p.122)

"The average man's fate is no longer in his own hands...but in those of
politicians, corporations, executives and remote, anonymous
technicians." (p.128)

"Technology has gotten the human race into a fix from which there is no
easy escape."(p.170)

"Those who are employed...will have to be ever more reliable, conforming
and docile, because they will be cells of a giant organism." (p.175)

I suggest you study the Manifesto closely and urge the jurors to view it
as more than "the ravings of a schizophrenic". The prosecution is using
Mr. K's writings against him. I suggest your team review the Manifesto
and use it in his defense. The defense needs all the resources it can
get.

This would not necessarily detract from your efforts to highlight Mr.
Kaczynski's mental disturbance. It would simply help jurors to
understand that "he may have problems, but in some ways he is similar to
us." 

Thank you for listening to my unsolicited opinion, and let me close by
congratulating your team on what you have already done and wishing you
the best of success in the future.

As well, nobody out there seems to have a clue what "the technological
system" meant. 

If Kaczynski was against ALL technology, he'd probably have gone off and
joined a Mennonite community. The idea is not a struggle against
"technology" per se, but against the cult of technologism and its desire
to implement complete control over people, to make their behaviour more
predictable and conforming with the technologist's standards. 

It is sad that people constantly misunderstand this. I don't think
Kaczynski ever wrote anywhere that portable radios, for example, are evil
in and of themselves; or ballpoint pens, or casiotone keyboards, or
whatever other banal examples of technology you might think of. The
problem's not "technology" itself, but those instances in which technology
is USED with an end in mind of controlling, brainwashing, or unnaturally
altering people and the environment in order to serve the ends of the
technologists and the people who make money off them.

Writers like William Barrett and Gabriel Marcel avoided this problem of
confusion, simply by referring to the enemy as "technique" -- so nobody
understood them, but at least nobody MISunderstood them.

Gabriel Marcel is interesting in that one of his ideas was that Mass Man
(i.e., the unthinking mass) is not only built and molded by technique, but
that the cult of technology also makes him forever unable to achieve a
high enough level of consciousness to ever GRASP any argument AGAINST
technology. Thus any argument, like Kaczynski's, will only ever seem to
fall on deaf ears (although there'll be a few "individuals" who will
actually be able to understand his concepts).

Nice to see someone besides me and Shadow is posting here.

body:
We are aboard a train which is gathering speed,
racing down a track on which there are an
unknown number of switches leading to unknown
destinations.  No single scientist is in the
engine cab and there may be demons at the switch.
Most of society is looking backward.
		Alvin Toffler, Future Shock (1970)
(quoting science fiction author Ralph Lapp)

We want a government based upon a science
of human behavior.  Nothing short of that will
produce a permanent social structure. ...
The trouble with the program of anarchy was
that it placed too much face in human nature.
		B.F. Skinner, Walden Two (1948)

Is it really humanly profitable to give up the
possibility of living a few years at Walden Pond,
so to say, for the privilege of spending a lifetime
in Walden Two?
		Lewis Mumford, Authoritarian and
Democratic Technics (1972)

The demise of appropriate technology as
a living social movement can be dated almost
to the hour and minute.  It occurred early in
the evening of Tuesday, November 4, 1980,
when it became clear that Ronald Reagan
had been elected President of the United States.
	Langdon Winner, The Whale and the Reactor:
A Search for Limits in an Age of Technology (1986)

[A] movement that exalts nature and opposes technology
must take a resolutely anti-leftist stance and must
avoid all collaboration with leftists.
Theodore J. Kaczynski a/k/a "FC" in
Industrial Society & Its Future (para. 214)

What is revealed in the end is that there is an
ideology in the technology itself.  To speak of
television as "neutral" and therefore subject
to change is as absurd as speaking of the
reform of a technology such as guns.
	Jerry Mander, Four Arguments For The
Elimination of Technology (1978)

Once regarded as the herald of enlightenment
in all spheres of knowledge, science is now
increasingly seen as a strictly instrumental
system of control.
	Murray Bookchin, The Ecology of Freedom:
The Emergence and Dissolution of Hierarchy (1982)

	BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING Y0U.
		George Orwell (Eric Blair),
Nineteen eighty four (1949)

But what good is it to pose questions of motives?
Of Why?  All that must be the work of some
miserable intellectual who balks at technical
progress.  The attitude of scientists, at any rate,
is clear.  Technique exists because it is technique.
The golden age will be because it will be.  Any
other answer is superfluous.
	Jacques Ellul, The Technological Society
(1954, tr. 1964)

	Forty years ago, no-one thought much about
smoking; Ronald Reagan with his Chesterfields
was just one instance of the glamour and
sophistication associated with cigarettes.
Computers and automation are now being sold
in much the same way that cigarettes were
purveyed three or four decades ago.
		Introduction, Questioning Technology:
A Critical Anthology, Ed. By John Zerzan and
Alice Carnes (1988)

[E]very hour that you're behind the keyboard is
sixty minutes that you're not doing something else.
		Clifford Stoll, Silicon Snake Oil,  (1995)

	Do you believe in a god?
	Do you have a soul?
	Can I buy a soul?
	What is the market price of a soul?
	Is your soul in mint condition?
		Edgar, a computer
		Exegesis, by Astro Teller (1997)

The real problem is not whether machines think
but whether men do.
		B.F. Skinner, Contingencies of Reinforcement, (1969)

[Computers] will become lifetime companions;
well get one at birth, take it everywhere, and
use it for everything.... Cats, of course, will
continue to ignore us.
	Gregory J.E. Rawlings, Slaves of the Machine:
The Quickening Computer Technology (1997)

	"Timetable for the future"
Parents can routinely choose characteristics
of their children through genetic engineering.
Probability: 50 percent
Year: 2025
Leading nation: United States
		Marvin Cetron and Owen Davies, Probable Tomorrows:
How Science and Technology Will
Transform Our Lives In The Next Century (1997)

Science and technology, like all original creations
of the human spirit, are unpredictable.  If we had
a reliable way to label our toys good and bad, it
would be easy to regulate technology wisely.
But we can rarely see far enough ahead to know
which road leads to damnation.  Whoever concerns
himself with big technology, either to push it
forward or to stop it, is gambling in human lives.
Freeman J. Dyson, Disturbing the Universe, (1979)

	Science is triumphant with far-ranging success,
but its triumph is somehow clouded by growing difficulties
in providing for the simple necessities
of human life on the earth.
		Barry Commoner, Science and Survival, (1966)

Men love to wonder, and that is the seed of science.
	Ralph Waldo Emerson, Society and Solitude (1870)

I think that engineering is what human beings,
deep down, want to do.  Not the only thing, but
one of the most basic and satisfying things.
Engineering is an activity that is fulfilling --
existentially...  To be human is to be technological.
When we are being technological we are being human.
		Samuel Florman, The Civilized Engineer, (1987)

All these belief systems share the fond hope
that by some sudden and dramatic epiphany,
this turbulent and troublesome world will
suddenly be put to right.  It is too much to hope
that even by 2050, people will have grown up
enough to reject such notions.  But we may hope
that by then the revolutionary spirit will have
largely worn itself out.
		T.A. Heppenheimer, The Real Future:
Tomorrow1s Technology Today (1983)

	A movement is pioneered by men of words,
materialized by fanatics and consolidated by men
of action.
	It is usually an advantage to a movement, and
perhaps a prerequisite for its endurance, that
these roles should be played by different men
succeeding each other as conditions require.
		Eric Hoffer, The True Believer (1963)

If the breakdown is sudden, many people will
die, since the world's population has become
so overblown that it cannot even feed itself any
longer without advanced technology.  Even if the
breakdown is gradual enough so that reduction
of the population can occur more through lowering
of the birth rate than through elevation of the death
rate, the process of de-industrialization probably
will be very chaotic and involve much suffering.
It is naive to think it likely that technology
can be phased out in a smoothly managed orderly way...
Theodore J. Kaczynski a/k/a "FC" in

The most selfish of all things is the independent
mind that recognizes no authority higher than its
own and no value higher than its judgment of truth.
		Ayn Rand, Atlas Shrugged (1957)

Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!   I say, let
our affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred
or a thousand ... simplicity of life and elevation
of purpose.
		Henry David Thoreau,  Walden (1854)

beyond the "quiet acts" of personal withdrawal
Mumford urges -- is to try to make the culture
of industrialism and its assumptions less invisible
and to put the issue of its technology on the
political agenda, in industrial societies as well
as their imitators.
Kirkpatrick Sale, Rebels Against The Future (1995)

the ills of extant technologies.  We can use the

movements and use these as means for rapid mass

	Joseph Agassi, Technology: Philosophical

	I have never advocated violence in any form.
I have always believed in education, in intelligence,
in enlightenment, and I have always made my appeal
to the reason and to conscience of the people.
		Eugene V. Debs, Address to the jury, September, 1918

	On the whole, new technical factors work in
favor of the dissemination of new ideas.
		Erich Fromm, The Revolution Of Hope:
Toward a Humanized Technology (1968)

	Perhaps Gene Roddenberry should have the
last word.  As he said on the twenty-fifth anniversary
of the Star Trek series, one year before his death:
The human creature is a remarkable creature,
one  with great potential, and I hope that Star Trek
has helped to show us what we can be if we believe
in ourselves and our abilities.
		Lawrence M. Krauss, The Physics of Star Trek (1995)

body:
Here's a summary of what's  really going on in the trial.  
Others have touched on this a bit:

++Warning: This discussion posits, for sake of arguement only,
that TK is the unabomer, a charge for which he has not been convicted.


The government's main concern in the unabomer case is to prevent
large numbers of people from espousing or even knowing about
his anti-tech and especially his anti-corporate views.  At 
first the best way to do this seemed obvious: kill him.
Hence the death penalty, with the procecution about to go to
great lengths to prove he's sane.

Then, once he asked to be his own lawyer, the gov't. realized 
that he could try to justify his actions by pointing out the
evils of tech. and  big corps.  (the defence advocated by
attorney Serra)  This would mean that every day CNN, NYT,
etc. would have to talk about all the bad things big corps.
have done...such a scenario is unacceptable for the govt.
Hence the fake suicide, and the new willingness to accept
a plea bargain.  They now figure he'll get less media attention
in jail his whole life (where he might be killed or suicided
anyway) than the attention he gets during the (monthlong?,
yearlong?) trial.  They will say they don't want a "circus
atmosphere" but what the don't want is a daily moral indictment 
of Exxon, GE, GM, etc.

Given the above, TK will face an interesting decision once he
is found competent: Should he accept the plea bargain?  According
to the Manifesto (#168.)

       Besides, we all have to die some                            
       time, and it may be better to die fighting for survival,
       or for a cause, than to live a long but empty and
purposeless            life. 


Hence he may feel that a life-or-death case will draw more attention
to his ideas than any prolific writings he may be able to produce
in jail.  What would you do if you were Ted?


o-w.k.

body:
Hi Renate,

Yes, you are right, Renate.  He approaches leftism "not so 
much a movement but rather a collection of related types."  
But that's common for extreme rightists, including those 
who are anarchistic.  

Kaczynski writes:
"When we speak of leftists in this article we have in mind 
mainly socialists, collectivists, 'politically correct' types, 
feminists, gay and disability activits, animal rights activists 
and the like."  (para. 7)

If you fall within these groups, he doesn't want your support --
he urges that his supporters not collaborate with such types.
Among EF!ers, he wants the support only of those who are
"thoroughly unleftist."  (para. 227)

His hatred of liberals is why he didn't get along with his 
parents.  They were traditional liberals.

I agree with Jorn that the manifesto is not rambling.  The
extensive arguments about leftists, however, struck many
commentators (like Kirkpatrick Sale) as totally unnecessary
to his Luddite argument.  Maybe it is -- maybe it isn't.  His
manifesto isn't just about technology:  it's more broadly
about his conception of freedom.

body:
THE THREE FACES OF THEODORE KACZYNSKI

Ross quoted from the Manifesto:
>HUMAN SUFFERING 
>167.  If the breakdown is sudden, many people
>will die, .... Even if the breakdown
>is gradual ...              ... the process
>of de-industrialization probably will be very chaotic
>and involve much suffering.  

This and the rest of the Manifesto constitutes the face TK wants
to show to the world -- that of a caring surgeon who must
reluctantly cause pain and suffering while amputating a limb, all
for the greater good of saving the patient's life.

TK's admission to the 1979 airplane bombing in notes found in his
cabin unmasks the private face which TK reveals only to himself.
[Copies of this and other admissions can be found at The Truth is
Redacted web site.]

  "Dec. 29, 1979: In some of my notes I mention a plan
   for revenge on society. Plan was to blow up an airliner
   in flight. Late summer and early autumn I constructed
   device. Much expense because had to go to Gr. Falls
   (Great Falls, Mont.) to buy material, including barometer
   and many boxes cartridges for the powder. I put more than
   a quart of smokeless powder in a can, rigged barometer so
   device would explode at 2000 ft. or conceivably as high
   as 3500 ft."
        
So plain old "revenge" and a desire to get even for some imagined 
wrong was TK's real reason for attempting to murder everyone on
board the American Airlines 727.  Here pain and suffering is
revealed as the whole purpose of the enterprise -- not some
unavoidable side effect.  But this is looking at things from the
point of view of TK's potential victims, which by the way
includes just about everyone alive at the time.  

What did taking "revenge on society" mean for TK himself?  We can
only speculate but he probably saw himself as avenging wrongs and
injustices so he would be able to view his own actions as
moralistic and noble.  And then there are the feelings of power
and self-importance he probably got from the taking on the whole
world and through his bombs being able to strike at whomever he
choses.  To use the slang of the 60's -- it would have a great
ego-trip for him.

What about TK's third face, the true face of Theodore Kaczynski?
Figuring that out is what makes this an interesting case.  Rather
than spoil anyone's fun, I'll leave that as a puzzle for the
reader.

DB

body:
wheaterj@aol.com (Wheaterj) wrote, in response to sloan@ishipress.com (Sam H
Sloan) 

"Friend, maybe you could illustrate the outmodedness of the ideas by quoting
and refuting an extract from the manifesto.
Many feel that these are in fact ideas whose time has come."
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------
Thank you Wheaterj! This is what I have been asking my friends to do, read the
manifesto, and give me their best arguments for or against. If someone can come
up with a true and logical reason why this document lacks merit, I would think
about it. So far, Dr. Kaczynski's work has had all the answers to their
arguments. (I still have questions that he wasn't able to address, based on the
necessity for brevity.) But, this was the most striking, passionate and well
reasoned document I have read in a long time.

I fear that most people feel they don't have time to read it, but do have time
to argue against it. It's kind of like preparing a report by reading the "Cliff
Notes". Of course, that's what our society does best. I prepare lots of reports
for management, and am careful not to put too many words in them, since that
seems to be a distraction for them, but lots of charts and graphs. Who needs,
or understands language anymore, when our society is increasingly graphical?
And who understands a good argument?

Dismissing this document out of hand doesn't qualify as a rebuttal to any of
its points. Adults should use their own logical powers to establish their own
conclusions, and then use argument to discover some truth.

To quote paragraph 110 of the manifesto (section dealing with "Some Principles
of History"), "The principles should be borne constantly in mind, and whenever
one reaches a conclusion that conflicts with them one should carefully
reexamine one's thinking and retain the conclusion only if one has good, solid
reasons for doing so."

I think that this is a good general reminder of how a logical argument should
work.

Thanks again!

body:
Alan Gore wrote:
"I can see this technology being used for, for example, to cause a sheep to
grow implanted human clone organs for use in human transplants. This is evil
because...?"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
-------
Well, for one thing, there are concerns about causing cross host diseases,
which could result in epidemics. For example, say there is a microbe whose host
is a sheep, and which may or may not be a serious threat to the sheep. In the
natural world, the microbe may not have any contact with humans. But, under the
conditions of cloning which mixes human genes with cellular material from other
species, the microbe could adopt a new host, namely human beings. While the
microbe may not have been a problem for the sheep, it could be a deadly killer
for humans. It may be no life saver at all, but the cause of a plague.

People in Europe are trying to oppose the import of genetically engineered food
(available at your local domestic supermarket, in case you didn't know it) for
similar reasons (crop destruction due to unknown variables being highest). (See
Business Week, Feb. 2, 1998, in the Science and Technology section, pages
62-63.)

Quite honestly, more thought is put into testing new software than is put into
what we do to our environment, which,  if changed too much, will no longer
provide life support for this society.

To paraphrase TK (on the principles of history), if a change is made that is
large enough to alter permanently a long-term trend, you cannot predict the
consequences of such changes. I think this applies here. The natural system of
genetics is surely a long term trend, as old as the earth itself.

I'm not even going to get into the ethical issues. But many pro-technology
people will admit that you have to draw the line somewhere.
