headers.Subject: The IMF and Consequences to Society

body:
If you revisit paragraph 196, "...It will be easier to destroy the industrial
system on a worldwide basis if the world economy is so unified that its
breakdown in any one major nation will lead to its breakdown in all
industrialized nations."

Enter the IMF, with its goal of stabalizing industrial economies. Congress is
about to debate funding the IMF with an additional $20 Billion US dollars. The
mainstream reporting is that if this isn't done, the effects of collapses in
other countries who are both our customers and our competitors would damage our
own economy. Various groups want to attach provisions to any US IMF fundings -
environmental policies, labor or human rights provisions, and other groups,
though of course, those which will be taken most seriously are the economic
interests. The corporate world is quite anxious that the IMF funding be passed
through Congress. Interesting enough, several Congressmen are not willing, due
to the above mentioned concerns. (I don't have their names, I just listen to
NPR, which I personally find to be the least biased source of news, when I feel
like listening to news at all.)

Meanwhile, I seem to have read somewhere that the Pope is encouraging poor
third world countries not to repay their IMF loans (which actually serve to
cripple those countries more, due to the large interest payments, and which
cause environmental degradation amongst other things.) The Pope is also
critical not only of communism, but of capitalism - he's not too happy with
what's going on in Poland. If anyone has more info on these subjects, I would
be interested.

Couple this with the "Year 2000" problem (and recently, the Washington Post
reported that there is a serious lack of programmers. I imagine there is a lack
of COBOL or other "legacy" (old programming languages) programmers to solve
this problem, which supposedly will bring down government, banking and other
industry systems.) The Year 2000 problem will start affecting people before the
year 2000, because the fiscal year will start in 1999. 

So, I am wondering, what is everyone on this newsgroup prepared to do? I would
welcome the collapse of the IMF, because I think it is a ruthless organization.
We can't predict the outcome of its collapse though.

This is just the sort of breakdown discussed in the "manifesto".

The members of this newsgroup have certainly represented the ideals in
paragraph 187 "On the more sophisticated level, the ideology should address
itself to people who are intelligent, thoughtful and rational. The object
should be to create a core of people who will be opposed to the industrial
system on a rational, thought-out basis, with full appreciation of the problems
and ambiguities involved, and of the price that has to be paid for getting rid
of the system. It is particularly important to attract people of this type, as
they are capable people and will be instrumental in influencing others."

I know I have done my small part in spreading the message, and will continue to
do so.

So, now we have a chance to make a difference. The future predicted in Ted's
work may be closer than we thought. His work was quite timely indeed. Perhaps a
little too close shaved for some.

What are we going to do about it?


Esjeje1@aol.com

shadow wrote:
 As for the

Wouldn't a new political party provide both an organization and platform
for the publicity to bring out such awareness and keep it up?  It would
also provide a legitimate means to collectively finance the effort.  The
reason the Democrats and Republicans are so afraid of a viable third
party is even if it does not have a majority it wouldn't need one. 
Merely by preventing either the Dems or Repubs from having a majority a
third party would either be the swing vote between them deciding issues
or if the Dems and Repubs united many of the radicals in both parties
would split off.  Either way, the stranglehold of the two parties would
be broken for the first time in a hundred years and we might have a
chance for real change.


> note 32 "it is even conceivable (remotely) that the revolution might
> consist only of a massive change of attitudes toward technology
> resulting in a relatively gradual and painless disintegration of the
> industrial system."

Is this the only means or hope TK holds out for peaceful change?  After
all, the original design of Democracy is supposed to allow for
Revolution without violence.  The average person, or majority, will
fight against violent revolution until such time as conditions have
become so bad that they are going hungry and losing loved ones.  Once
things have gone this far unless there is a distinct outside oppressor
nearly all chance of controlling the outcome is lost. Don't get me
wrong, I like the IDEA of anarchy it is just that the resultant rule of
force which inevitably arises is a definite step back.  (Even though all
rule is eventually base on force some systems do manage to insulate
greater numbers of people from its exercise than others, as well as to
use it in a clearly regulated and predictable manner)
	In other words is it not better to make ourselves heard with votes than
with deaths, especially since it is death we are trying to avoid?

Ummm,,,,this is a common misconception, but it's not true that 1/3 of
the manifesto is devoted to the anti leftist rant. Here's the breakdown:
Para.6-32 deal with leftists, and it is not at all a blanket
condemnation of ALL leftists, because at (23) he qualifies his argument
with this line: "this is only a rough indication of a general tendency
of leftism".
>From there he goes on to the subject of autonomy, which he says is a
basic need that has been denied in our society. This seems like a
tangent till we get to the main point, which is how people are
psychologically damaged by the technocratic society.

Only at the end (213-230) does Ted get back onto the leftists. This
leaves a total of 43 leftist-oriented paragraphs, with a total of 188
non-leftist paragraphs. LEt's see, that's approx. 2/9ths or maybe .2 or
maybe .15 or something that a mathematician like Ted can tell us. Now I
don't usually get this picky when analyzing the Manifesto, but I'm just
getting tired of that mindless bromide "1/3 of the manifesto is a
leftist rant", which is another bit of boilerplate prose like the
epithet "RAMBLING".

> So he certainly screwed himself as a revolutionary in
> terms of tactics, as leftists are the ones who tend
> to be more environmentally aware.

This is true, but if one reads it closely one realizes that Ted is
talking about the Stalinist-type leftist who extolls Progress &
behavioral engineering & has made Russia one of the most polluted
nations on earth. And once again, in 228., Ted qualifies his argument by
saying that "some individuals meet some of the criteria ... you will
just have to use your own judgment." This is pretty reasonable-sounding,
coming from someone everyone thinks of as a schizo, a maniac, etc. If
the author hadn't been a bomb-maker, I would just think of him as a
plain old college professor having an afternoon bull session w/ his
students!

I wouldn't say that Vonnegut didn't read Hoffer but I see a large
difference in your quote of Hoffer and mine of Vonnegut(I realize
Vonnegut is not considered a serious thinker by many but he does make
piercing observations of life and relates them in a humorous enough
manner that they don't encourage people to commit suicide or blow things
up.)
Hoffer is speaking of three 'succeeding' people while Vonnegut has three
people working as a 'team', or at the same time.  All of Vonnegut's team
would fall into Hoffer's catagory of "men of words".  Vonnegut then
distinquishes between the types of men of words necessary:1) genius or
original thinker, 2) one of public standing who will more or less
'second' the original thoughts as having validity, and 3)an explainer or
person with the common touch who can make new ideas understandable to
all.
I would think Vonnegut has very little use for fanatics and would
consider all men capable of action if properly motivated.  Hoffer sounds
like a recipe for violent revolution while Vonnegut sounds like a
revolution of the mind.  I think changing the way people think, honestly
and without deception, is the more effective and result oriented method.

Certainly, the above statement does exhibit some of TK's weaknesses.
Art appreciation is seldom limited to either leftist liberals or
rightest conservatives.  While liberals may be more open to change and
new forms of art when they first appear entire schools of art which
develop over many years are seldom established without broad-based
appreciation.
	I don't know what school of art TK was referring to above: Surrealism
and Cubism, to name only a couple, are also modern art. Perhaps this
lack of appreciation, or perhaps even ignorance, for art which has been
a relief from the stress of life for thousands of years all the way back
to cave drawings is one of the reasons TK went to the extremes he did.
This does not invalidate his thinking it only shows what can happen if
all of one's education is in math and science with no human relief.  TK
becomes an example of his own thesis: excessive reliance on science and
technology leads to self destruction.

On 1998-02-10 scrapie@rigel.cyberpass.net(scrapie) said:
 sc>Para 84:  "a surrogate activity that is directed toward an
 sc>artificial goal that the individual pursues for the sake of the
 sc>"fulfillment" that he gets from pursuing the goal, not because he
 sc>needs to attain the goal itself."
 sc>This is another great instance of projection, and it requires that
 sc>we accept his earlier assertions about the artificiality of goals
 sc>he doesn't himself approve of.
 sc>It's also interesting, to me at least, to contrast this with the
 sc>considerable body of thought, most clearly defined for me in
 sc>Buddhist teachings but present also in some Jewish and Christian
 sc>teachings, about the utility of recognizing that attaining goals,
 sc>ultimately, is never necessary - it's the act of pursuing them, and
 sc>the state of mind you're in while pursuing them, which
 sc>distinguishes you.
 sc>TK rejects that line of reasoning - and is in fact making a false
 sc>consciousness argument about it.  (To be fair, he's actually not
 sc>saying anything about state of mind when pursuing what he sees as
 sc>legitimate "power process" goals.)

 sc>Para 92:  This is interesting;  he essentially denies moral agency
 sc>to scientists.  A letter published this week in Nature from a group
 sc>of people working on the Convention on Biological Diversity points
 sc>out "Whether or not this protocol will provide for the
 sc>consideration of social and economic issues is as yet undecided."
 sc>This point is made critically - the authors of the letter are
 sc>imploring the larger community of scientists to make that
 sc>consideration an *explicit* goal because they recognize that as it
 sc>now stands, it is an *implicit* goal and they are required to
 sc>consider it but not voice their considerations.
 sc>They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social
 sc>implications" explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being
 sc>given an ethical agency, and that they need to be able to act on it
 sc>in the open.
 sc>In talking with people who I think have worked in what are to me
 sc>genuinely negative fields of research - weapons design at Lawrence
 sc>Livermore, for instance - I find that those who are directing and
 sc>actively engaged in the work are there because they think they are
 sc>doing the right thing for the country, even with all the risks
 sc>their work entails, and that by doing the right thing for the
 sc>country, they do the right thing for the world.  These people are
 sc>actively aware of and engaging their moral agency - in a direction
 sc>which I choose not to.
 sc>The people who seem unwilling to do so are bright people who act
 sc>more in support than in directing the work.  They see employment in
 sc>the field as ethically neutral, as just a legal job, and don't like
 sc>thinking about the costs and benefits of the work.

 sc>Para 96:  Concludes with:  "In order to get our message before the
 sc>public with some chance of making a lasting impression, we've had to
 sc>kill people."  I wonder if TK realizes the extent to which he's not

stalinist leftist types.
See 227 where Ted admits that "it is still far from clear what we mean
by the word "leftist". several surrounding paragraphs reflect the same
disclaimers. In one place he even leaves us the option of "you will have
to judge for yourself". this conciliatory approach is at odds with the
more forceful tone of other parts of the manifesto.

> Para 29:  Where does this line of reasoning extend to?  TK seems to be
> arguing that the scholastic and economic inequalities which were
> maintained for hundreds of years in the US between whites and blacks are
> somehow essential to the maintenance of blackness.

No, he is just debunking the superficial notion of a black culture which
mostly involves making Black folks good little cogs in the machine just
like white folks, only letting them have their rap music & soul food.
Perhaps there are things in genuine traditional *african* culture that
would be more desirable from Ted's point of view.


> The discussion of the "power process" - how much of this is accurate
> sociology, and how much of this is TK projecting what *he* felt about
> being distanced from the Noble Savage by Society onto everyone?

Most of it is the latter. I don't think that's a problem. I didn't read
the Manifesto expecting it to be a highly researched sociological tract
complete with boring surveys, statistics & footnotes. I've seen enough
of those unreadable things. The Manifesto is one writer's
*beliefs/opinions*--- and it is so much better than the abovementioned
dry, pseudo-objective socio-tracts that it reads like a bestseller by
comparison.

> 
> Para 61:  How much of this discussion of mere obedience at work can be
> read in light of what we now know about TK working at a job much like the
> one he's describing here but *working for his brother,* and being
> essentially ordered by his brother to stop treating one of his coworkers
> bizarrely?

Plenty of others have had jobs like that too. McDonalds, data entry,
graphics production. The other major category of work is Sales &
Management, where you have to do more than what you're told: you have to
CARE about the company's goals too. Oh, then there's jobs like nursing,
where you Can't do what you care about, because it's against doctor's
orders. (in my case, it means forcing poor suffering 95-year old
bedridden patients to stay alive & suffer, because of our
pseudo-compassionate "life"-valuing society... oops, I'm digressing.)

> Para 69:  TK should've tried visiting Africa before praising the
> "stoicness" in the face of the risk of disease.  

of course no one wants to die of a disease. I understand that in India
people know they can die from bathing in the polluted Ganges, but they
don't seem to care... the good karma from the holy river outweighs life
& death.

On the other hand, look at our society's fear of death & the lengths we
go to to deny disease. See above par. about nursing & look at how people
will stay at jobs they hate in order to retain insurance.

> 
> Para 73:  Communes have been attempted periodically to escape the
> pressures outlined in this paragraph.  Almost without exception, they've
> failed within a span of a very few years.  (And those communities which
> have succeeded in maintaining their identity base their rejection of
> society less on such mundane topics as who works for whom and why than
> they do on a deeply-held religious faith.)

Do a web search on the Twin Oaks community in Virginia. Twin Oaks has
been around for 30 years. It's a very successful commune and I think the
big appeal is the "work credit" system. People are required to work a
certain number of credits--an hour equals a credit, whether it's
management or dishwashing. This gets rid of hierarcy & inequality. They
can do a variety of chores at a variety of times. This gets rid of the
rigid   9-5 schedule that is so dehumanizing. Also, it's a small
community, so everyone is cooperating w/everyone else rather than
working for a big fat cat boss. 
I think it's a pretty good way of life myself, and I'd be there except
my family wouldn't want to move. 

[discussion of birthrate/anthropolgy snipped. I think these are
peripheral issues here. I'm not even sure why Ted included them. The
REAL point of the manifesto, in my opinion, starts at about par. 111.
"Tech. industrial society cannot be reformed">

> Para 84:  "a surrogate activity that is directed toward an artificial
> goal that the individual pursues for the sake of the "fulfillment" that
> he gets from pursuing the goal, not because he needs to attain the goal
> itself."
> 
> This is another great instance of projection, and it requires that we
> accept his earlier assertions about the artificiality of goals he doesn't
> himself approve of.

I can't argue with that. Everyone does this in their writing. It's kind
of a "Duhhh" thing. I hate woods-destroying bulldozers because *I* like
to hike in the woods. There's also the intellectual rationalization,
"trees create oxygen" but that's not what drives the emotion.

> Para 87:  The Motives of Scientists.  I found this section to be
> particularly weak.  I think that again, because of his isolation even
> when he was in an academic setting, he didn't give sufficient weight to
> the notion that there are people who really are just curious, and get a
> great deal of satisfaction from engaging that curiosity.

Here's where the projection is strongest. Don't forget, Ted was a
mathematician who was concerned with the behavior of circles &
lines--not the most interesting field of study.

> Also, I expect TK would suggest that examining the abundance of lead
> isotopes to study the age of the solar system is of no conceivable
> interest to anyone.  Yet the scientist who started that work at Caltech
> in the early 60's ultimately forced the oil companies and car companies
> to give up on using leaded gasoline because of the public health threat
> posed by lead settling from tailpipes.  It's sort of surprising to see
> someone with so much formal training who doesn't appreciate the odd turns
> which research can take.

Yeah, but in general Ted hates science. I'm sure he rightly despises the
Space Program. Which is where we always hear the argument about how pure
science always leads to useful commercial applications. Like Ted cares!

> Para 89:  The last sentence is a criticism of scientists' motives.
> However, those motives are just fine - exactly as TK states them - with a
> number of systems of belief:  being here, now, as Leary would encourage
> us - not focusing on the goal (as TK would urge us to) but on the
> journey.

I think Ted is missing something: the same abstract satisfaction a
scientist gets from solving a problem is what HE gets from doing a
carving (or maybe from making a bomb.)

> They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social implications"
> explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being given an ethical
> agency, and that they need to be able to act on it in the open.

some scientists may have protested unethical things like the H-Bomb, but
if they did, not enough people listened to them. At this point, if 10
scientists protest cloning and even got all the governments to ban it,
there's still another asshole who will do cloning in his basement. How
to prevent runaway science from creating disasters? by SMASHING SCIENCE,
that's how. Smash the Universities, terrorize or kill the scientists ,
destroy the factories and burn the technical books.

Now I'm not saying I would advocate such a thing... but when following
this line of reasoning, one finally understands what was going on in the
Unabomber's head when he sent bombs to universities. After all... that's
where science comes from, isn't it... from institutions of higher
learning. This is why he bombed professors as well as corporate execs. 

All that power process stuff seems to be window dressing to me. When
taking Ted's 1971 essay into account, it seems that what he fears is
runaway science & progress & what it has done and still may do to this
planet. If he hates science, the universities are the logical target.

You can say he is evil, unethical, etc... but illogical he ain't.
 
> Para 96:  Concludes with:  "In order to get our message before the
> public with some chance of making a lasting impression, we've had to
> kill people."  I wonder if TK realizes the extent to which he's not made
> a lasting impression, but has simply become another media commodity -
> even in the hands of some of his supporters.  Unapack sends a copy of the
> Manifesto out with every order of Unabomber goods they sell through their
> site - but I wonder how many of the buyers are pitching it and using the
> stickers merely for their admittedly quite good Situationist humor
> value?

Yup. I'm not sure I understand situationism... but I'm sure Lydia
realizes that any time you get someone to laugh at the system, you're
doing your little bit to undermine it. If the people are too lazy to
read the manifesto, I guess there's nothing you can do. unless you can
attach electrodes to their head & feed it in. :)

Thanks for posting this thoughtful essay. Next time, take one or 2
paragraphs. Unfortunately it's very hard for me to get computer time to
answer anything any longer. (I have at least 2 other computer users in
the family competing for time.)

--Shadow

body:
It's interesting that everyone agrees that fighting the Nazis was a good thing
to do, but some think that what TK has done is a bad thing. I firmly believe
that TK was fighting for a valid cause. But, let's leave aside the issue of
whether violence is justified, and look at some social comparisons.

TK discussed the breakdown of the family in  paragraph 51, "The breakdown of
traditional values to some extent implies the breakdown of the bonds that hold
together traditional small-scale groups...a technological society HAS TO weaken
family ties and local communities if it is to function efficiently. In modern
society an individual's loyalty must be first to the system and only
secondarily to a small-scale community, because if the internal loyalties of
small-scale communities were stronger than loyalty to the system, such
communities would pursue their own interests at the expense of the system." See
also footnote 7, and paragraph 50 which discusses the lip service given to
"family values".

Everyone has seen examples of this breakdown of the family.

One of the cornerstones of the Nazi regime was the Hitler youth. Its purpose
was to indoctrinate the youth to idolize Hiltler's "values". Families whose
children were not members were suspect. Families had to conform, with the
result that parents who were against Hitler's ideas were unable to pass those
values down to their children, and saw them become loyal Nazis. The family was
broken down, even as propaganda extolled the values of the good family.

I'll be interested to see the conclusions that are drawn.

body:
Ross wrote:

>sjj, you say you are in favor of unionism -- and are against 
>violence.  TK is *against* unionism and in favor of the destruction
>of industrial society.  It's not clear to me what ideas of TK's
>you support.  I expect he would not favor collective bargaining.
>

In fact, I never said I was in favor of unionism as it exists today. In an
argument about the air traffic controllers, I noted that many people today do
not have the opportunity to join unions. I asked how the air traffic
controllers' fight was different than the workplace battles many non-unionized
workers face. I never said that I found the current union system to be the
solution to the massive problems that corporate-industrial society has created.

In fact, I am in favor of the decline of the corporate industrial society. I
recall a time, not long ago, when it wasn't so invasive. I don't see that a
gradual return to a simpler lifestyle equates violence. I say it should be
gradual, because the state of our world got this way gradually, even though it
seems as if it happened overnight. It would be like the world going on a
"diet", not necessarily pleasant, but not a bad thing either, and for a very
positive goal.

TK stated in footnote 32, "It is even conceivable (remotely) that the
revolution might consist only of a massive change of attitudes toward
technology resulting in a relatively gradual and painless disintegration of the
industrial system..." I do admit that the possibilities of something more
devastating exist, but I think that my purpose is to find and work for the
easier solution, because I think that such a solution has a better chance of
being realized. In any case, most sane people will admit that the consequences
of our current trend will result in far greater devastation. Quite honestly,
the (human) world will probably not end in our lifetimes, but if the current
rate of growth and progress, (and human and environmental degradation)
continues,  it's not many generations off. And Ross, all those parks and golf
courses that you like will be sacrificed long before then.

In the face of the power of today's corporate power structure, the ability of
the individual to fight for himself is severely limited. I said, in the posting
you are refering to, that people who belong to a union have a little more power
against the corporate structure than the average person. I also bemoaned the
state of today's labor unions, which have become less representative of their
members and more representative of their leaders. In fact, I consider the
activists of the Hay Market Massacre to be much truer representatives of labor,
because these people were fighting for themselves, something I previously
posted on.

TK never said that people shouldn't fight for their rights. He did question the
motives of leftist groups, those engaged in struggles that personally had
nothing to do with them. I have less trouble with this portion of the manifesto
than some other people seem to have, because I have noticed that such types do
tend to be more concerned about the "having" of a battle than the actual goals.
So, in this sense, the current union structure is not much of a help, because
it has become part of the power structure. But I still cannot forget the labor
activities of the past, where the people concerned engaged in struggles for
their own rights. I am in favor of workers having their voices heard in battles
with the corporate rulership.

Of course, the corporate world has tightened its grip on society in the past
century, and have replaced governments as the real seats of power. There have
been so many buy-outs and consolidations of companies that it is impossible to
escape the corporate leadership of this world. Does this mean that ordinary
people should just sit back and take it?

I think that if people could feel that defending themselves sometimes works,
they will feel that their other goals could likewise meet with success. Many
people I talk to about various concerns of modern life seem more resigned to
rather than accepting of it. I don't think that the corporate lifestyle is
inevitable.

In the "Power Process" section, TK discussed the necessity for having goals. He
also said that it was necessary for people to attain some of their goals,
through their own struggle. Perhaps a successful fight against the corporate
world would enable people to tackle other personal battles. Many people relate
to the problems discussed in TK's book, even if they don't relate to its
author.

On your second point, I said that, like most people, I do not favor violence. I
never said that I didn't favor a radical solution, because I do. Radical and
violent are not synonyms.

I am encouraged by a new trend - increasingly popular books about living a
simpler life. This is a gentle kind of non-compliance that I find most
appealing. Titles such as "Inner Simplicity" and "Simplify Your Life" by Elaine
St. James, and "Simple Abundance - A Daybook of Comfort and Joy", by Sarah  Ban
Breathnach, preach the gospel of distinguishing between what you need, and what
you are told to want. They encourage people to stop recreational shopping, get
out of debt, don't watch too much TV, stop reading magazines (vehicles for
commercials), go to the library instead of buying books, etc. They also
encourage people to have fun, and not to do things they don't like. Quite the
opposite of the corporate message. These books are meant to be day by day
companions, not read at a shot, and then forgotten. Their message is that life
is too complicated but that you can do something to restore your tranquility.
Of course, if eveyone paid them heed, the consumer index would be in big
trouble. Ideas like these are a first step in a radical resistance at the level
of the people, which of course is what a grass-roots movement is.

There are also books about living a more self sustaining life-style, and
getting off the power grid. It does take a while for ideas to take root, but I
think we are just at the beginning. I am trying to spread the word that you can
be free, enjoy your life, connect to nature and live a happy life without
listening to or complying with the powers that be. I want people to know that
they can fight back.

I do not recall saying anything that was contrary to the basic ideas TK
expressed in "Industrial Society and its Future", but if I did, then I was just
building on them, and so much the better. TK hoped for a group of thoughtful
people to discuss the issues. It seemed to me that he realized the issues
deserved more thought than even one genius could provide. I don't think he
expected this thoughtful group of people to be "yes-men" to all of his ideas;
what's the point of a discussion in that case? I think this is why he expressed
doubts about some of his suggestions - it's a great strategy for getting
discussion going. His main concern is stated in the introductory paragraphs of
his book. The rest of it was a well argued, point following point, framework
for the discussion. That is what I want to be talking about!


Esjeje1@aol.com

There are several issues in this article. The jokes, the public's impression

As far as the jokes go, I don't think they mean much. There are jokes about

day. Truly mean spirited jokes don't raise laughter.

body:
Lauren,

I applaud your interest in this topic - the Unabomber story has so many
intriguing elements to it.

In the essay, "Industrial Society and its Future", aka the Unabomber Manifesto,
Ted Kaczynski makes a number of arguments to prove his point that "The
Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for the human
race". 

He argues that, to be happy, people need goals and some chance of attaining
their goals. They also need personal control over their own lives, which is
generally slipping away from people. He talks about the powerful industrial
technological society's role in breaking down the family. He also discusses the
feelings of purposelessness that people have in today's world, and the
consequences, such as addiction to things like drugs, TV, spending money you
don't have, which modern people use to get themselves through their lives.

You might want to use some of those themes, and tie them in with your
observations about people and things in the news. For example, a few months
ago, on 20/20 or 60 minutes or one of those, there was a segment about heroin
addiction amongst high school students in a well off town in Texas, and there
had been a rash of suicides there a few years earlier, which also made the
news. I wish I had more specific info.

In the "manifesto", look up paragraphs 37, 42, 50, 51, 66 and footnote 21, for
starters, although if you are going to take on this rather complicated theme,
there are many more related paragraphs.

Another intersting theme might be the way technology starts out as optional,
and then becomes necessary. You might want to explore the effects on the
environment, or on people. An example out of the manifesto relates to the
automobile. Most people didn't own one when they first came out, but now most
people couldn't do without one. We can get to travel much more than our
ancestors, but we also have air pollution, the stress of being in traffic every
day, and dangerous rude drivers to contend with. Another example is the built
in obsolecense of most products that we are encouraged to buy.  You might want
to think about other examples, and discuss those, and their effects. See
paragraph 127 of the manifesto.

There was also a section called, "The 'Bad' Parts of Technology Cannot be
Separated from the 'Good' Parts". How do you see the balance between the good
and bad parts of technology? I refer you to a Washington Post article about the
intrusion of database technology into people's lives. You might want to reflect
on this and other subjects that you can think of.

See paragraphs 121 - 124 of the manifesto, and 

http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/WPlate/1998-03/10/084l-031098-idx.html

Yet another idea - the difference between "freedom" and "permissiveness",
discussed in paragraphs 94 and 72, and elsewhere. What would life be like if
people people were truly free, instead of being granted "freedom" by some
power? How much real freedom do we have?

Of course, Dr. Kaczynski addressed many issues about modern life, which are all
related to each other, just like a spider web - touch one thread and it affects
another. But, that is life.

My last suggestion, if you haven't done so already, is read the manifesto. You
very well might find a topic there that you find more interesting than those I
suggested. You can find it all over the net.

Two other interesting sites (for starters, there are plenty of others) on some
background information you may want:

http://www.unabombertrial.com/
http://www.paranoia.com/unapack/

Hope this helped and Good Luck on your paper!


SJJ

  made life unfulfilling, have subjected human beings to indignities, have led

  suffering as well) and have inflicted severe damage on the natural world.
  The continued development of technology will worsen the situation.
  It will certainly subject human beings to greater indignities and inflict
  greater damage on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater social
  disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased physical
  suffering even in "advanced" countries.

2. The industrial-technological system may survive or it may break down. If it
survives, it MAY eventually achieve a low level of physical and psychological
suffering, but only after passing through a long and very painful period of
adjustment and only at the cost of permanently reducing human beings and many
other living organisms to engineered products and mere cogs in the social
machine.
  Furthermore, if the system survives, the consequences will be inevitable:
  There is no way of reforming or modifying the system so as to prevent it from

  revolution against that form of society. This is not to be a POLITICAL

body:
Industrial Society and the Future

The Power Process

33.  Human beings have a need (probably based in biology) for something that
we will call the "power process."
  This is closely related to the need for power (which is widely recognized)
  but is not quite the same thing.
  The power process has four elements.
  The three most clear-cut of these we call goal, effort and attainment of
  goal.
  (Everyone needs to have goals whose attainment requires effort, and needs to
  succeed in attaining at least some of his goals.)
  The fourth element is more difficult to define and may not be necessary for
  everyone.
  We call it autonomy and will discuss it later (paragraphs 42-44).

34.  Consider the hypothetical case of a man who can have anything he wants
just by wishing for it.
  Such a man has power, but he will develop serious psychological problems.
  At first he will have a lot of fun, but by and by he will become acutely
  bored and demoralized.
  Eventually he may become clinically depressed.
  History shows that leisured aristocracies tend to become decadent.
  This is not true of fighting aristocracies that have to struggle to
  maintain their power.
  But leisured, secure aristocracies that have no need to exert themselves
  usually become bored, hedonistic and demoralized, even though they have
  power.
  This shows that power is not enough.
  One must have goals toward which to exercise one's power.

35.  Everyone has goals; if nothing else, to obtain the physical necessities
of life: food, water and whatever clothing and shelter are made necessary by
the climate.
  But the leisured aristocrat obtains these things without effort.
  Hence his boredom and demoralization.

36.  Nonattainment of important goals results in death if the goals are
physical necessities, and in frustration if nonattainment of the goals is
compatible with survival.
  Consistent failure to attain goals throughout life results in defeatism, low
  self-esteem or depression.

37.  Thus, in order to avoid serious psychological problems, a human being
needs goals whose attainment requires effort, and he must have a reasonable
rate of success in attaining his goals.

To avoid this, a movement that exalts nature and opposes technology
> must take a resolutely anti-leftist stance and must avoid all
> collaboration with leftists

body:
> At any rate, I don't see how you could avoid ostracizing the majority if
> you're going to tell them that no, they're not happy to have their own
> cars, television sets, and ready supply of processed foods - and that, in
> fact, you think the entire system which makes these things possible needs
> to be dismantled, and that many of them and their children need to die.

That depends on who this "majority" is. Naturally all of us (even
myself) would not be *happy* to have my food supply yanked & my kids
slaughtered tomorrow. 
Plus I'm sure that you could go into an audience of ignorant imbeciles
(out of the movie Fahrenheit 451, let's say) and say "Hey, those
enviro's are coming to cart away your TV sets!!" and incite mass
hysteria.


Nevertheless a lot of people with even limited intelligence realize that
this planet is headed for big trouble. If we could see into the future &
realize that our overpopulation & exploitation are heading us toward the
brink... many of us would prefer to cut back on our luxuries and
conserve now. People have accepted "inconveniences" and "sacrifices"
already (recycling, vegetarianism, environmental laws). People have
accepted the necessity for change... and our "leaders" and capitalist
Daddies have lagged behind. (You'd think that by now someone would have
marketed alternative energy equipment with the same enthusiasm as they
have marketed the better mega-software package of the month.) I think a
lot of us would accept cultural alternatives that would cut down on our
auto dependence & power consumption... but that would require
cooperation, not our culture's present worship of me-first materialism &
greed.

They would probably be more accepting of the planetary ethos if not for
the competing ethos of the capitalists that says "ME FIRST" and "MORE"
and tells them that "those environmentalists are a bunch of left-wing
wackos who are stealing our rights".

> 214. To avoid this, a movement that exalts nature and opposes technology
> must take a resolutely anti-leftist stance and must avoid all
> collaboration with leftists.

This is one of Ted's big mistakes. There is ALREADY a movement that
exalts nature & opposes tech. It's called EARTH FIRST! and it is NOT
"leftist". If anything, it is "pagan". Earth First! has been fiercely
defending Nature (see my earlier messages about the Tree Sitters) and
that has nothing to do with "leftism". Ted needed to get a clue. I'd get
him a subscription to Earth First Journal if I thought they'ld let him
have it.

> This leaves him open, primarily, to rightist revolutionaries and pure
> anarchists as members of his cadre;  the latter are in relatively short
> supply compared to the former.
> 
> There's a very interesting group of people, primarily artists by vocation
> rather than political sorts, with a useful take on modern society which
> is neither left nor right.  These folks are known as the Situationists;
> they probably reached their apex of influence during the uprising in
> Paris in 1968. 

Thanks, I have always been curious about them. And I think their
successor today is UNAPACK. One might call them "quality of life"
anarchists or Luddites. And I think their number is much larger than you
think, they are just unaware & unorganized. They are the people who say
"turn off the TV and refuse to buy the products".
If all of these people could become conscious of themselves and become a
movement... we'd see some big changes. Perhaps that should be our goal. 

Which brings me back to the original subject of this post: Luddite
poetry. "Live your life as an act of rebellion!"

body:
Ted's take on morality is a bit confusing.

> 25.  The moral code of our society is so demanding that no one can think, feel
> and act in a completely moral way.
>   For example, we are not supposed to hate anyone, yet almost everyone hates
>   somebody at some time or other, whether he admits it to himself or not.

I'm not sure. Perhaps in the 50's there was a time when people were
never supposed to say anything bad about anyone. Particularly, women
were socialized to always be "nice". Now in the 90's people have
cultivated a culture of "sanctioned agression" (TV's favorite phrase is
"I'm gonna kick your ass!")

It is true that one cannot express "hate" along ethnic lines. LIkewise
among what Ted would call "leftists" and I would call "wishy-washy New
Agers", people can't express a "negative vibration". LIkewise in the
born-again Christian subculture, one simply can't express hate; one has
to put on a front of "forgiveness" and pray to be "delivered" from the
bad feelings.
So the question of hate/anger is far more complex than Ted's analysis.

>   Some people are so highly socialized that the attempt to think, feel and act
>   morally imposes a severe burden on them.
>   In order to avoid feelings of guilt, they continually have to deceive
>   themselves about their own motives and find moral explanations for feelings
>   and actions that in reality have a nonmoral origin.
>   We use the term "oversocialized" to describe such people.

This is definitely true among born again Christians & other spiritual
groups. I speak as a survivor of the former group!! In "mainstream"
society, one goes to a shrink to deal with guilt.
I wish Ted would elaborate on "feelings and actions that have a nonmoral
origin". Which feelings are those? Just about everything has a moral
basis. Unless he is talking about the simple struggle to survive. 

Morality is incredibly complex. A vegetarian decides that it is immoral
to buy into the worldwide factory farming of animals by consuming their
product. This person can still get plenty of food from the local market.
But a mountain hermit can shoot a squirrel to keep from starving & that
isn't an immoral act.

> 
> 26.  Oversocialization can lead to low self-esteem, a sense of powerlessness,
> defeatism, guilt, etc.
>   One of the most important means by which our society socializes children is
>   by making them feel ashamed of behavior or speech that is contrary to
>   society's expectations.
>   If this is overdone, or if a particular child is especially susceptible to
>   such feelings, he ends by feeling ashamed of HIMSELF.
>   Moreover the thought and the behavior of the oversocialized person are more
>   restricted by society's expectations than are those of the lightly
>   socialized person.
>   The majority of people engage in a significant amount of naughty behavior.
>   They lie, they commit petty thefts, they break traffic laws, they goof off
>   at work, they hate someone, they say spiteful things or they use some
>   underhanded trick to get ahead of the other guy.
>   The oversocialized person cannot do these things, or if he does do them he
>   generates in himself a sense of shame and self-hatred.
>   The oversocialized person cannot even experience, without guilt, thoughts
>   or feelings that are contrary to the accepted morality; he cannot think
>   "unclean" thoughts.
>   And socialization is not just a matter of morality; we are socialized to
>   conform to many norms of behavior that do not fall under the heading of
>   morality.
>   Thus the oversocialized person is kept on a psychological leash and spends
>   his life running on rails that society has laid down for him.
>   In many oversocialized people this results in a sense of constraint and
>   powerlessness that can be a severe hardship.
>   We suggest that oversocialization is among the more serious cruelties that
>   human beings inflict on one another.

I think the bigger problem isn't "morality", so much as simple
constraint on our every day lives. Society constrains us by the fact
that we are forced to spend an hour in a car every day, forced to spend
1/3 of our salary on insurance, forced to spend every day in a dank
office. And when we go home we are unable to find release in peaceful
natural surroundings, because the developers have destroyed every
vestige of nature and forced us to live in a concrete maze. We also
can't relax by going on a walk & meeting friends, because our culture
has so situated us physically & socially that such simple/natural
behavior is impossible.

So in theory we are very "free" in this society--free to write what we
want, free to open our own business or buy what we want, free to go to
the church of our choice, etc. But in reality we feel like rats running
on treadmills & have no clue how to get off.

The fact that we know we are "free" in theory causes us to be even more
frustrated and out of touch with our feelings; if we are dissatisfied,
we wonder "what's wrong with me??" and think of all those poor refugees
who would give anything to live as we do. And then we add "guilt" to the
rest of our frustration. Finally we can't stand it anymore & dull our
feelings by watching TV.
 
> 27.  We argue that a very important and influential segment of the modern left
> is oversocialized and that their oversocialization is of great importance in
> determining the direction of modern leftism.

Lose the "leftism" stuff, Ted, it's about EVERYONE in this society.
"Left" or "right" just refers to which targets you are going to blame
for the current mess.
The Left tends to blame those on top; the Right blames those on the
bottom.

> 
> 31.  We realize that many objections could be raised to the foregoing
> thumbnail sketch of leftist psychology.
>   The real situation is complex, and anything like a complete description of
>   it would take several volumes even if the necessary data were available.
>   We claim only to have indicated very roughly the two most important
>   tendencies in the psychology of modern leftism.

This is a passage that no one seems to have read. Everyone trumpets the
sound-bite that "Ted hates all leftists & is therefore a right-winger". 
Here Ted himself cautions that his analysis is incomplete & rough.

 
> 32.  The problems of the leftist are indicative of the problems of our society
> as a whole.

Here is another really important sentence.


>   The main reasons why these values have become, so to speak, the official
>   values of our society is that they are useful to the industrial
>   system. Violence is discouraged because it disrupts the functioning of the
>   system. Racism is discouraged because ethnic conflicts also disrupt the
>   system, and discrimination wastes the talent of minority-group members who
>   could be useful to the system. Poverty must be "cured" because the
>   underclass causes problems for the system and contact with the underclass
>   lowers the moral of the other classes. Women are encouraged to have careers
>   because their talents are useful to the system and, more importantly because
>   by having regular jobs women, become better integrated into the system and
>   tied directly to it rather than to their families. This helps to weaken
>   family solidarity. (The leaders of the system say they want to strengthen
>   the family, but they really mean is that they want the family to serve as
>   an effective tool for socializing children in accord with the needs of the
>   system. We argue in paragraphs 51,52 that the system cannot afford to let the
>   family or other small-scale social group be strong or autonomous.)

Here Ted speaks of "the system" as if it is a sinister "Lord Daddy
Lombrosis" who sits around scheming "hmmm, how can we brainwash &
enslave everyone?"
Which is where I disagree. Much as I LIKE to make "The System" into this
sort of evil scapegoat, I have to be intellectually honest & say that I
don't see this sort of sinister plotting happening--at least not yet. I
think attempts to help poor people, stop domestic violence etc. are
well-meaning attempts to improve the quality of life. Of course, when
the bureaucracy tries to legislate such areas of human behavior, they
generally bungle the effect and end up with the side effect of far too
much regimentation & control. "affirmative action" is a prime example.

And so ends today's scholarly manifesto analysis (collective sigh of
relief!)
--Shadow

body:
Ross wrote:

>Scott, on this general question of active courting, 
>consider TK in a gym class consisting solely of 
>revolutionaries who are willing to take active steps
>in destroying all industrial society.
>
>TK, in the role of coach, says: "Okay, all on the left politically, 
>step over here.  All on the right, step over here.  All you
>revolutionaries, who are apolitical, stay where you are.
>Now, you on the left, get out of here, we don't want you.
>
>How many apolitical revolutionaries do you think there are?
>Is that committed minority going to be apolitical?  

Paragraph 7, "But what is leftism? During the first half of the 20th century
leftism could have been practically identified as socialism. Today the movement
is more fragmented and it is not clear who can properly be called a
leftist...What we are trying to get at in discussing leftism is not so much a
movement or an idealogy as a psychological type..."

Paragraph 28, "...the left takes an accepted moral principle, adopts it as its
own, and then accuses mainstream society of violating that principle..."

Paragraph 29, "Here is an illustration of the way in which the oversocialized
leftist shows his real attachment to the conventional attitudes of our society
while pretending to be in rebellion against it..."

Paragraph 191, "One should think twice before encouraging any other social
conflict than that between the power holding elite (which wields technology)
and the general public (over which technology exerts its power)..."

I think that TK is using an untraditional definition of leftism that is very
different than the definition others here are using. Maybe he should have
coined a new word for his concept. The leftist, as defined by TK is attached to
the system, and is accusatory of the public; the revolutionary is supposed to
fight against the system without alienating the public.

Being concerned about the environment or the social problems described in the
manifesto does not automatically make one a leftist. Expecting society to do
something about it, or giving up your own power to a collective could qualify
you as such.

TK wasn't too kind to the conservatives either, which most people associate
with the right. He did call them fools, in paragraph 50, after all.

I'm not sure how political most people are - they are mainly concerned about
their own lives, not about the "right" or "left". TK wrote about things that
have provoked a great deal of personal soul searching, and that supercedes any
political label that one might attach to me or other such supporters. In this,
I don't think I'm unique.

body:
Esjeje!,

You make good points.  I'll quote another oft-cited passage on TK's
use of the term of "leftists" and then make some rambling comments.  

TK writes:
"When we speak of leftists in  this article we have in 
mind mainly socialists, collectivists, 'politically correct' 
types, feminists, gay and disability activists, animal rights 
activists and the like."

I think TK's use of the term is the common one.  And I think
his reaction to leftists is more Rush Limbaugh-like than
we realize.  He didn't get along with his parents because
of their politics.  Limbaugh characterizes leftists in terms
of their psychological type all the time.  That's part of the
standard ad hominem attack.  Just like leftists attack rightists as
selfish.  (They are, you know).

Note that a rightist and a leftist thinks conservatives are fools, not someone
who is apolitical.

TK felt that a long essay was necessary, lest the expression
of his ideas be imprecise.   But the truth is usually simpler than that.

Here, the notion of an apolitical revolutionary is misleading --
if you are a revolutionary you are extremely political (e.g.,
for example, opposed to all technology).  I once knew a great
guy who was focused solely on the threat of nuclear war (in 1984 at
Berkeley).  I don't know that his obsessive focus was any more or less valid
than TK's.  But like TK, he was very political.  Focus on a single 
issue doesn't make it apolitical.

Ross,

Now for some rambling thoughts of my own.

Well, we are both guilty of only quoting parts of paragraph 7. One part we both
left out is, "But not everyone who is associated with these movements is a
leftist."

So, I don't think that TK is necessarily against anyone connected with,
"socialists, collectivists, 'politically correct' types, feminists, gay and
disability activists, animal rights activists and the like."

It's not certain to me who TK would approve of as supporters, other than a
small group of thoughtful people, as he expressed hope for. I guess he saw a
contradiction between his description of "leftism" and thoughtfulness.

The other part of paragraph 7 that we both left out was, "Thus, what we mean by
"leftism" will emerge more clearly in the course of our discussion of leftist
psychology (Also, see paragraphs 227-230.)"

I have never listened to Rush Limbaugh, (and don't plan to either) so you may
have me there. I wouldn't disagree with you on rightists being selfish. We've
seen a bit of that in a series of postings from a stubborn capitalist a few
weeks ago.

I'm not sure why TK didn't get along with his parents. I have a feeling that it
was something more than their politics. Of course, rebelling against their very
public liberal politics might have done something for him, but other reasons
might exist for his ideas on "leftism". It's hard to say. Maybe he will clarify
this question in his next writings, since he did want the opportunity to rebut
any criticisms of his arguments.

I don't disagree that revolutionaries are political. I just wonder if "right"
and "left" are the only labels available for them.

not normal for human societies. There is good reason to believe that
primitive man suffered from less stress and frustration and was better
satisfied with his way of life than modern man is. It is true that not all was

We attribute the social and psychological problems of modern society to
the fact that that society requires people to live under conditions radically
different from those under which the human race evolved and to behave in ways
that conflict with the patterns of behavior that the human race developed
while living under the earlier conditions. It is clear from what we have
already written that we consider lack of opportunity to properly experience
the power process as the most important of the abnormal conditions to which
modern society subjects people. But it is not the only one. Before dealing
with disruption of the power process as a source of social problems we will
discuss some of the other sources

Among the abnormal conditions present in modern industrial society are
excessive density of population, isolation of man from nature, excessive
rapidity of social change and the break-down of natural small-scale
communities such as the extended family, the village or the tribe

It is well known that crowding increases stress and aggression. The degree
of crowding that exists today and the isolation of man from nature are
consequences of technological progress. All pre-industrial societies were
predominantly rural. The Industrial Revolution vastly increased the size of
cities and the proportion of the population that lives in them, and modern
agricultural technology has made it possible for the Earth to support a far
denser population than it ever did before. (Also, technology exacerbates the
effects of crowding because it puts increased disruptive powers in people's
hands. For example, a variety of noise-making devices: power mowers, radios,
motorcycles, etc. If the use of these devices is unrestricted, people who want
peace and quiet are frustrated by the noise. If their use is restricted,
people who use the devices are frustrated by the regulations. But if these
machines had never been invented there would have been no conflict and no
frustration generated by them

For primitive societies the natural world (which usually changes only
slowly) provided a stable framework and therefore a sense of security. In the
modern world it is human society that dominates nature rather than the other
way around, and modern society changes very rapidly owing to technological
change. Thus there is no stable framework

The conservatives are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional
values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and economic
growth. Apparently it never occurs to them that you can't make rapid, drastic
changes in the technology and the economy of a society without causing rapid
changes in all other aspects of the society as well, and that such rapid
changes inevitably break down traditional values

The breakdown of traditional values to some extent implies the breakdown
of the bonds that hold together traditional small-scale social groups. The
disintegration of small-scale social groups is also promoted by the fact that
modern conditions often require or tempt individuals to move to new locations,
separating themselves from their communities. Beyond that, a technological
society HAS TO weaken family ties and local communities if it is to function
efficiently. In modern society an individual's loyalty must be first to the
system and only secondarily to a small-scale community, because if the
internal loyalties of small-scale communities were stronger than loyalty to
the system, such communities would pursue their own advantage at the expense
of the system

Suppose that a public official or a corporation executive appoints his
cousin, his friend or his co-religionist to a position rather than appointing
the person best qualified for the job. He has permitted personal loyalty to
supersede his loyalty to the system, and that is "nepotism" or
"discrimination," both of which are terrible sins in modern society. Would-be
industrial societies that have done a poor job of subordinating personal or
local loyalties to loyalty to the system are usually very inefficient. (Look
at Latin America.) Thus an advanced industrial society can tolerate only those
small-scale communities that are emasculated, tamed and made into tools of the
system

Crowding, rapid change and the breakdown of communities have been widely
recognized as sources of social problems. But we do not believe they are
enough to account for the extent of the problems that are seen today

A few pre-industrial cities were very large and crowded, yet their
inhabitants do not seem to have suffered from psychological problems to the
same extent as modern man. In America today there still are uncrowded rural
areas, and we find there the same problems as in urban areas, though the
problems tend to be less acute in the rural areas. Thus crowding does not seem
to be the decisive factor

On the growing edge of the American frontier during the 19th century, the
mobility of the population probably broke down extended families and
small-scale social groups to at least the same extent as these are broken
down today. In fact, many nuclear families lived by choice in such isolation,
having no neighbors within several miles, that they belonged to no community
at all, yet they do not seem to have developed problems as a result

Furthermore, change in American frontier society was very rapid and deep.
A man might be born and raised in a log cabin, outside the reach of law and
order and fed largely on wild meat; and by the time he arrived at old age he
might be working at a regular job and living in an ordered community with
effective law enforcement. This was a deeper change

that which typically
occurs in the life of a modern individual, yet it does not seem to have led to
psychological problems. In fact, 19th century American society had an
optimistic and self-confident tone, quite unlike that of today's society

justified) that change is IMPOSED on him, whereas the 19th century
frontiersman had the sense (also largely justified) that he created change
himself, by his own choice. Thus a pioneer settled on a piece of land of his
own choosing and made it into a farm through his own effort. In those days an
entire county might have only a couple of hundred inhabitants and was a far
more isolated and autonomous entity than a modern county is. Hence the pioneer
farmer participated as a member of a relatively small group in the creation of
a new, ordered community. One may well question whether the creation of this
