only so long as they are outsiders and the technological system is
controlled by non-leftists. If leftism ever becomes dominant in society, so
that the technological system becomes a tool in the hands of leftists, they
will enthusiastically use it and promote its growth. In doing this they will
be repeating a pattern that leftism has shown again and again in the past.
When the Bolsheviks in Russia were outsiders, they vigorously opposed
censorship and the secret police, they advocated self-determination for
ethnic minorities, and so forth; but as soon as they came into power
themselves, they imposed a tighter censorship and created a more ruthless
secret police than any that had existed under the tsars, and they oppressed
ethnic minorities at least as much as the tsars had done. In the United
States, a couple of decades ago when leftists were a minority in our
universities, leftist professors were vigorous proponents of academic
freedom, but today, in those universities where leftists have become
dominant, they have shown themselves ready to take away from everyone else's
academic freedom. (This is "political correctness.") The same will happen
with leftists and technology: They will use it to oppress everyone else if
they ever get it under their own control.

 217. In earlier revolutions, leftists of the most power-hungry type,
repeatedly, have first cooperated with non-leftist revolutionaries, as well
as with leftists of a more libertarian inclination, and later have
double-crossed them to seize power for themselves. Robespierre did this in
the French Revolution, the Bolsheviks did it in the Russian Revolution, the
communists did it in Spain in 1938 and Castro and his followers did it in
Cuba. Given the past history of leftism, it would be utterly foolish for
non-leftist revolutionaries today to collaborate with leftists.

 218. Various thinkers have pointed out that leftism is a kind of religion.
Leftism is not a religion in the strict sense because leftist doctrine does
not postulate the existence of any supernatural being. But for the leftist,
leftism plays a psychological role much like that which religion plays for
some people. The leftist NEEDS to believe in leftism; it plays a vital role
in his psychological economy. His beliefs are not easily modified by logic
or facts. He has a deep conviction that leftism is morally Right with a
capital R, and that he has not only a right but a duty to impose leftist
morality on everyone. (However, many of the people we are referring to as
"leftists" do not think of themselves as leftists and would not describe
their system of beliefs as leftism. We use the term "leftism" because we
don't know of any better words to designate the spectrum of related creeds
that includes the feminist, gay rights, political correctness, etc.,
movements, and because these movements have a strong affinity with the old
left. See paragraphs 227-230.)

 219. Leftism is totalitarian force. Wherever leftism is in a position of
power it tends to invade every private corner and force every thought into a
leftist mold. In part this is because of the quasi-religious character of
leftism; everything contrary to leftists beliefs represents Sin. More
importantly, leftism is a totalitarian force because of the leftists' drive
for power. The leftist seeks to satisfy his need for power through
identification with a social movement and he tries to go through the power
process by helping to pursue and attain the goals of the movement (see
paragraph 83). But no matter how far the movement has gone in attaining its
goals the leftist is never satisfied, because his activism is a surrogate
activity (see paragraph 41). That is, the leftist's real motive is not to
attain the ostensible goals of leftism; in reality he is motivated by the
sense of power he gets from struggling for and then reaching a social
goal.[35]

 Consequently the leftist is never satisfied with the goals he has already
attained; his need for the power process leads him always to pursue some new
goal. The leftist wants equal opportunities for minorities. When that is
attained he insists on statistical equality of achievement by minorities.
And as long as anyone harbors in some corner of his mind a negative attitude
toward some minority, the leftist has to re-educated him. And ethnic
minorities are not enough; no one can be allowed to have a negative attitude
toward homosexuals, disabled people, fat people, old people, ugly people,
and on and on and on. It's not enough that the public should be informed
about the hazards of smoking; a warning has to be stamped on every package
of cigarettes. Then cigarette advertising has to be restricted if not
banned. The activists will never be satisfied until tobacco is outlawed, and
after that it will be alco hot then junk food, etc. Activists have fought
gross child abuse, which is reasonable. But now they want to stop all
spanking. When they have done that they will want to ban something else they
consider unwholesome, then another thing and then another. They will never
be satisfied until they have complete control over all child rearing
practices. And then they will move on to another cause.

220. Suppose you asked leftists to make a list of ALL the things that were
wrong with society, and then suppose you instituted EVERY social change that
they demanded. It is safe to say that within a couple of years the majority
of leftists would find something new to complain about, some new social
"evil" to correct because, once again, the leftist is motivated less by
distress at society's ills than by the need to satisfy his drive for power
by imposing his solutions on society.

221. Because of the restrictions placed on their thoughts and behavior by
their high level of socialization, many leftists of the over-socialized type
cannot pursue power in the ways that other people do. For them the drive for
power has only one morally acceptable outlet, and that is in the struggle to
impose their morality on everyone.

222. Leftists, especially those of the oversocialized type, are True
Believers in the sense of Eric Hoffer's book, "The True Believer." But not
all True Believers are of the same psychological type as leftists.
Presumably a truebelieving nazi, for instance is very different
psychologically from a truebelieving leftist. Because of their capacity for
single-minded devotion to a cause, True Believers are a useful, perhaps a
necessary, ingredient of any revolutionary movement. This presents a problem
with which we must admit we don't know how to deal. We aren't sure how to
harness the energies of the True Believer to a revolution against
technology. At present all we can say is that no True Believer will make a
safe recruit to the revolution unless his commitment is exclusively to the
destruction of technology. If he is committed also to another ideal, he may
want to use technology as a tool for pursuing that other ideal (see
paragraphs 220, 221).

 223. Some readers may say, "This stuff about leftism is a lot of crap. I
know John and Jane who are leftish types and they don't have all these
totalitarian tendencies." It's quite true that many leftists, possibly even
a numerical majority, are decent people who sincerely believe in tolerating
others' values (up to a point) and wouldn't want to use high-handed methods
to reach their social goals. Our remarks about leftism are not meant to
apply to every individual leftist but to describe the general character of
leftism as a movement. And the general character of a movement is not
necessarily determined by the numerical proportions of the various kinds of
people involved in the movement.

224. The people who rise to positions of power in leftist movements tend to
be leftists of the most power-hungry type because power-hungry people are
those who strive hardest to get into positions of power. Once the
power-hungry types have captured control of the movement, there are many
leftists of a gentler breed who inwardly disapprove of many of the actions
of the leaders, but cannot bring themselves to oppose them. They NEED their
faith in the movement, and because they cannot give up this faith they go
along with the leaders. True, SOME leftists do have the guts to oppose the
totalitarian tendencies that emerge, but they generally lose, because the
power-hungry types are better organized, are more ruthless and Machiavellian
and have taken care to build themselves a strong power base.

225. These phenomena appeared clearly in Russia and other countries that
were taken over by leftists. Similarly, before the breakdown of communism in
the USSR, leftish types in the West would seldom criticize that country. If
prodded they would admit that the USSR did many wrong things, but then they
would try to find excuses for the communists and begin talking about the
faults of the West. They always opposed Western military resistance to
communist aggression. Leftish types all over the world vigorously protested
the U.S. military action in Vietnam, but when the USSR invaded Afghanistan
they did nothing. Not that they approved of the Soviet actions; but because
of their leftist faith, they just couldn't bear to put themselves in
opposition to communism. Today, in those of our universities where
"political correctness" has become dominant, there are probably many leftish
types who privately disapprove of the suppression of academic freedom, but
they go along with it anyway.

226. Thus the fact that many individual leftists are personally mild and
fairly tolerant people by no means prevents leftism as a whole form having a
totalitarian tendency.

227. Our discussion of leftism has a serious weakness. It is still far from
clear what we mean by the word "leftist." There doesn't seem to be much we
can do about this. Today leftism is fragmented into a whole spectrum of
activist movements. Yet not all activist movements are leftist, and some
activist movements (e.g.., radical environmentalism) seem to include both
personalities of the leftist type and personalities of thoroughly un-leftist
types who ought to know better than to collaborate with leftists. Varieties
of leftists fade out gradually into varieties of non-leftists and we
ourselves would often be hard-pressed to decide whether a given individual
is or is not a leftist. To the extent that it is defined at all, our
conception of leftism is defined by the discussion of it that we have given
in this article, and we can only advise the reader to use his own judgment
in deciding who is a leftist.

228. But it will be helpful to list some criteria for diagnosing leftism.
These criteria cannot be applied in a cut and dried manner. Some individuals
may meet some of the criteria without being leftists, some leftists may not
meet any of the criteria. Again, you just have to use your judgment.

 229. The leftist is oriented toward largescale collectivism. He emphasizes
the duty of the individual to serve society and the duty of society to take
care of the individual. He has a negative attitude toward individualism. He
often takes a moralistic tone. He tends to be for gun control, for sex
education and other psychologically "enlightened" educational methods, for
planning, for affirmative action, for multiculturalism. He tends to identify
with victims. He tends to be against competition and against violence, but
he often finds excuses for those leftists who do commit violence. He is fond
of using the common catch-phrases of the left like "racism, " "sexism, "
"homophobia, " "capitalism," "imperialism," "neocolonialism " "genocide,"
"social change," "social justice," "social responsibility." Maybe the best
diagnostic trait of the leftist is his tendency to sympathize with the
following movements: feminism, gay rights, ethnic rights, disability rights,
animal rights political correctness. Anyone who strongly sympathizes with
ALL of these movements is almost certainly a leftist. [36]

230. The more dangerous leftists, that is, those who are most power-hungry,
are often characterized by arrogance or by a dogmatic approach to ideology.
However, the most dangerous leftists of all may be certain oversocialized
types who avoid irritating displays of aggressiveness and refrain from
advertising their leftism, but work quietly and unobtrusively to promote
collectivist values, "enlightened" psychological techniques for socializing
children, dependence of the individual on the system, and so forth. These
crypto-leftists (as we may call them) approximate certain bourgeois types as
far as practical action is concerned, but differ from them in psychology,
ideology and motivation. The ordinary bourgeois tries to bring people under
control of the system in order to protect his way of life, or he does so
simply because his attitudes are conventional. The crypto-leftist tries to
bring people under control of the system because he is a True Believer in a
collectivistic ideology. The crypto-leftist is differentiated from the
average leftist of the oversocialized type by the fact that his rebellious
impulse is weaker and he is more securely socialized. He is differentiated
from the ordinary well-socialized bourgeois by the fact that there is some
deep lack within him that makes it necessary for him to devote himself to a
cause and immerse himself in a collectivity. And maybe his (well-sublimated)
drive for power is stronger than that of the average bourgeois.

But not every leisured aristocrat becomes bored and demoralized. For
example, the emperor Hirohito, instead of sinking into decadent hedonism,
devoted himself to marine biology, a field in which he became distinguished.
When people do not have to exert themselves to satisfy their physical needs
they often set up artificial goals for themselves. In many cases they then
pursue these goals with the same energy and emotional involvement that they
otherwise would have put into the search for physical necessities. Thus the
aristocrats of the Roman Empire had their literary pretentions; many
European aristocrats a few centuries ago invested tremendous time and energy
in hunting, though they certainly didn't need the meat; other aristocracies
have competed for status through elaborate displays of wealth; and a few
aristocrats, like Hirohito, have turned to science

We use the term "surrogate activity" to designate an activity that is
directed toward an artificial goal that people set up for themselves merely
in order to have some goal to work toward, or let us say, merely for the
sake of the "fulfillment" that they get from pursuing the goal. Here is a
rule of thumb for the identification of surrogate activities. Given a person
who devotes much time and energy to the pursuit of goal X, ask yourself
this: If he had to devote most of his time and energy to satisfying his
biological needs, and if that effort required him to use his physical and
mental facilities in a varied and interesting way, would he feel seriously
deprived because he did not attain goal X? If the answer is no, then the
person's pursuit of a goal X is a surrogate activity. Hirohito's studies in
marine biology clearly constituted a surrogate activity, since it is pretty
certain that if Hirohito had had to spend his time working at interesting
non-scientific tasks in order to obtain the necessities of life, he would
not have felt deprived because he didn't know all about the anatomy and
life-cycles of marine animals. On the other hand the pursuit of sex and love
(for example) is not a surrogate activity, because most people, even if
their existence were otherwise satisfactory, would feel deprived if they
passed their lives without ever having a relationship with a member of the
opposite sex. (But pursuit of an excessive amount of sex, more than one
really needs, can be a surrogate activity

In modern industrial society only minimal effort is necessary to satisfy
one's physical needs. It is enough to go through a training program to
acquire some petty technical skill, then come to work on time and exert very
modest effort needed to hold a job. The only requirements are a moderate
amount of intelligence, and most of all, simple OBEDIENCE. If one has those,
society takes care of one from cradle to grave. (Yes, there is an underclass
that cannot take physical necessities for granted, but we are speaking here
of mainstream society.) Thus it is not surprising that modern society is
full of surrogate activities. These include scientific work, athletic
achievement, humanitarian work, artistic and literary creation, climbing the
corporate ladder, acquisition of money and material goods far beyond the
point at which they cease to give any additional physical satisfaction, and
social activism when it addresses issues that are not important for the
activist personally, as in the case of white activists who work for the
rights of nonwhite minorities. These are not always pure surrogate
activities, since for many people they may be motivated in part by needs
other than the need to have some goal to pursue. Scientific work may be
motivated in part by a drive for prestige, artistic creation by a need to
express feelings, militant social activism by hostility. But for most people
who pursue them, these activities are in large part surrogate activities.
For example, the majority of scientists will probably agree that the
"fulfillment" they get from their work is more important than the money and
prestige they earn

For many if not most people, surrogate activities are less satisfying
than the pursuit of real goals ( that is, goals that people would want to
attain even if their need for the power process were already fulfilled). One
indication of this is the fact that, in many or most cases, people who are
deeply involved in surrogate activities are never satisfied, never at rest.
Thus the money-maker constantly strives for more and more wealth. The
scientist no sooner solves one problem than he moves on to the next. The
long-distance runner drives himself to run always farther and faster. Many
people who pursue surrogate activities will say that they get far more
fulfillment from these activities than they do from the "mundane" business
of satisfying their biological needs, but that it is because in our society
the effort needed to satisfy the biological needs has been reduced to
triviality. More importantly, in our society people do not satisfy their
biological needs AUTONOMOUSLY but by functioning as parts of an immense
social machine. In contrast, people generally have a great deal of autonomy
in pursuing their surrogate activities. have a great deal of autonomy in
pursuing their surrogate activities

body:
Buried in the rest of the news this week, I found the following interesting:

"NPR's Peter Overby reports that dozens of corporate sponsors have contributed
eight million dollars to help defray the cost of hosting the NATO summit. The
U.S. government is paying the rest of the bill -- 15 million dollars. The
companies have given cash, goods and services for the right to be called the
"NATO Host Committee." Critics say the U.S. is selling access to government
officials. "

http://www.npr.org/ramfiles/me/19990423.me.05.ram

"("We live in a world in which relatively few people - maybe 500 or 1,000 -
make the important decisions" - Philip B. Heymann of Harvard Law School, quoted
by Anthony Lewis, New York Times, April 21, 1995.)" Quoted by TK in para. 67 of
ISAIF.

I'm just waiting to see the commercials - "Official Sponsor of the NATO Summit"
or some such... $8million seems like such a drop in the bucket, compared to
talks of $10 billion or so as a proposed contribution to the NATO "action" in
Kosovo. I wonder whose great idea this was? Is it possible that campaign
finance reform is just getting to be a bit too popular of an issue? Is this a
sign of things to come, a way around what CFR is supposed to accomplish?

-Susan

For the record, I believe everyone is entitled to their beliefs.  What I
don't appreciate are hypocritical smears and intimidation.  People should be
able to express their views without apprehension that they might say the
wrong thing.

That said, I think it's great that David Duke is running for Congress.  I
don't like him personally, but at least he is something different.  I would
be just as pleased to see a Marxist or socialist running for Congress, to be
honest.  I want to see diversity.  I yearn for the days of nationalism,
especially.  Centrism spoils the party when there is too much of it.  Some
may argue that it brings stability to the nation, but let's face it, there
are some consequences.  (Well, that's another topic.)

I don't appreciate the clustering of me with David Duke.  Of course, it's
inevitable given the shift to the left that has occured since the '60s.
Anything that is different is bound to be labelled an -ist something, either
implicitly or explicitly.  But that's okay, I've gotten used to it, plus
those lame pejoratives have lost the sting they once had! ;o)

I'm also sick of crackers like that lady on Newsweek who contributes for the
McGlaughlin Group on PBS, who spew centrist, liberal, do-gooder garbage.  I
can just imagine the suburban house she lives in; it's gotta be huge!  It
takes someone who's really good at not offending anyone to make it as far
within the media as she has, I would guess (maybe I'm wrong, oh well, just
intuition.)

Getting back to the topic, I hate the KKK.  They are illiterate and have
absolutely NO class.  Basically, what they do is carry around Bibles and use
their religion to condone racism (or whatever else they believe.. incest?).
I am atheist; they think I'm going to hell.

David Duke and his degenerate, freckled face, barbarian-descended clones
wouldn't last a day in Madrid or Barcelona.  The Falangists would easily
kick their pale asses, and drive them to the Pyrenees!  Anti-Catholic punks.
Those people need to learn some history.  If it wasn't for the Roman emperor
Constantine there wouldn't even be any protestant sects.  People would still
be pagans, I suppose.

Why?  It's exactly the same logic as in the presentation of the DNA
evidence.  There's no sequence data in Turchie, only a statement that the
DNA known to originate with Ted puts him in a group which could have sent
the FC documents to Tyler - and that group is quite large, 1 to 5 % of the
total population.  

Honestly, if the DNA workup had been admitted on the simpler inclusionary
logic, but the cake phrase had been obliged by the legal system to be held
up - at least rhetorically - as a unique and probative usage, I'd be
worried about how flummoxed anyone in a white coat could make someone
wearing the more traditional black robe...  

> Instead, in both of Douglas' books and the Turchie affidavit, it was 
>represented as a mistake, peculiar -- unique -- to TK and the Unabomber 
>(albeit in a single-sentence paragraph).   (My view, btw, is that there clearly 
>was probable cause in search of the cabin).  

I disagree on how Turchie presented it, unless there's a second invocation
I missed:  

199. In paragraph 185 of the UNABOM Manuscript (Attachment 2), it is stated
"...well, you can't eat your cake and have it too." In a letter signed by
Theodore Kaczynski, to his mother Wanda  Kaczynski, date unknown, Theodore
Kaczynski compares "... the increase in the complexity of our social
organization that actually make necessary the erosion of privacy and
freedom. We will be sacrificing some of the materialistic benefits of
technology, but  there just isn't any other way. We can't eat our cake and
have it  too."

200. It is noted by your affiant that the common use English  Language
phrase is, "You can't have your cake and eat it too!"

This was the only mention I could find of the phrase in Turchie, and in
context, para 200 is less important than the similarity in the longer
passage in para 199 with elements of ISAIF's reasoning.  

>I mainly mean to criticize Mr. Douglas, as this sort of "profiling"
>is his field of expertise.  What's the point of such analysis if it's just flat
>wrong?  More importantly, why is he including it in a second book many months
>after the point has been widely made, including in a defense brief?

It does remain an uncommon usage.  I haven't read Douglas so I don't know
what kind of hay he's making with it.  

In general, the Turchie presentation of the textual similarities is pretty
complicated, and a lot of it relies on material that I don't think is back
in the public domain - letters from Ted to David and Wanda.  So we're left
focused on material that is public, and the media were frequently
presenting the simplest possible explanations of what was being done in
Turchie's presentation.  The "cake" phrase is one that could be seized on
as it was simple to explain and uncommon.  

A nugget I hadn't caught before in the affidavit:  

204. Your affiant is aware that other individuals have conducted analyses
of the UNABOM Manuscript [_redaction_] determined that the Manuscript was
written by another individual, not Theodore Kaczynski, who had also been a
suspect in the investigation.

Boy, I'd love to know what was redacted there.  It certainly sounds as if
the FBI had access to stuff written by someone else who was a good
candidate for the writing, but not for the sending.  A lot of Turchie
devotes itself to establishing that Ted could have mailed or placed the
devices on the relevant dates - and presumably their "other individual"
wasn't a viable suspect to them based on their assumptions that 

a) FC was in fact just one person, not a member of any group and

b) their "other individual" could not have mailed or placed documents or
bombs on at least some of the relevant dates.  

-Peter

Prisoner Rape, and described his experience behind bars after being arrested
for protesting the Vietnam War.  Well, the ACLU, left wing activists, and
friends of his have made him into a hero.  Well, I think he was a punk --
and nothing more than that.

I think the heroes were those brave soldiers who fought and died for our
country.  I certainly didn't agree with the war, didn't agree with some of
our tactics, but damn it, those kids didn't want to be there; they risked
their lives for our country.  Yes, the puppet government we supported in
South Vietnam was corrupt, and communist sympathy there was pervasive.  But
look at what happened as soon as we deserted the effort: 8 million South
Vietnamese fled into exile and 200,000 died in the seas, wanting to escape
Communist oppression.

The average age of our troops was 19; these were kids!  At one point 100
were dying a day.  What was Jane Fonda doing?  Sitting on her fat leftist
arse reaping the rewards of capitalism and waving a Viet Cong flag while
they were fighting and dying.  Bitches like her make me sick; I WANT HER TO
FUCKING DIE.  I saw the public broadcasting special "Dear America: Letters
from Vietnam" and was deeply inspired, I felt pride in our country, right or
wrong I admired to valor of the soldiers.  And I wasn't even born yet during
the war.

To think of those cowardly reprobates, being priveleged college kids who
evaded the draft, spitting on our soldiers (many of whom were black and
hispanic) upon their return makes me sick.

Stephen Donaldson was not a hero, he was a punk.  A weak suburban white
punk.

It was easy for him to protest a war, but would he have been willing to
fight and die for anything?  Well, one thing I know for sure, he wasn't
willing to fight for his manhood while he was incarcerated.  He was
repeatedly raped behind bars, unwilling or unable to at least ATTEMPT to
defend himself.  Moreover, while he was getting violated he felt that he was
paying for the sins of society; he felt he deserved it!

Here he shows his self-hate and mental weakness:

"There were times when I felt like I was paying for all the sins of the
white race."

Here he describes the racially seething atmosphere in prison:

"Some guys were really, ah, were really rough, and they'd make racial
comments, for example, 'Your ass belongs to the black man. Don't you ever
forget it.'  Stuff like that, you know."

I think there are many more Steven Donaldson's in our society; Ted Kaczynski
described it as a disease.  TK took a major detour in the beginning of the
Manifesto just to talk about it.  These types are sheep; they will rarely,
if ever, challenge any fundamental beliefs of society but will latch onto
already accepted beliefs and gripe about people not following them enough.
They will do this under ANY system because they not only blithely follow the
the status quo, but worse, they are oversocialized COWARDS.

Being politically correct is NOT REBELLIOUS; it is conformity.  It is
fighting to preserve and enforce values which are already ingrained in our
society.

Author: Pyro <Valderrey@email.msn.com>
Date: 1999/07/27

> Enough of the blather.  We know what political correctness is, and
> those who vehemently deny its existance even moreso.  Political
> correctness is presuming that you are "automatically right" because
> your opinion or view holds greater emotional appeal than your
> counterparts.  The politically correct elite have also instilled
> within the public the notion, that those who challenge the core
> beliefs that they propagate are evil, wicked, and have comitted SIN.

   Yes, this paragraph seems agreeable until you reach the last few
 words.  It would be an overstatement to claim that such elements as
 "evil" and "sin" are fictions propagated by a "politically correct
 elite" and/or -only- by them.  Ridding ourselves of such "politically
 correct elite" would not eliminate "sin" but instead wreck havoc on
 attempts to discern what such terms could mean.  Someone's claim of a
 word without meaning (for them) doesn't invalidate another's search for
 meaning, and if "evil" or "sin" really don't have meaning then there'd
 be nothing lost if that putative "absense of meaning" were re-verified.
 The existence of manipulative propaganda on the part of a media elite
 doesn't disprove an underlying reality which may or may not conform to
 their highly questionable and not-so-sublimated subliminal agenda.

   It may, furthermore, be critical to take cognizance of the fact that
 when stating "... _we_know_ what political correctness is..." there is
 still nothing implied which asserts the knowledge as being -coherent-,
 i.e. the definition applied by one individual may not necessarily be
 in correspondence with another's definition, because each individual
 might independently assert personal claims to a certain aspect of PC.
 Thereby, something is intrinsically faulty when abiding in "knowledge"
 traced to inherent solipsism. (see: _Personal_Identity_, J.Perry, ed)


> _Politically_Incorrect_ is not a forum for vigorous discussion.  The
> show is a front for the elites to say, "you see, PC really is a joke,
> and we can talk about all issues openly." The reality is, the more
> serious issues involving politically correct repression are not dealt
> with on the show.

    Also much agreement here:  do viewers take note of that show's
  frequent commercial interruptions?    :-)  :-)  :-)


> Larry King clever? Yes, clever for having a closet PC'er pretending
> to be representative of the masses of repressed non-PC'ers, and being
> able to shut down the opposition with their superficial, tendentious
> discourse.

    Ah yes, and clever because Larry King is unabashedly PC.


> Science requires objectivity.  We can theorize all that we want, can
> even come to believe that dinosaurs and humans lived side by side, but
> that does not change reality.  Of course, PC'ers can continue to
> believe that blacks, whites, and Asians have _equal_ intellectual
> potential, that they all have _equal_ athletic ability, that whites
> can be great pugilists too, but blacks have succeeded
> disproportionately simply because they tried harder, having been
> been excluded from the professions.

    Group inequalities are stipulated herein, but unless you're willing
  to dispute _Brown_vs._Board_of_Education_ (1954), a legal precendent
  exists which asserts economic benefit to the nation via desegregation.


> But when PC'ers begin to impede on the rights on non-PC'ers I am going
> to raise a fuss.  When the head of the psychology department at the
> University of Delaware tells Linda Gottfredson that she cannot receive
> funds to study innate differences among the races because it is
> "racist", someone has to blow the horn.  PC'ers can believe in the
> tooth fairy for all I care, but when they work on hindering the rights
> of people who seek the truth, when it happens to conflict with their
> fairy-tale utopic vision, I will have to protest.

   I admit to some confusion here.  Weren't you about to posit a claim
 that racial differences had already been established, and sufficient
 evidence already published?  If so, why the additional duplication from
 Ms. Gottfredson?  I thought affirmative action programs were premised
 upon acceptance of racial variations, even as terms of "race/ethnicity"
 aren't clearly defined (example: "Caucasians" can claim 'black' ethnic
 affiliation if disadvantaged by being raised within a black ghetto).

   Next, you've provided a characterization of what the term "PC" might
 entail, in "presuming one is automatically right," yet while you do
 that you are nonetheless quick on the draw to assert "rights" without
 any documentation in law literature, e.g. "rights of non-PC'ers" who by
 definition, were -absent- any statement of being "automatically right."
 Perhaps we'll need to sharpen our discussion on this point:  the First
 Amendment Right is not constructed upon analysis of whether someone is
 or is not "PC" but upon constitutional rights of minorities against an
 unjust oppression by the majority.  A "PC" attribute might not fall so
 neatly along the lines of being or not being a member of a minority or
 the majority, particularly in context to where boundary gerrymandering
 was drawn, from which the notions of "minority/majority" got extracted.

   If we're to run with a notion that "non-PC'ers" are not automatically
 right then it's incumbent upon "non-PC'ers" to sustain their burden of
 proof at each step in the argument, a burden they should be eager and
 -willing- to obtain since "not being automatically right" was their
 existential condition, according to your provided characterization.


> I was merely pointing out that we all have innate tendencies which
> influence how we end up, the ideas we come to accept. It is well known
> among psychologists that "liberals" and "conservatives" _think_
> differently. That's not to say we have absolutely no free will, or
> ability to drastically change our core beliefs. I am just pointing out
> that, in my opinion, genetics may play a role in influencing the
> belief system we come to accept. Capiche?

    If you'd say that "ability to drastically change our core beliefs"
  is also an "innate tendency" then the "innate tendencies" are not
  immutable, even without genetic mutation and genetic bioengineering.
  First you're asserting (as fact?) that "we all have innate tendencies
  which influence how we end up..." but later you state this as simply
  your "opinion" so which case is it going to be?


<< Was TK a fascist? >>
> Honestly, I don't think so.  But I believe he has tendencies toward
> fascism. I believe he has even contacted Dr. Pierce in the past.

    Yet TK's manifesto specifically invokes "non-political revolution."
  How could he possibly be a (political) fascist?

         "4. We therefore advocate a revolution against the industrial
         system.  This revolution may or may not make use of violence:
         it may be sudden or it may be a relatively gradual process
         spanning a few decades. We can't predict any of that. But we
         do outline in a very general way the measures that those who
         hate the industrial system should take in order to prepare the
         way for a revolution against that form of society. This is not
         to be a POLITICAL revolution. Its object will be to overthrow
         not governments but the economic and technological basis of
         the present society."


> << I think you'll need to restart your analytical engine: opposition
> to High-Technology is an opposition to fascism, and opposition to all
> forms of social controls so popular with fascists that were enabled
> by means of High-Technological spying and privacy infringements. >>

> Oh, please. Ask the Polish who were more oppressive: the communists or
> fascists? I have an uncle who left socialist Cuba to fascist Spain,
> and came to admire Generalissimo Franco.  Now before you spew a
> bromidic retort, he happens to be married to a woman who is part
> black, and has no feelings of racism.  He also has 4 degrees.

  Fine -- now here's the bromidic retort as expected:

    Any totalitarian state can be serviced by that High-Technology TK
  identifies as their core means of asserting social controls over the
  masses, from the left or right.  The fact that your uncle who was not
  documented in Poland, nor in TK's manifesto, and has no necessary
  bearing upon your own views nor upon this exchange, admired defunct
  facists from a safe distance, has a trophy wife by way of chic racial
  tokenism, and allows you brief non-racist respite coupled with that
  obvious inspiration toward sheepskin appropriation and other sundry
  "golden fleece" awards, says nothing about the itemized sub-point to
  this particular thread, i.e. opposition to fascism (a special case of
  totalitarian regimes in general) follows from opposition to forms of
  High-Technological encroachment upon imaginative freedoms.

         "... But what kind of freedom does one have if one can use it
         only as someone else prescribes? FC's conception of freedom is
         not that of Bolivar, Hu, Chang or other bourgeois theorists.
         The trouble with such theorists is that they have made the
         development and application of social theories their surrogate
         activity. Consequently the theories are designed to serve the
         needs of the theorists more than the needs of any people who
         may be unlucky enough to live in a society on which the
         theories are imposed."

  Conservatives do not improve upon that quest for freedom by "the
  average individual" because they simply promote "the power of Big
  Business" by whipping up resentment against "Big Government" --

         "13. (Paragraph 66) Conservatives' efforts to decrease the
         amount of government regulation are of little benefit to the
         average man. For one thing, only a fraction of the regulations
         can be eliminated because most regulations are necessary. For
         another thing, most of the deregulation affects business
         rather than the average individual, so that its main effect is
         to take power from the government and give it to private
         corporations. What this means for the average man is that
         government interference in his life is replaced by
         interference from big corporations, which may be permitted,
         for example, to dump more chemicals that get into his water
         supply and give him cancer. The conservatives are just taking
         the average man for a sucker, exploiting his resentment of Big
         Government to promote the power of Big Business."


> << TK's demolition of the right is much harsher than his supposed
> (ironic) "literary criticism" of left-leftism. >>

> You have absolutely no clue. TK spent a great portion of the Manifesto
> bashing political correctness and leftism.  He bashed people like you,
> who enjoy playing semantics and spewing superfluous drivel rather than
> to cut to the issues.  The one measly sentence in which he referred to
> conservatives as "fools" has given trolls like you justification for
> pretending he was leftist all along.  The real world isn't black and
> white, you know.

     He said the revolution he advocates is -similar- to the French and
   Russian revolutions, which each were leftist:

         "181. As we stated in paragraph 166, the two main tasks for
         the present are to promote social stress and instability in
         industrial society and to develop and propagate an ideology
         that opposes technology and the industrial system. When the
         system becomes sufficiently stressed and unstable, a
         revolution against technology may be possible. The pattern
         would be similar to that of the French and Russian
         Revolutions. French society and Russian society, for several
         decades prior to their respective revolutions, showed
         increasing signs of stress and weakness. Meanwhile, ideologies
         were being developed that offered a new world view that was
         quite different from the old one. In the Russian case,
         revolutionaries were actively working to undermine the old
         order. Then, when the old system was put under sufficient
         additional stress (by financial crisis in France, by military
         defeat in Russia) it was swept away by revolution. What we
         propose in something along the same lines."


     He mentioned that "true believers" of either form -- leftists or
   (rightwing) nazis -- presented "a problem" and would not "make a
   safe recruit to the revolution" particularly if he is "committed
   also to _another_ ideal" (such as some racially eugenic agenda):

         "222. Leftists, especially those of the oversocialized type,
         are True Believers in the sense of Eric Hoffer's book, "The
         True Believer." But not all True Believers are of the same
         psychological type as leftists.  Presumably a truebelieving
         nazi, for instance is very different psychologically from a
         truebelieving leftist. Because of their capacity for
         single-minded devotion to a cause, True Believers are a
         useful, perhaps a necessary, ingredient of any revolutionary
         movement.  This presents a problem with which we must admit we
         don't know how to deal. We aren't sure how to harness the
         energies of the True Believer to a revolution against
         technology. At present all we can say is that no True Believer
         will make a safe recruit to the revolution unless his
         commitment is exclusively to the destruction of technology. If
         he is committed also to another ideal, he may want to use
         technology as a tool for pursuing that other ideal (see
         paragraphs 220, 221)."


     He's clearly opposed to "eugenics" because that would amount to an
   unnatural "manufactured product," additional "government regulation,"
   and the (arbitrary) imposition of "medical ethics" determined by some
   'elite' scientific soviet, or "needs of the industrial-technological
   system."  So TK would thereby be opposed to racial goals concurrent
   with either "eugenic" or "dis-eugenic" agendas:

         "122. Even if medical progress could be maintained without the
         rest of the technological system, it would by itself bring
         certain evils.  Suppose for example that a cure for diabetes
         is discovered. People with a genetic tendency to diabetes will
         then be able to survive and reproduce as well as anyone else.
         Natural selection against genes for diabetes will cease and
         such genes will spread throughout the population. (This may be
         occurring to some extent already, since diabetes, while not
         curable, can be controlled through the use of insulin.) The
         same thing will happen with many other diseases susceptibility
         to which is affected by genetic degradation of the population.
         The only solution will be some sort of eugenics program or
         extensive genetic engineering of human beings, so that man in
         the future will no longer be a creation of nature, or of
         chance, or of God (depending on your religious or
         philosophical opinions), but a manufactured product.

         "123. If you think that big government interferes in your life
         too much NOW, just wait till the government starts regulating
         the genetic constitution of your children. Such regulation
         will inevitably follow the introduction of genetic engineering
         of human beings, because the consequences of unregulated
         genetic engineering would be disastrous.  [19]

         "124. The usual response to such concerns is to talk about
         'medical ethics.' But a code of ethics would not serve to
         protect freedom in the face of medical progress; it would only
         make matters worse. A code of ethics applicable to genetic
         engineering would be in effect a means of regulating the
         genetic constitution of human beings.  Somebody (probably the
         upper-middle class, mostly) would decide that such and such
         applications of genetic engineering were "ethical" and others
         were not, so that in effect they would be imposing their own
         values on the genetic constitution of the population at large.
         Even if a code of ethics were chosen on a completely
         democratic basis, the majority would be imposing their own
         values on any minorities who might have a different idea of
         what constituted an "ethical" use of genetic engineering. The
         only code of ethics that would truly protect freedom would be
         one that prohibited ANY genetic engineering of human beings,
         and you can be sure that no such code will ever be applied in
         a technological society. No code that reduced genetic
         engineering to a minor role could stand up for long, because
         the temptation presented by the immense power of biotechnology
         would be irresistible, especially since to the majority of
         people many of its applications will seem obviously and
         unequivocally good (eliminating physical and mental diseases,
         giving people the abilities they need to get along in today's
         world). Inevitably, genetic engineering will be used
         extensively, but only in ways consistent with the needs of the
         industrial-technological system. [20]"

   So we're not dealing with "one measly sentence" but a constellation
 of antipathies attached to the prospect of right-wing fascism.  Even
 if the "real world" isn't Black and White, TK's manifesto asks of the
 reader to consider the portion that might be, or is.


> (re:  "feeble" minds)
> I think many of these people have the _potential_ to think for
> themselves, to widen their intellectual horizons, but for whatever
> reason(s) have not reached their full potential.

    Ok, that was another diagnosis, now what is your proposal?


> << How can you be certain that McCarthyism lasted only a few years?
> More likely the same McCarthyism was driven underground and sublimated
> into a corrosive litmus-test of politically "correct/incorrect," eh?
>>

> Oh, please, is being called a "commie" really as devastating as being
> called a racist, today? Do you remember the OJ Simpson trial? Saying
> "nigger" became worse than committing a murder.  Mike Tyson has a
> tattoo of Mao Tse-tung on his arm, yet no one says anything.  Imagine
> if a white boxer had a tattoo of Adolf Hitler or Mussolini.  What a
> fuss the PC'ers would make! By all accounts Mao is responsible for
> more civilian deaths than Hitler and Mussolini combined.  But, oh
> yeah, those Chinese landowners and peasants were not God's Chosen,
> so they don't count.

     Trying to follow your tenous "thread" of logic:  were you saying
  that being called a "commie" -should- be more devastating in light of
  uncontested accounts?  So McCarthyism still simmers on your burner?
  I think that was my point exactly.


> (re: "hatred" towards mother-killers)
> You need to get a clue.  I implied, if this individual cared for his
> mother to any infinitesimal degree, manifesting hatred towards the
> killer would have been a sign of health.

     Even if "hatred" for the sinner, rather than the sin, were to
   improve your effective response, why would we need to spell out a
   "_right_ to hate" using formal legalistic terms?  Does one require
   non-specific "right" in order to manifest hatred?  Seems to me an
   oxymoron and _non-sequitur_.  Hate exists even without "rights."


> << Alright, let's go there. How many "races" are there? On what
> source of information did you base your assessment? What of the
> prospect and evidence of interbreeding? When is "racial purity"
> achieved if Hitler was 25% Jewish? >>

> Rationalization.  Funny, people like you who are eager to deny the
> existence of race are usually the most race conscious.  One guy who
> was arguing with me over the existence/non-existence of race, had his
> handle as "Sixftblkman".  Another would repeatedly refer to whites as
> "crackers."

    These are strawmen.  I don't deny the existence of race, nor of
  implicit racism which follows from racial distinctions.  Even the
  notion of being "color-blind" implies some "colorization" out there
  from which one is assuming deliberate blindness.  My difficulty
  occurs when I'm trying to resolve all cases of people into what may
  seem to be rather arbitrary and -temporal- indicators of racial
  distinction.  There seem to be increasing numbers that do not fit
  nicely into their proper pigeonholes, so the "race" concept is not
  a well-formed notion.  The web-link you've provided also sources
  other documents that more precisely target a "Bayesian statistical
  analysis" of racial phenotype differences.  However, as an employer
  I'd be presented with an individual who was not considered in the
  cited study, and furthermore the impacted minorities who follow up
  such studies are likely to take pains to obliterate former conceptual
  categories, so that the former divisiveness instead becomes blurred.
  For example, if someone is criticized as "not being sufficiently
  educated" in a certain context (an IQ-test) they may 'retaliate' by
  educating themselves in that manner so as to satisfy the requirements
  and diminish the validity of former findings.  So today we have many
  minority lawyers, doctors, engineers, computer programmers, and Chess
  players.  Unless you're prepared to defeat Grandmaster Maurice Ashley
  at Chess, I don't think you've got a strong argument on the IQ-side.

    However, the IQ-test argument was itself premised upon whether a
  given individual, or class of individuals, finds some means of "fit"
  within the corporate "industrial-technological system" that TK rails
  against.  TK is saying the ITS has failed us, is failing us, and will
  itself fail someday, perhaps dooming planetary life to extinction.
  His thesis is that if sustainable 'survival' will be our long-term
  objective then the ITS needs to be revamped, revised, reformed, or
  tossed entirely, to be replaced by some agrarian model that does not
  consume or waste non-renewable resources and does not support the
  dubious agenda of overpopulation/war/poverty cycles, or Spenglerian
  rise and fall of civilizations, because today's methods of warfare
  have moved the debate into a twilight-zone realm that does not exempt
  civilians from international conflict.  IQ has meaning only if it is

body:
jumangi@my-deja.com wrote:

>   Yes, this paragraph seems agreeable until you reach the last few
> words.  It would be an overstatement to claim that such elements as
> "evil" and "sin" are fictions propagated by a "politically correct
> elite" and/or -only- by them.

No, it's not an overstatement.  Leftists and right-wingers have different
tendencies and ways of thinking.  In some conservative circles, saying "God
is dead" would be considered blasphemy, but saying "nigger" or "spic"
wouldn't bother anyone.  On the other hand, in some leftist circles you
could get away with the former and not the latter.  Morality is relative,
and you will find sanctimonious people of all walks of life.  Leftists are
self-righteous in their own way, and so are conservatives.  Of course, there
may be significant overlap.

Believe me, leftists, who are more secular, can demonize people pretty
badly.  Do you remember Mark Furman?  I'm not saying he was a good guy, I'm
just making a point.  (I do think they took what he said WAY out of
proportion, however -- I digress).

> Ridding ourselves of such "politically
> correct elite" would not eliminate "sin" but instead wreck havoc on
> attempts to discern what such terms could mean.

"Wreck havoc".  <smirck> ;o)

> Someone's claim of a
> word without meaning (for them) doesn't invalidate another's search for
> meaning, and if "evil" or "sin" really don't have meaning then there'd
> be nothing lost if that putative "absense of meaning" were re-verified.
> The existence of manipulative propaganda on the part of a media elite
> doesn't disprove an underlying reality which may or may not conform to
> their highly questionable and not-so-sublimated subliminal agenda.

Look, all I am saying is that there are lots of people out there who are
easily swayed by what the media dishes out.  They may or may not be
stupid -- although the stupid ones may be more easily swayed.  Even smart
people may be given to being influenced by dubious information which is
perpetually pounded into their heads.  When the controlled media tells
society to be watchful of certain types of people, and tells them what
behaviors are appropriate and inappropriate in a specific context, it's
bound to have some influence.  Because a large segment of the population are
not avid readers, their primary source of information is the mass media.

The media loves to take advantage of people's misfortunes, and disasters.
What happened following the deaths of Princess Diana and JFK Jr. are
examples.  The media benefitted in a sick way from both incidents, through
increased ratings.  When news of "racism" hits the screen, people listen.
The media then exploits -- often greatly exaggerates -- such incidents
without much concern as to how they might be provoking racial tensions in
society.  There can be real consequences when the media disseminates
information in a careless manner.

>   It may, furthermore, be critical to take cognizance of the fact that
> when stating "... _we_know_ what political correctness is..." there is
> still nothing implied which asserts the knowledge as being -coherent-,
> i.e. the definition applied by one individual may not necessarily be
> in correspondence with another's definition, because each individual
> might independently assert personal claims to a certain aspect of PC.
> Thereby, something is intrinsically faulty when abiding in "knowledge"
> traced to inherent solipsism. (see: _Personal_Identity_, J.Perry, ed)

You have a point.  People may have their own interpretations of what
political correctness is.  Even Ted Kaczynski had a hard time establishing a
definition for it.

>    Group inequalities are stipulated herein, but unless you're willing
>  to dispute _Brown_vs._Board_of_Education_ (1954), a legal precendent
>  exists which asserts economic benefit to the nation via desegregation.

Wow.  An admission to differences!  I'm impressed.

>   I admit to some confusion here.  Weren't you about to posit a claim
> that racial differences had already been established, and sufficient
> evidence already published?  If so, why the additional duplication from
> Ms. Gottfredson?

Why should scientists stop seeking to find the truth?  Should mathematicians
have been complacent when Archimedes found the value of pi?  Should we stop
trying to find out more about the underwater world and be satisfied with
what Jacques-Yves Cousteau found?  Who are you to tell Linda Gottfredson
that we know enough about racial differences for her to bother to try to
find more on the subject?  Moreover, how do you know she is not married? ;o)

> I thought affirmative action programs were premised
> upon acceptance of racial variations, even as terms of "race/ethnicity"
> aren't clearly defined (example: "Caucasians" can claim 'black' ethnic
> affiliation if disadvantaged by being raised within a black ghetto).

Affirmative action, from what I understand, was intended to fight perceived
discrimination against minorities in hiring.  It then turned into a system
of demanding quotas, without regard to merit -- and companies which did not
comply, or were perceived as not complying, were guilty of racism until
proven innocent.

>   Next, you've provided a characterization of what the term "PC" might
> entail, in "presuming one is automatically right," yet while you do
> that you are nonetheless quick on the draw to assert "rights" without
> any documentation in law literature, e.g. "rights of non-PC'ers" who by
> definition, were -absent- any statement of being "automatically right."

I am not talking about law.  I am talking about perception as to what is The
Truth.

> Perhaps we'll need to sharpen our discussion on this point:  the First
> Amendment Right is not constructed upon analysis of whether someone is
> or is not "PC" but upon constitutional rights of minorities against an
> unjust oppression by the majority.  A "PC" attribute might not fall so
> neatly along the lines of being or not being a member of a minority or
> the majority, particularly in context to where boundary gerrymandering
> was drawn, from which the notions of "minority/majority" got extracted.
>
>   If we're to run with a notion that "non-PC'ers" are not automatically
> right then it's incumbent upon "non-PC'ers" to sustain their burden of
> proof at each step in the argument, a burden they should be eager and
> -willing- to obtain since "not being automatically right" was their
> existential condition, according to your provided characterization.

I agree.  I think we all have a responsibility to back up our arguments.  As
I pointed out, leftists tend to be more secular.  They take socially valued
ideas with religious fervor.  Many things they make an issue out of gets
into subjective territory, which cannot really be proven or disproven; they
are just perceptions.

>    If you'd say that "ability to drastically change our core beliefs"
>  is also an "innate tendency" then the "innate tendencies" are not
>  immutable, even without genetic mutation and genetic bioengineering.
>  First you're asserting (as fact?) that "we all have innate tendencies
>  which influence how we end up..." but later you state this as simply
>  your "opinion" so which case is it going to be?

C'mon, you are being silly.  Some people have biological tendencies which
may influence the ideology they will come to accept.  For example, some
years ago psychologists found that people with _extremely_ dominant and
authoritative personalities were attracted to fascism/Nazism.  It seems
plausible that these aren't the only people who are influenced by genes.  I
don't mean to sound like a biological determinist; I am just being
realistic.  Humans don't have the ability to be anything they want to be.
Not everyone can be a nuclear physicist, for example.  Some people may be
more flexible than others.  However, no gene (as far as I know) has yet been
isolated to conclusively prove this view.

>    Yet TK's manifesto specifically invokes "non-political revolution."
>  How could he possibly be a (political) fascist?

According to Ross, TK contacted Dr. Pierce.  If this is true, it blows your
fansasy right out of the window.

>  Fine -- now here's the bromidic retort as expected:
>
>    Any totalitarian state can be serviced by that High-Technology TK
>  identifies as their core means of asserting social controls over the
>  masses, from the left or right.  The fact that your uncle who was not
>  documented in Poland, nor in TK's manifesto, and has no necessary
>  bearing upon your own views nor upon this exchange, admired defunct
>  facists from a safe distance, has a trophy wife by way of chic racial
>  tokenism, and allows you brief non-racist respite coupled with that
>  obvious inspiration toward sheepskin appropriation and other sundry
>  "golden fleece" awards, says nothing about the itemized sub-point to
>  this particular thread, i.e. opposition to fascism (a special case of
>  totalitarian regimes in general) follows from opposition to forms of
>  High-Technological encroachment upon imaginative freedoms.

Wow.  You really went off on a tangent.  First off, my uncle is not racist.
In fact, he insists there is black in the family.  He has always preferred
darker women.  Now, you may have a predilection for taking women as tokens,
but there is no need for you to project your sexually deviant inclinations
onto this forum!

You also driveled some platitudinous remarks, as expected.  Why must you
equate any system which seeks to take people's freedoms away with fascism?
Do you think governments, which are spuriously non-fascist, can only do good
or something?  You need to wake up from your dream.  Read about history and
current events.

>     He said the revolution he advocates is -similar- to the French and
>   Russian revolutions...

He was referring to strategy, not ideology.  Nice try, though.

>     He mentioned that "true believers" of either form -- leftists or
>   (rightwing) nazis -- presented "a problem" and would not "make a
>   safe recruit to the revolution" particularly if he is "committed
>   also to _another_ ideal" (such as some racially eugenic agenda)..

He also said "true believers" were an indispensable part of any movement.  I
agree that he would oppose any eugenic idea (at least one involving control
via technology).

>     He's clearly opposed to "eugenics" because that would amount to an
>   unnatural "manufactured product," additional "government regulation,"
>   and the (arbitrary) imposition of "medical ethics" determined by some
>   'elite' scientific soviet, or "needs of the industrial-technological
>   system."  So TK would thereby be opposed to racial goals concurrent
>   with either "eugenic" or "dis-eugenic" agendas:

Eugenics is very natural.  Do you prefer skanks?  Is dependency on welfare
the primary trait you look for in women?  Do you prefer women with
non-symmetrical facial features?  If so, well, never mind.  Almost everyone
practices some degree of eugenics, consciously or subconsciously.

>     Trying to follow your tenous "thread" of logic:  were you saying
>  that being called a "commie" -should- be more devastating in light of
>  uncontested accounts?  So McCarthyism still simmers on your burner?
>  I think that was my point exactly.

No, I don't care to push my views on society.  I think the smears are bad,
either way.  I have socialist relatives who I deeply respect.

>     Even if "hatred" for the sinner, rather than the sin, were to
>   improve your effective response, why would we need to spell out a
>   "_right_ to hate" using formal legalistic terms?  Does one require
>   non-specific "right" in order to manifest hatred?  Seems to me an
>   oxymoron and _non-sequitur_.  Hate exists even without "rights."

You are the one drawing strange conclusions.  You keep on bringing up issues
of jurisprudence when there is no basis to do so.

>    These are strawmen.  I don't deny the existence of race, nor of
>  implicit racism which follows from racial distinctions.  Even the
>  notion of being "color-blind" implies some "colorization" out there
>  from which one is assuming deliberate blindness.  My difficulty
>  occurs when I'm trying to resolve all cases of people into what may
>  seem to be rather arbitrary and -temporal- indicators of racial
>  distinction.  There seem to be increasing numbers that do not fit
>  nicely into their proper pigeonholes, so the "race" concept is not
>  a well-formed notion.

Are you talking about mixed-race people?  When different races of dogs
interbreed it does not take away the fact that different races pre-existed
and still exist.

>    However, the IQ-test argument was itself premised upon whether a
>  given individual, or class of individuals, finds some means of "fit"
>  within the corporate "industrial-technological system" that TK rails
>  against.

TK brought up leftist rejection of the utility of IQ tests first!  He used
it as an example of liberal intolerance and, to paraphrase him, "rejection
of science and rationality."

>  TK is saying the ITS has failed us, is failing us, and will
>  itself fail someday, perhaps dooming planetary life to extinction.
>  His thesis is that if sustainable 'survival' will be our long-term
>  objective then the ITS needs to be revamped, revised, reformed, or
>  tossed entirely, to be replaced by some agrarian model that does not
>  consume or waste non-renewable resources and does not support the
>  dubious agenda of overpopulation/war/poverty cycles, or Spenglerian
>  rise and fall of civilizations, because today's methods of warfare
>  have moved the debate into a twilight-zone realm that does not exempt
>  civilians from international conflict.  IQ has meaning only if it is
>  inextricably tied to the survival of individuals, groups and society.

Perhaps to monitor any eugenic or dysgenic trends in the non-technological
society, IQ tests might be of use?  Would TK be happy leading a bunch of
halfwits within his quasi-Neolithic utopia?

Regards,
Pyro

body:
From: Pyro <Valderrey@email.msn.com>

(re: overstatements of "elite" controllers)
> ... what I am saying is that the elite effectively ingrains ideas
> of what is "good" and "bad", "just" and "unjust", etc., within the
> public, who, in large part, are unable to decide for themselves the
> merit of such propaganda.  Am I making this too complicated?

    Yes, you are making it too complicated, because you also spoke of
  (biological) "innate tendencies" that influence outcome.  How can
  the "elite" have all that control -- ingraining their ideas -- when
  (as you say) "innate tendencies" already provide the organism's
  assertions of "good" / "bad" in matters of destiny, etc. ???


> jumangi@my-deja.com wrote:
>> That puts the cart before the horse, however, since enlightenment
>> philosophy at the core of nation-building in this country spoke of
>> government of the people and that just governments derived powers
>> only by consent of the governed.
>
> Why do you have to dish out so many truisms?

    Enlightenment Philosophy is not National Socialism.  Capiche?


>> Concurrent then, with "loss of control" over information flow by
>> politico/religious hierarchies through widespread -democratization-
>> of an electronic publishing industry, the notion that dissemination
>> of "political corrections" should proceed entirely from those who
>> maintain tight grips on mass-media is weakening.
>
> There are countless academics who have had a difficult time
> publishing their works deemed "inappropriate" by corporate elites who
> either have their own biases and want to repress certain ideas they
> don't agree with or perhaps they are concerned over the image of
> their company.

    I checked out the Christopher Brand frap and found simply that an
  Academic publishing company reneged on an agreement to publish.  It
  must have been something rather serious for them to change horses in
  the middle of the stream on an 11th-hour notice, but of course it is
  a privilege of any publishing house to do these sorts of things. This
  doesn't stop Christopher Brand from finding another publisher.


> In many so-called Western Democracies propagating certain _ideas_ via
> internet can get you arrested.  Many organizations are pushing for
> this in America.  I don't see this trend reversing.  So you can jot
> down your notion of "the democratization of publishing" on your fist
> and stick it where the sun don't shine.

    Would my fist "get arrested" that way?  What other kinds of
   critically important "arrests" do you feel ought to be published?
   I've tried to make it patently clear for you that I'm stipulating
   "racial differences" for the purposes of these exchanges.  Were
   there any points at contention you thought needed establishment on
   the "racial variations" issue?  Is there some critical conclusion
   you haven't yet advanced that follows from observations concerning
   "racial differences or variations?"


(re: origins of the notions of "evil" & "sin")
> I have never said it was _only_ PC'ers who are self-righteous.  I
> have stated repeatedly that both secular and non-secular people have
> their own ideas of what is "evil" and "sin".

    So now you've cavitated to my point:  that indeed it -was- your
  "overstatement" to suggest that notions of "evil" & "sin" existed
  only on account of propagation from the "politically correct elites."


> Some people confuse equality under the context of law with equality
> in ability. I'm not one of those.

   Since the Supreme Court didn't make that conflation I'm concluding
  now that you agree with _Brown_vs._Board_of_Education_ (1954).


>> Nobody is stopping scientists from seeking truth, nor is anyone
>> stopping Ms. Gottfredson from conducting research.
>
> Tell that to J. Philippe Rushton, who was almost fired for talking
> about race differences. They did nail Christopher Brand of Edinburgh
> University, however.

    Haven't bothered to follow those cases.  Were half-a-dozen other
  academics waiting in the wings to assume their publishing and/or
  teaching positions?  How does losing one's job prevent one from
  seeking (or finding) truth?  And is that distinct from The Truth?

    Regarding Christopher Brand:  this guy was mixing up race theory
  with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.
  They might independently each qualify for scholarly inquiry, however
  I would imagine that combination of the two was understandably being
  received as inappropriate, running along just a wee bit too far down
  that garden path of seduction for pedagogical tastes.  TK had already
  anticipated such developments as pathological trends inherent to the
  "industrial-technological system" with:

   ._______________________________________________________________.
   |                                                               |
   |     "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes,   |
   |      such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]"   |
   |_______________________________________________________________|


  and we may note TK's juxtaposition of "abuse" with "hatred" in the
  two overlapping incongruous contexts which nailed Christopher Brand.

    Now Ms. Gottfredson was offered $177,541 by the Pioneer Fund to
  conduct research (www.s-light.demon.co.uk/stories/genewar06.htm, or
  www.ferris.edu/ISAR/Institut/pioneer/search.htm). When her University
  (who is the employer) intervened to say she could not accept those
  moneys on the grounds of something similar to an academic "conflict of
  interest" then Ms. Gottfredson was faced with a -choice- to continue
  teaching or to resign and run with the Pioneer Fund.  Nobody doubts
  that $177,541 would have been the bottom of the barrel for her, nor
  that she might have sought employment at another University where she
  could also accept Pioneer Funds.  The crux of this issue centers on
  whether Universities can rightfully exert controls over their faculty
  by conditioning employment according to standards they are free to
  develop internally.  Of course, with regards to the Law and Higher
  Education, appeals processes remain available for those who wish to
  take it to the courts, yet I couldn't locate any litigation which may
  have documented that eventuality.  I agree that any case-law in that
  area might be of interest.  A University does not expect professorial
  staff energies to be diverted away from obligations at teaching and
  core-curricular refinement.  Furthermore the University is sometimes
  itself in a precarious funding position and is by no means completely
  independent of its obligation to the surrounding business community
  or to taxpayers.  "Academic freedom" is a nice-sounding phrase, yet
  for all intents and purposes we might say that it is mythological in
  certain controversial areas, and isn't exempt from the drumbeat of
  those objectionably platitudinous charges.  The issues being worked
  aren't so much those establishing mensuration of "racial variation"
  in a rapidly-changing educational context and/or compositional mixing
  but what to do about social policy, given stipulation of parameters.


>> What novel conclusions had you expected Ms. Gottfredson to draw?
>
> It is conventionally -- and erroneously -- believed that social
> inequalities are necessarily the result of discrimination. Plenty of
> evidence points to significant differences among individuals, groups,
> and races as far as intelligence, specifically. Given the extent of
> diversity in our society, and the pervasive belief that there is some
> sort of bogey man holding certain groups down, and given that we have
> not conclusively proven to what _extent_ these differences might be
