> Regarding Christopher Brand: this guy was mixing up race theory
> with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.

Um, no.  He got into two seperate controversies, one of which was used as a
pretext to get rid of him for his unpopular views over the other, unrelated
issue.

The first controversy began as he openly asserted that the races differ in
intelligence, among other things, obviously.  The second controversy began
when he asserted that psychological studies have shown that children who are
of above-average intelligence who have sex with adults, in which the child
is willing to engage in the act, do not end up with psychological conflicts
when they get older, generally.  That's all he said.  While it did not go
well with the Puritanical cretins in the UK, it was scientifically accurate.

(re: Kaczynski quote)
> | "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes, |
> | such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]" |

Sounds to me like something Dick Armey or George Bush Jr. would say.

> Now Ms. Gottfredson was offered $177,541 by the Pioneer Fund to
> conduct research (www.s-light.demon.co.uk/stories/genewar06.htm, or
> www.ferris.edu/ISAR/Institut/pioneer/search.htm). When her University
> (who is the employer) intervened to say she could not accept those
> moneys on the grounds of something similar to an academic "conflict of
> interest" then Ms. Gottfredson was faced with a -choice- to continue
> teaching or to resign and run with the Pioneer Fund. Nobody doubts
> that $177,541 would have been the bottom of the barrel for her, nor
> that she might have sought employment at another University where she
> could also accept Pioneer Funds. The crux of this issue centers on
> whether Universities can rightfully exert controls over their faculty
> by conditioning employment according to standards they are free to
> develop internally.

Absolutely.  I think standards are extremely important, especially in
universities.  However, there is a critical distinction between firing a
professor because he is a non-productive louse and firing one merely because
he holds unpopular views, even though he does his job well.  You are showing
the arrogance PC'ers hold, which I have been talking about.  Who are you, or
the chancellor of a university, or anyone else, to tell a professor he
should resign because his work is "improper", even as the professor has
engaged in groundbreaking work and has contributed to an area of science to
which few or none can match?

> "Academic freedom" is a nice-sounding phrase, yet
> for all intents and purposes we might say that it is mythological in
> certain controversial areas, and isn't exempt from the drumbeat of
> those objectionably platitudinous charges. The issues being worked
> aren't so much those establishing mensuration of "racial variation"
> in a rapidly-changing educational context and/or compositional mixing
> but what to do about social policy, given stipulation of parameters.

How are we to establish effective social policies if we don't know why
things are the way they are?

(re: race differences and genes)
> The "conclusive proof" is available by creating opportunities and
> allowing them to succeed or to wash-out in higher-education courses.

This sounds nice, but you need to be specific as to what you mean by
"opportunities".  I mean, I just applied for a job and because I am
"Hispanic" (by the absurd technicality of subconscious racist Anglo-Saxon
do-gooders) I am fairly confident I will get the job, and be automatically
given more points on the cognitive exam than my white counterparts (even
though I would have scored higher than virtually all of them without the
help).  Yes, sounds like an oppressive system.

> It seems to me, however, that once deciding opportunities should not
> be allowed (on pretext of "genetic" impairment applied to classes of
> individuals rather than to the individuals themselves) then one would
> effectively -sabotage- a viability of any further "conclusive proof"
> in the evaluative context of those higher-education courses.

_Non-sequitur_.  Ms. Gottfredson, and other race-realist academics, are not
out to keep certain groups from having the same opportunities as everyone
else.  They are out to find and expose the truth; they are trying to be
objective.

> The
> notion of pre-judging individuals based on "genetic" profiling might
> have been similar to the former Soviet Union's testing practices for
> pre-determining life stations, but is inconsistent with democratic
> principles in the free society based on individual rights.

Geneticists in the Soviet Union were sent to gulags.  It seems to me the
analogy involving the Soviet Union would have worked better if you had used
PC'ers instead of race-realist professors

(re: is TK a closet Nazi?)
> If we're to avoid media bias it might be worthwhile to move toward
> the direction of being like a court room.

You have convinced me that TK has never contacted any Nazi organization. :-)

However.. as you pointed out, media bias against Kaczynski was shown by
their clumping him with neo-Nazis.  This reinforces my view of how people
use the "Nazi" label to smear, especially those who are clearly _not_ Nazis,
who happen to be "undesirable", or have undesirable opinions.

> Double-negatives don't necessarily render a positive, and also
> one might dislike certain political groups because they are -not-
> sufficiently radical, or simply because they do not share common
> interests (i.e. were "hippie protestors" conversant in "boundary
> functions" and/or general mathematical topics?).

Oh, c'mon.  The liberal professors egged on the radicals of the '60s.  It
seems to me you are doing some rationalizing -- and you are good at it (I
don't mean this in an offensive way).

> The closest I can find, from the Manifesto, is TK's affiliation
> with anarchism, which is completely at variance to the corporate
> right-wing, or to platitudinous National Socialism, since TK used
> the phrase "our particular brand of anarchism" in footnote #34.
> Elsewhere TK is extraordinarily verbose on how both "right-wing"
> and "left-wing" desire High-Technology as a means of controlling
> their organizations and national electorate. The bottom line is
> that TK cannot be categorized even remotely near the right-wing.

Platitudinous National Socialism?  A platitude is an over-used word or
phrase.  While the Nazis undoubtedly had many platitudes in their day, their
slogans are fairly obscure to the general public today.  National Socialists
are merely at one extreme, and the PC'ers are diametrically at the opposing
end.

(re: "commies" and McCarthyism)
> So smear McCarthyism could be justified upon organizations
> advocating violence against the state?

Where would we draw the line?  The Communists in the '50s were perceived as
very threatening to the state; we were in a Cold War.  Communists were
stealing nuclear secrets and handing them to the Soviets.  I hate the
current state of affairs, and hope the system collapses.  But I don't
advocate violence against the system, or to anyone in particular.  I just
hope it self-destructs -- and it may, who knows. . .

Modern day fascists seem to hold views more in line with what the Founding
Fathers believed.  The Founding Fathers were far more racist than most
realize.  (By Founding Fathers I mean American Revolutionaries, in case you
are not American).

(re: nature's "IQ-testing")
> How did you determine that 'nature' had a will? Wouldn't a "will"
> entail a purpose, and then an organizational destiny or _teleos_?
> Which terms would the atheist propose to employ for a universe with
> ulterior -personality- apparently on behalf of these human critters?

What I mean is, humans, having greater intellectual capacity than all other
creatures, have been able to manipulate their environment at an unparalleled
level.  Humans have been able to destroy forests and to make innumerable
species of animals extinct or endangered.  These are truisms, I know.  With
technology, humans have lost harmony with the natural world.  Living in the
suburbs and in filthy, polluted cities, typing into computers, etc., we live
artificial lives.  As time goes by it will get worse and worse.  Although in
many ways technology will benefit mankind.

I think we are doing many things against the laws of nature.  I find Taoism
to be an interesting nontheistic religion which emphasizes this point.

> Maybe you can assist me with the task of sorting out the points
> presented by Ms. Gottfredson's paragraph above. She notes that the
> multiculturalists want to impose a "Western view of reality" while
> claiming that they exaggerate "differences among American subgroups"
> and trivialize "contrasts among societies across other continents."
> However, the "Western view" was constructed from Europe, West Asia,
> North Africa, and America -- so hasn't Ms. Gottfredson engaged in
> _prima-facia_ trivialization of intercontinental differences by
> invoking the "Western view" phrase?

Yes, the "Western view" has been shaped by many different cultures and
civilizations, but it has developed into something distinct.  And no, she is
not trivializing other cultures, but exposing the ethnocentrism of those who
want to impose this adulteration of antecedent cultures and civilizations.
The West has gotten very decadent, and is hated in most of Arabia, as well
as in many other parts of the world -- and rightly so!

YANKEES GO HOME!!!

> I find it most perplexing that we should be "conscious" at all in
> what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos. Perhaps you were about
> to offer non-pedantic explanation that should dispel all perplexity?
> It would seem that pedantry saves bandwidth if leading to correctness
> and truth, whereas non-communicative carelessness wastes resources.

First at all, in this "what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos", this
state of "conciousness", which even you recognize to exist, should be a
matter of fulfillment and joy rather that an element of perplexity and
despair.  To reach that "correctness or TRUTH", you have to equate it with
BEAUTY.  Yes, TRUTH = BEAUTY. (Please, do not ask me what is beauty).

Yes, it is in the eyes of the beholder.

It is in nature; it is in the rumor of the breeze caressing the trees, in
the sound ot the rain, in the singing of a bird, and in a flower.

It is in an aria by Puccini , "Ave Maria" by Schubert, Mozart and Bach's; it
is in poetry and literature.

It is in a still life by Cezanne, a landscape by Monet, and "Las Meninas" by
Velazquez; it is in Picasso's works, Giotto and Fra Angelico's.

It is in Praxiteles', in Berninis', Donatello's, and Michelangelo's; it is
in the Parthenon, as well as in the church of Notre Dame and the new
Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao.

It is in the smile of a child, as well as in making love to the woman you
desire.

It is in a good cup of wine, as well as in the freshness of a glass of water
when you are thirsty.

It is in the dignity of common and humble people.

It is in the fluttering of a butterfly, and being able to hear the voice of
your conscience.

Yes my friend, this element that you are referring to as "conciousness" is
the _tabula_ that can bring you to awareness and give you the ability to
appreciate beauty, which again = TRUTH.

After so many years of civilization, it appears that we haven't moved too
far from that Socratic statement: "There is only one thing I know, and that
is that I know nothing."  (Is this the correct quotation?) Anyway, JB, you
are right about the fact that we are insignificant and with a very limited
perception of the immensity of the universe.  But remember, the TRUTH is
your TRUTH -- and manifests from your own capacity to appreciate beauty.

Regards,
Pyro

body:
> (re: overstatements of "elite" controllers)
> Author: Pyro <Valderrey@email.msn.com>
> I am glad you brought this up.  I believe we are influenced greatly
> by both environment and culture, but truths regarding the influence
> of genes on our outcome, in terms of extent, has been greatly
> suppressed.  When I suggested that genes might play a role on the
> outcome of our political affiliations, it was a statement based on
> intuition.  It would be very difficult to prove conclusively that
> some gene or set of genes makes one a "conservative" or "liberal", a
> "fascist" or "Marxist", etc.  Again, I believe that genes _may_ serve
> as one of many influences to the outcome of one's political
> affiliation.

    Well, were those "truths" being suppressed here?  Now that we
  have both perspectives "in balance" where can we go from here?


> Another point I would like to bring up is that minority groups which
> are more passionate about their beliefs can often get ahold of a
> disproportionate amount of power, through sheer will.  So, you can
> just imagine how effective propaganda can be if it can stimulate the
> more passionate types.

    Was the goal to make propaganda more effective or less effective?


> (re: origins of the notions of "evil" & "sin")
>> So now you've cavitated to my point: that indeed it -was- your
>> "overstatement" to suggest that notions of "evil" & "sin" existed
>> only on account of propagation from the "politically correct elites."

> This subtopic doesn't seem to be going anywhere.  I never said it was
> only PC'ers who are sanctimonious, and that notions of "good" and
> "evil" are spread just by "PC elites." I just pointed out that many
> PC'ers go around smearing people because they have different
> viewpoints, and carry a "holier than thou" attitude.  I believe you
> misconstrued what I said, which is nothing new.

    There's a method to my madness as follows:  you're suggesting now
  that in addition to having a "presumption" or "perception" of being
  "automatically right" that (an additional characterization) "PC'ers"
  are sanctimonious with "'holier than thou' attitudes."  It's very
  important to nail down the semantics of what you propose to say,
  because that's not too far from locating similar attitudes on the
  part of those who -critique- the "PC'ers" and/or "Jews" -- as you
  have done on this newsgroup.  As with Orwell's _Animal_Farm_ when
  I see the same tactics employed by both human capitalists and pigs
  then I can't very well distinguish the two anymore.  Later on herein
  I will be presenting a diagram with _relative_scaling_ for "degrees"
  of the "PC-attribute" you might wish to measure, so that if one may
  claim "higher-PC" over the "PC'ers" then one can play one-upmanship
  on the "holier than thou" attitude, thus becoming even more like an
  "enemy" one hates.  As for those who "smear" we have ample evidence
  from -you- of racist (anti-semitic) smearing, and I don't see how
  you can avoid the charge of being sanctimonious, "holier than them,"
  or "automatically right" (you appear to be without self-criticism),
  and in bed with those you claim are your "PC" enemies.

    If I've misconstrued, please feel free to straighten out what seems
  to be the major disconnect and discrepancy from the part of "pyro."


> (re: harassment of J. Philippe Rushton)
> Professor Rushton had always received excellent reviews from his
> superiors at the school until he drew controversy.  Once again,
> nice try.

    Prof. Rushton's research seemed to indicate that large brain-size
  implied small penis-size, and vice-versa, that large penis-size
  was highly correlated with small brain-size.  Are you claiming that
  "scientific results" of that type should -not- be controversial?
  Some professors are famous for stirring up "harassment" in order to
  popularize their findings.


> I think firing, or harassing, professors because they hold unpopular
> views, or teach unpopular _facts_, doesn't bode well for nations
> claiming to be democratic.

     At least in a free democracy we can hear of the news, because
   many other systems of government would have no publicity at all.
   There's the major difference in a nutshell.


>> Regarding Christopher Brand: this guy was mixing up race theory
>> with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.

> Um, no.  He got into two seperate controversies, one of which was
> used as a pretext to get rid of him for his unpopular views over the
> other, unrelated issue.

> The first controversy began as he openly asserted that the races
> differ in intelligence, among other things, obviously.  The second
> controversy began when he asserted that psychological studies have
> shown that children who are of above-average intelligence who have
> sex with adults, in which the child is willing to engage in the act,
> do not end up with psychological conflicts when they get older,
> generally.  That's all he said.  While it did not go well with the
> Puritanical cretins in the UK, it was scientifically accurate.

    If there were "controversies" then there's some legitimate dispute
  as to alleged "science" and "accuracy."  How did (some) psychologists
  determine that there were no "conflicts" afterwards?  Even preventive
  medicine has difficulty resolving longitudinal studies.  It's much
  more difficult to define "health" than "disease" and there are still
  unresolved issues even for definitions of "mental disease" much less
  claiming to know what is "mental health."  Furthermore, an absense
  of "psychological conflicts" does not imply no impairment to mental
  health functioning.  Social taboos are not aribtrary but were also
  components of an evolving picture of human existence, and cannot be
  summarily dismissed.  We still haven't solved problems defining IQ,
  particularly if IQ is measured according to "fit" in a dysfunctional
  "industrial-technological system" causing planetary despoilation.
  So, in what sense do we know what is "above-average intelligence" if
  we haven't determined what are the genuine contributory factors for
  (natural) intelligence?

    I don't think pedophilia is defensible, even if there were "no
  detectable psychological conflicts" (rationalization par excellance)
  because these are not the sole criterion for determining whether the
  subversion and seduction of young people is deleterious to their life
  functioning.  Meeting the psychological minimum is not the measure of
  all things.  A question is not whether pedophilia impaired individuals
  below the minimal criteria for functioning, but whether possibilities
  for excellence above and beyond "minimal" standards were impaired to
  any degree whatsoever.  Once again a most vivid and horrific example
  of logical fallacy within the nut-house called pop-psychology.

                ( Matthew 18:6, Mark 9:42, Luke 17:2 )


> (re: Kaczynski quote)
>> |  "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes,   |
>> |   such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]"   |
>
> Sounds to me like something Dick Armey or George Bush Jr. would say.

     Your point being .... ?


>(re: Ms. Gottfredson and $177,541 in Pioneer Funds)
> ... I think standards are extremely important, especially in
> universities.  However, there is a critical distinction between
> firing a professor because he is a non-productive louse and firing
> one merely because he holds unpopular views, even though he does his
> job well.  You are showing the arrogance PC'ers hold, which I have
> been talking about.  Who are you, or the chancellor of a university,
> or anyone else, to tell a professor he should resign because his work
> is "improper", even as the professor has engaged in groundbreaking
> work and has contributed to an area of science to which few or none
> can match?

    Nobody stopped Ms. Gottfredson from continuing her research, as is
  the perogative of any professional desirous of scientific integrity.
  Nobody told Ms. Gottfredson that she should resign on account of her
  "work."  So far, the issue presented to her concerned a University
  Policy prohibitive of the receipt of funds from a "special-interest
  group" identified as racist.  The chancellor, the board of regents,
  the president:  all are beholden to outside factors stemming from a
  state legislature, the taxpayers, obligation to alumni, the business
  community.  Any component of the process is subject to review and/or
  replacement if deemed unsuitable.  Ms. Gottfredson could have pursued
  litigation yet decided against it, if Pioneer Funds were so all-fired
  critically important.  I'll ask you again:  what were the conclusions
  you expected Ms. Gottfredson to reach, and what possible impact would
  any potential conclusion have upon shaping social policy concerns?


> (re: race differences and genes)
>> The "conclusive proof" is available by creating opportunities and
>> allowing them to succeed or to wash-out in higher-education courses.

> This sounds nice, but you need to be specific as to what you mean by
> "opportunities".  I mean, I just applied for a job and because I am
> "Hispanic" (by the absurd technicality of subconscious racist
> Anglo-Saxon do-gooders) I am fairly confident I will get the job, and
> be automatically given more points on the cognitive exam than my
> white counterparts (even though I would have scored higher than
> virtually all of them without the help).  Yes, sounds like an
> oppressive system.

     I agree that affirmative action hiring quotas shouldn't work by
   adding points to a "cognitive exam" (if that's really the case).
   There's no advantage in disguising affirmative action as something
   else.  In fact those who might oppose affirmative action, could on
   principle be those the programs were designed to benefit.  The fact
   that opposition to affirmative action does not stem from those who
   "benefit to excess" indicates their degree of insecurity and greed.
   I would prefer my resume to reflect hiring by merit rather than by
   affirmative action.  If you don't sense "oppression" then perhaps
   you're not sufficiently challenged.  May I recommend the library?


>> It seems to me, however, that once deciding opportunities should not
>> be allowed (on pretext of "genetic" impairment applied to classes of
>> individuals rather than to the individuals themselves) then one would
>> effectively -sabotage- a viability of any further "conclusive proof"
>> in the evaluative context of those higher-education courses.

> _Non-sequitur_.  Ms. Gottfredson, and other race-realist academics,
> are not out to keep certain groups from having the same opportunities
> as everyone else.  They are out to find and expose the truth; they
> are trying to be objective.

    If they're just diddling each other with sociological narcissism
  then that's yet another argument there upon academic irrelevance.
  "Objectivity" is not the singular goal of science, by the way, since
  we are also interested in obtaining data that provides some answers
  to the question of how to chart social policy.  If Ms. Gottfredson's
  work isn't going to inform us about social policies, then where was
  the "statement of purpose" motivating her studies?  A _sequitur_ to
  my fundamental argument still remains even if it's not going to apply
  (as -you- claim) to Ms. Gottfredson, or "other race-realist academics"
  (though there are, undoubtedly, many "race-realist academics" who are
  acutely attuned to potential social policy effects of their research).
  Thereby a "flip side" of that issue presented itself when you asked:


(re: "academic freedom" and/or that fundamental question)
> How are we to establish effective social policies if we don't know
> why things are the way they are?

    ... yielding a "chicken-and-egg" dilemma.  To unravel it, let's ask
  first if the "role of science" can possibly provide answer(s) to "why
  things are the way they are" or -- more pragmatically -- whether we
  may expect of science only a function of fulfilling "theory creation"
  and provisional explanation of data.  A "science" claiming to offer
  answers to fundamental "why" questions runs the risk of not anymore
  being science but becoming "scientism," i.e. science arrogating an
  expertise over regions of inquiry formerly assigned to religion. TK's
  view seems to be that religion won't be replaced by science -- and he
  seems to state that religion most definitely should not be replaced
  by those aspects of "science" which are High-Technology -- so one
  could adopt, or share, TK's views wholesale or dispute them outright
  or in part, which seems to be the point of focus for this newsgroup.


> (re: is TK a closet Nazi?)
>> If we're to avoid media bias it might be worthwhile to move toward
>> the direction of being like a court room.

> You have convinced me that TK has never contacted any Nazi
> organization. :-)

    This admission seems to be rather important, since Ross Getman had
  stated his reason for abandoning a.f.u. was due to -your- insistence
  on conflating TK with Nazism, and now you owe an apology to Ross for
  mischaracterizing his statements.


> However.. as you pointed out, media bias against Kaczynski was shown
> by their clumping him with neo-Nazis.  This reinforces my view of how
> people use the "Nazi" label to smear, especially those who are
> clearly _not_ Nazis, who happen to be "undesirable", or have
> undesirable opinions.

    I'm in agreement that "media bias" occurs through miscategorization
  via "clumping" since a presumption on the part of mass-media is that
  "news consumers" have neither an interest nor the sophistication for
  factual details which lead to differentiation of cases, distinguishing
  TK from other unrelated incidents, even as we all recognize generally
  that "justice" initially requires case-by-case treatment for meeting
  the requirements of due process and equal protection.  Often as not,
  the news reporters themselves lack the interest and sophistication to
  provide accurate and thorough coverage, and in more than a few cases
  the news reporters are simply corporate shills, or puppets of statist
  agenda.  Debates about "journalistic ethics" are largely unresolved
  and ongoing, and are usually unhelpful when discussed after the fact,
  which unfortunately is also most usually the situation.  With regards
  to TK, a feature of TK's peculiar violent methods must have prejudiced
  mass-media against the possibility of a reasoned forum for carefully
  detached and insightful remarks.  "Who people are" and "what they do"
  are also too often conflated by an overtly simplistic/reductionistic
  mass-media.  Mass-media is itself merely an aggregate of individual
  contributions, and each of those individuals is operating from some
  simplistic/reductionistic "world-view" or perspective on things, so
  the sum of parts might be nothing more than "more parts" and never
  attain wholism.  One doesn't locate wholism simply by summation since
  there might be many different approaches to obtaining an addition of
  many highly-unrelated discrete components.  Philosophical wholism
  usually needs to proceed from a notion of completedness or closure,
  as with drawing a circular (or spherical) boundary.  Mass-media seems
  unwilling to entertain that idea, opting instead for their peculiar
  brand of asinine chaos.  The marketplace is an inferior as judge of
  cultural forms, however, servile journalists seem to take their cues
  primarily from marketplace fashions rather than depicting long-range
  perspectives from which activity in the present-tense can better be
  coordinated.  There is resistance to forms of wholism that are drawn
  too narrowly, or without sufficient dimensionality, so understanding
  of higher-dimensional properties (i.e. packing, density, tangency,
  codings, lattices, algebraic geometry, etc.) may be the prerequisite
  for constructed wholism with sufficiently comprehensive boundaries.
  Again, most journalists are woefully undereducated in mathematics.

    If mass-media was labelled "PC" and if this forum can attain a
  level of non-spin objectivity unavailable in mass-media, then perhaps
  it's also appropriate to demolish the "PC" notion.  It's paradoxical
  to assert positions "more correct" than "political correctness" since
  that notion introduces fluidity and redefinition of terms.  Rather
  than polarizing perspectives and propositional statements into two
  boxes labelled "PC" & "non-PC" it may be helpful to consider complex
  spectra of views running, more or less, along two intersecting axis:


                                   true                e
                            c        |
            a                        |       d
                  b                  |
                                     |                   f
                                     |
     politically incorrect ----------+---------- politically correct
                                     |
           j          l              |     g                 i
                                m    |
                 k                   |               h
                                     |
                                   false


  with letters (a...m) identifying a number of sample "positions" on the
  chart.  I'm hoping we can work from this diagram, or one similar, and
  if you'd like to propose an alternative then by all means do so.  It's
  essential to disentangle any -necessary- association of "PC"/"non-PC"
  with notions of "true"/"false" (or other variations: "The True", etc).
  If there's a position qualifying as both "non-PC" and "true" then it
  can be identified by marking its location on the diagram somewhere
  nearby to letter "a." Positions in general, however, might not all be
  aligned along a diagonal running from "a" through "h" since we might
  also encounter perspectives and views which run along a diagonal from
  "k" through "e" and so all over the map of this diagram. A fundamental
  identifier distinguishing these two axis may be provided by contextual
  comparison:  the "correct" or "incorrect" according to politics was
  determined by socio-political alignments, something akin to majority
  will.  A "true" or "false" axis boils down to insertion of individual
  assessment, evaluation, review, and/or initiation of perspectives that
  may or may not be in accord with the majority.  The diagram itself can
  be subjective when two individuals disagree over phenomena along the
  horizontal axis (such as differences among polling results), and will
  be subjective when two individuals encounter variances along vertical
  axis estimations of the relative "truth" or "falsity" of some given
  propositional construct.  The relative "degree of subjectivity" to
  such diagrams is simply accumulated "measure of statistical variance"
  among positions (a...m) and (a'...m') -- unprimed and primed diagrams
  -- obtained by summing:

   ___
   \
     \   A*A'*(a - a')^2 + B*B'*(b - b')^2 + C*C'*(c - c')^2 ...
     /
   /___


  for each of the diagrammed positions (a...m) and (a'...m') with their
  corresponding relative weight factors (A...M) and (A'...M') assigned
  to each of the positions in the diagrams, since not all individuals
  will necessarily regard a given set of propositional statements, or
  positions, or perspectives, or views, as equally weighted.  They might
  want to introduce measures of _relative_importance_ to variations from
  their precise locations, as placed within their respective bi-axial
  correspondence frames.

    Perhaps we can avoid the clumping of "media bias" once developing
  an understanding for categorical taxonomy of perspectives, according
  to the generalized characterization for orthogonal axis utilized for
  representing the relationship between an individual and society, and
  then by comparison, among individuals and societies.  Elsewhere on
  this newsgroup you have criticized (say) "Jews" for being "too PC,"
  however if they are to sustain -your- criticism, then in that context
  -you- wish to propose they are -not- "PC" -- or are "non-PC" -- and
  so we would have the confusion of contexts and thereby an intrinsic
  paradox to what appears to be untenable:  your anti-semitism asks an
  audience to accept that some group could be "non-PC" because they are
  "too PC" so you'd need to establish the precise manner in which that
  diagram has "wrap around" -- of which there are several varieties --
  providing some justification for why you've chosen a particular model.
  If, instead you wish -not- to communicate by clarifying those points
  sufficiently, then the  'net.consequence'  of your "theorization"
  runs the risk of becoming little more than a fart in the wind.  Also,
  if hyperspace "wrap around" (such as the video-game *Asteroids*) is
  your 'solution' or explanation of why a "PC" group could be relabelled
  as "non-PC" then you'd also need to describe just what is implied by
  an ordering relation on horizontal and/or vertical axis.

    Furthermore, since this is the newsgroup  "alt.fan.unabomber"  any
  reference to "Nazis" should be related in some manner to the topic of
  discussion, as to how and what TK advocated, and whether or not there
  is agreement/disagreement, and perhaps why or why not, etc.  Had TK
  been targeting "semites" or were such affiliations incidental?  The
  three contexts for "nazi" in his Manifesto occur in:

      (a) par.83 -- how the "power process" for identifying with mass
    movements is "exploited by the fascists, nazis, and communists."

      (b) par.161 -- how behavioral psychology is also an instance of
    "technical advance" for "controlling human beings" though "not ...
    impressively successful."  TK says there are "growing numbers ...
    who ... are rebels against the system:  welfare leaches, youth
    gangs cultists, satanists, nazis, radical environmentalists,
    militiamen, etc."  Interpreting this paragraph is difficult, since
    TK is diagnosing ills of the system as inherent pathologies to the
    "industrial-technological system."  Evidence of the pathology is
    being provided by increasing numbers of rebels.  Then, among the
    itemized groups listed, TK includes "radical environmentalists"
    as if there should be some kind of guilt-by-association.  This is
    a confusing passage since "radical environmentalism" might be a
    popular term with some personality types, so why is TK associating
    them with leaches, cultists, gangs, satanists, nazis, militiamen?
    There is a double-take "irony" involved in that passage:  TK is
    (1) saying that "radical environmentalists" (however commendable)
    are also themselves evidence of pathology in a crumbling ITS.
    However para.161 was discussing how "to integrate these techniques
    into a functioning social system" via "educational psychology" and
    some possible "advances relating to human behavior."  So TK is also
    (2) sounding a call to those who might be "leaches, cultists, gangs,
    satanists, nazis, militiamen, etc." to consider taking up a banner
    of "radical environmentalism."  The placement of "environmentalism"
    among those other groups was woefully incongruous, yet we might
    take into account that TK was/is a mathematician, perhaps with some
    sense of humor:  "The teachers are too busy taking knives and guns
    away from the kids to subject them to the latest techniques for
    making them into computer nerds."  TK will detail those "latest
    techniques" in the final sentence of para.161, slipping in a bit of
    subliminal programming.  TK was a professor, and very likely still
    remains a 'teacher' actively engaged in "taking knives and guns
    away from kids" also through "radical environmentalism" -- a third
    irony -- perhaps an exquisite interpretation available only for
    those inclined by higher mathematics, which is neither the same as
    high technology nor scientism.

      (c) par.222:  The irony agains run thick.  TK invokes a reference
    to "True Believers" and then trots out a proposition concerning an
    assertion of -attribute- for those "True Believers" (as if we really
    can be all that knowledgeable about a phenomenon poorly understood).
    How can anyone be certain that "not all True Believers are of the
    same psychological type as leftists" ? The only source for possible
    certainty seems to follow from the general condition that it's not
    unsafe to assume Venn diagrams for concept apprehension. TK follows
    with:  "Presumably" (sic!) "a truebelieving nazi, for instance is
    very different psychologically from a truebelieving leftist."  Well
    of course, wasn't that Hitler's point-of-contention against the
    German communist party?  Why, then, is TK saying "presumably" ?  It
    is an _obvious_point_ not requiring presumption!  Again, TK asks
    those who would be "nazis" to consider "psychological differences."
    Eric Hoffer's books were among many titles directed at analyzing the
    causes of Nazi Germany.  The phenomenon of a "True Believer" was
    being identified as a -problem- within the human condition, so the
    the book _The_True_Believer_ was designed to be an anti-nazi tract.
    Like Hoffer, TK pokes fun at "leftists" but considers them far less
    dangerous to sustainable civilization than nazis.  "This presents a
    problem with which we must admit we don't know how to deal."  (This
    is a statement of -perplexity- !) "We aren't sure how to harness the
    energies of the True Believer to a revolution against technology."
    (Because such harnessing would itself be a behavioral technology.)
    Then TK sets about "harnessing" them anyway:  "...no True Believer
    will make a safe recruit to the revolution unless his commitment is
    exclusively to the destruction of technology..." because TK advances
    the "definition via negative" attempting to 'hook' the reader into
    accepting a particular interpretation of what TK thinks the person
    identified as "True Believer" should be.  In order to understand
    what paragraph #222 is about some investigation needs to proceed on
    the semantic merits of what the word "technology" means, and why TK
    thinks it needs destruction in order to save the human species.

   There was -no- invocation of "race agenda" or "pedophilia" involved
  in TK's narrowly stated goal of exclusive commitment.  In what way,
  then do people like J.Phillip Rushton, Chris Brand, or Ms.Gottfredson
  bear upon TK's description of his revolution?  Either relevance, or
  that "True Believer" will -not- make a "safe recruit."   Q.E.D.


>> Double-negatives don't necessarily render a positive, and also
>> one might dislike certain political groups because they are -not-
>> sufficiently radical, or simply because they do not share common
>> interests (i.e. were "hippie protestors" conversant in "boundary
>> functions" and/or general mathematical topics?).

> Oh, c'mon.  The liberal professors egged on the radicals of the '60s.
> It seems to me you are doing some rationalizing -- and you are good
> at it (I don't mean this in an offensive way).

    Not all liberal professors were throwing eggs, so who is actually
  doing the "rationalizing" here?  Rational thinking is distinct from
  rationalizing, because rational thinking is open-minded while the
  device of rationalizing is employed to justify a closed-mind.  The
  closed mind works by -presuming- a conclusion and then attempting to
  fit facts into some peculiar twist.  You would suggest for us that
  "any professor who did not egg on the '60s radicals" could not be a
  liberal, which is the sort of untenable hypothesis that could proceed
  only from a closed-mind.  Your example (above) provided illustration
  of not only "rationalization" but also "rationalization with covert
  projection" (claiming -others- are that cause of "rationlization").


>> The closest I can find, from the Manifesto, is TK's affiliation
>> with anarchism, which is completely at variance to the corporate
>> right-wing, or to platitudinous National Socialism, since TK used
>> the phrase "our particular brand of anarchism" in footnote #34.
>> Elsewhere TK is extraordinarily verbose on how both "right-wing"
>> and "left-wing" desire High-Technology as a means of controlling
>> their organizations and national electorate. The bottom line is
>> that TK cannot be categorized even remotely near the right-wing.

> Platitudinous National Socialism? A platitude is an over-used word or
> phrase.  While the Nazis undoubtedly had many platitudes in their
> day, their slogans are fairly obscure to the general public today.
> National Socialists are merely at one extreme, and the PC'ers are
> diametrically at the opposing end.

    We have a new (complex) model, now, where you can try a recasting
  of your political chart.  There are -many- instances of what may
  constitute a "fringe" (extremist) group.  When speaking of "opposite"
  one might refer to "inverting about X-axis" or "inverting about Y"
  or "inverting about both" or introducing a new/previously unanalyzed
  dimension.  It is quite obviously a mistake to claim that one group
  might have some (conspiratorial) connection to another simply because
  both can be considered extremist.  As for platitudes, the literature
  of _Mein_Kampf_ has been analyzed for its "plethora of proverbs" --
  of which Hitler was well versed -- and most acknowledge Hitler as a
  master deceptionist with propaganda.  The fundamental question still
  remains:  why were so many deceived by Hitler's insane program which
  led Germany into yet another plan of self-destruction?  His war was
  (paradoxically) the destruction of Germany and its people, completely
  -unlike- an agenda to "destroy technology" which is non-specific, has
  no nationalism, is not directed at any racial group, considers the
  longest-range viewpoint possible, does not involve political activity,
  is not interested in leading large numbers of "true believing" sheep,
  is uninterested by economic self-aggrandizement or conquests of more
  territory.  No resemblance between propaganda and anti-propaganda.


> (re: "commies" and McCarthyism)
>> So smear McCarthyism could be justified upon organizations
>> advocating violence against the state?

> Where would we draw the line? The Communists in the '50s were
> perceived as very threatening to the state; we were in a Cold War.
> Communists were stealing nuclear secrets and handing them to the
> Soviets.  I hate the current state of affairs, and hope the system
> collapses.  But I don't advocate violence against the system, or to
> anyone in particular.  I just hope it self-destructs -- and it may,
> who knows. . .

> Modern day fascists seem to hold views more in line with what the
> Founding Fathers believed.  The Founding Fathers were far more racist
> than most realize.  (By Founding Fathers I mean American
> Revolutionaries, in case you are not American).

    Well yes, the embarassment of a Civil War is the legacy of -their-
  original Constitution, though a few had the prescience to speculate
  upon likelihood of modification to a living document.  One might also
  instead say that the War of Independence had much to do with forcing
  an institution of government, even prematurely, by enshrining a 3/5th
  qualification for slave designation.  They also passed a Constitution
  in the absense of Thomas Jefferson who at that time was in France, so
  it could be argued that business community conservatives, rather than
  exponents of an Enlightenment Philosophy, set those wheels into motion
  for subsequent War during the 1860s.  Where does one stop drawing the
  boundary for "Founding Fathers" -- is Lincoln included in that group,
  particularly when noticing his magnificent memorial in Wash., D.C.?
  So, there were "whigs" / "tories" / "federalists" / "republicans" --
  with significant points of departure among them -- and to claim some
  monolithic tendency on the part of "Founding Fathers" is to ignore
  the reading of history that you have devotedly espoused.  Prior to
  inception of the Civil War, importation of African slaves had been
  already banned; many plantations were gradually setting free their
  slaves.  The 1860s Civil War was fought primarily over "Succession
  versus Union" and only secondarily on abolition.  The Emancipation
  Proclamation set -nobody- free because those southern territories
  already conquered had already released their slave holdings, whereas
  those southern territories not yet conquered were not abiding by the
  terms of Northern declarations anyway.  That was simply Lincoln's
  propaganda during the course of the Civil War.


> (re: nature's "IQ-testing")
>> How did you determine that 'nature' had a will? Wouldn't a "will"
>> entail a purpose, and then an organizational destiny or _teleos_?
>> Which terms would the atheist propose to employ for a universe with
>> ulterior -personality- apparently on behalf of these human critters?

> What I mean is, humans, having greater intellectual capacity than all
> other creatures, have been able to manipulate their environment at an
> unparalleled level.  Humans have been able to destroy forests and to
> make innumerable species of animals extinct or endangered.  These are
> truisms, I know.  With technology, humans have lost harmony with the
> natural world.  Living in the suburbs and in filthy, polluted cities,
> typing into computers, etc., we live artificial lives.  As time goes
> by it will get worse and worse.  Although in many ways technology
> will benefit mankind.

    For evidence of "greater intellectual capacity" you point to
  manipulation of the environment, dominance over nature, technological
  development and lost harmony, artificial lives, etc.  In what sense
  were you saying "nature" had a 'will' when you've outlined how nature
  has been dominated by humans with a "greater intellectual capacity"
  (greater than whom -- nature?).  How do you measure the "intellectual
  capacity" of nature in order to determine which is the greater?  Much
  in your paragraph indicated the sorry lacuna of your (mis)education.


> I think we are doing many things against the laws of nature.  I find
> Taoism to be an interesting nontheistic religion which emphasizes
> this point.

     Where in Taoism was it said that we do many things against the
   laws of nature?


>> Maybe you can assist me with the task of sorting out the points
>> presented by Ms. Gottfredson's paragraph above. She notes that the
>> multiculturalists want to impose a "Western view of reality" while
>> claiming that they exaggerate "differences among American subgroups"
>> and trivialize "contrasts among societies across other continents."
>> However, the "Western view" was constructed from Europe, West Asia,
>> North Africa, and America -- so hasn't Ms. Gottfredson engaged in
>> _prima-facia_ trivialization of intercontinental differences by
>> invoking the "Western view" phrase?

> Yes, the "Western view" has been shaped by many different cultures
> and civilizations, but it has developed into something distinct.
> And no, she is not trivializing other cultures, but exposing the
> ethnocentrism of those who want to impose this adulteration of
> antecedent cultures and civilizations. The West has gotten very
> decadent, and is hated in most of Arabia, as well as in many other
> parts of the world -- and rightly so!  ...  YANKEES GO HOME!!!

   Wouldn't imposition of ethnocentricism be one component of what she
 identifies as the "Western view?"  Even if "yankees" went home where
 would that home be:  America, Europe, West Asia or North Africa? There
 would still remain a "Western view" which for all intents and purposes
 hasn't changed.  What assurances does one retain that a "Western view"
 would evaporate once "yankees" go home?  "Yankees" certainly are not
 the sole proponents of a "Western view," particularly a view which we
 say has been "shaped by -many- different cultures and civilizations."


>> I find it most perplexing that we should be "conscious" at all in
>> what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos. Perhaps you were about
>> to offer non-pedantic explanation that should dispel all perplexity?
>> It would seem that pedantry saves bandwidth if leading to correctness
>> and truth, whereas non-communicative carelessness wastes resources.

(re: "consciousness" -- "pedantry" -- "bandwidth")
> First at all, in this "what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos",
> this state of "conciousness", which even you recognize to exist,
> should be a matter of fulfillment and joy rather that an element of
> perplexity and despair.

    An initial perplexity consists of how "consciousness" could even
  exist without vision and personality to the cosmos -- I think you
  glossed over that point -- yet that lack of vision and personality
  was amply provided by your statement of adherence to atheism.  It's
  not trivial to "remove God" from the picture because in order to do
  so, certain obligations persist for filling the void remaining as a
  consequence to removal.  One of God's many former functions was to
  provide means for social organization and administration of justice.
  TK notes several times how "leftism" tends to fill the void once
  God (and/or religion) are annihilated, but -never- claims that such
  replacement occurs from the right-wing.  TK's "criticism of the left"
  in this context might be interpreted as criticism of the irreligious:


        "218. Various thinkers have pointed out that leftism is a kind
         of religion. Leftism is not a religion in the strict sense
         because leftist doctrine does not postulate the existence of
         any supernatural being. But for the leftist, leftism plays a
         psychological role much like that which religion plays for
         some people.  ... "

    TK's criticism of religion occurs in context to conservative abuse
  (exploitation/manipulation) of religious true-believers "as cheap and
  transparent support for narrow, short-sighted selfishness ... or ...
  cynically exploited to make easy money ... or has degenerated into
  crude irrationalism ... or is simply stagnant," with each observation
  highly correlated to problems inherent to the conservative status-quo.


        "30. (Paragraph 184) A further advantage of nature as a
         counter-ideal to technology is that, in many people, nature
         inspires the kind of reverence that is associated with
         religion, so that nature could perhaps be idealized on a
         religious basis. It is true that in many societies religion
         has served as a support and justification for the established
         order, but it is also true that religion has often provided a
         basis for rebellion. Thus it may be useful to introduce a
         religious element into the rebellion against technology, the
         more so because Western society today has no strong religious
         foundation.

        "Religion, nowadays either is used as cheap and transparent
         support for narrow, short-sighted selfishness (some
         conservatives use it this way), or even is cynically exploited
         to make easy money (by many evangelists), or has degenerated
         into crude irrationalism (fundamentalist Protestant sects,
         "cults"), or is simply stagnant (Catholicism, main-line
         Protestantism). The nearest thing to a strong, widespread,
         dynamic religion that the West has seen in recent times has
         been the quasi-religion of leftism, but leftism today is
         fragmented and has no clear, unified inspiring goal.

        "Thus there is a religious vaccuum in our society that could
         perhaps be filled by a religion focused on nature in
         opposition to technology.  But it would be a mistake to try to
         concoct artificially a religion to fill this role. Such an
         invented religion would probably be a failure.  Take the
         "Gaia" religion for example. Do its adherents REALLY believe
         in it or are they just play-acting? If they are just
         play-acting their religion will be a flop in the end.

        "It is probably best not to try to introduce religion into the
         conflict of nature vs. technology unless you REALLY believe
         in that religion yourself and find that it arouses a deep,
         strong, genuine response in many other people."

    Perplexity is -not- the same as despair.  It is -not- "joy" which
  finds amusement at the expense of others, through excoriation by race
  or religion, such as your anti-semitic remarks on this newsgroup.
  _Ecclesiastes_ says "anger is better than mirth, but joy is better
  than anger."  You have been confusing "joy" with "mirth" because
  you still haven't moved beyond "anger."  Perplexity is prerequisite
  for an open-mind distinguishing rational thinking from rationalizing.


(re:  truth=beauty)
> Yes, it is in the eyes of the beholder.

    There are numerous problems with your rhapsodizing, which you might
  discover yourself by following up on studies of philosophy.  To begin
  with, those "innate tendencies" (found in Plato) do not square with
  Plato's distinction of truth (eternal) from beauty (mutable), nor with
  investigation of reality versus appearances.  J.S.Mill quite obviously
  overstated when saying "truth is beauty, beauty truth, that is all ye
  can know and all ye need to know..." What horsepucky! Must have been
  "toungue-in-cheek" because there's quite a bit more to know than just
  his simple reductionist statement.  A doctrine of ignorance, Mr. Mill!

    Furthermore:  beauty is subjective, as you say, but we consider the
  project of inquiry into truth as potentially objective, not merely as
  "your truth" and "my truth" but improved correlations as among those
  diagrams mentioned herein.  Study them well, grasshopper.


> After so many years of civilization, it appears that we haven't moved
> too far from that Socratic statement: "There is only one thing I
> know, and that is that I know nothing."

    As I had previously mentioned, the Athenian Council found Socrates
  wanting, even with all his disingenuous pretensions to ignorance.
  How did Socrates "know" which questions to ask?   :-)




         - regards
         - jb

matches.quote:
Almost everyone will agree that we live in a deeply troubled society. One
of the most widespread manifestations of the craziness of our world is
leftism, so a discussion of the psychology of leftism can serve as an
introduction to the discussion of the problems of modern society in general

But what is leftism? During the first half of the 20th century leftism
could have been practically identified with socialism. Today the movement is
fragmented and it is not clear who can properly be called a leftist. When we
speak of leftists in this article we have in mind mainly socialists,
collectivists, "politically correct" types, feminists, gay and disability
activists, animal rights activists and the like. But not everyone who is
associated with one of these movements is a leftist. What we are trying to
get at in discussing leftism is not so much a movement or an ideology as a
psychological type, or rather a collection of related types. Thus, what we
mean by "leftism" will emerge more clearly in the course of our discussion
of leftist psychology (Also, see paragraphs

Even so, our conception of leftism will remain a good deal less clear
than we would wish, but there doesn't seem to be any remedy for this. All we
are trying to do is indicate in a rough and approximate way the two
psychological tendencies that we believe are the main driving force of
modern leftism. We by no means claim to be telling the WHOLE truth about
leftist psychology. Also, our discussion is meant to apply to modern leftism

body:
THE PSYCHOLOGY OF MODERN LEFTISM

6. Almost everyone will agree that we live in a deeply troubled society. One
of the most widespread manifestations of the craziness of our world is
leftism, so a discussion of the psychology of leftism can serve as an
introduction to the discussion of the problems of modern society in general.

7. But what is leftism? During the first half of the 20th century leftism
could have been practically identified with socialism. Today the movement is
fragmented and it is not clear who can properly be called a leftist. When we
speak of leftists in this article we have in mind mainly socialists,
collectivists, "politically correct" types, feminists, gay and disability
activists, animal rights activists and the like. But not everyone who is
associated with one of these movements is a leftist. What we are trying to
get at in discussing leftism is not so much a movement or an ideology as a
psychological type, or rather a collection of related types. Thus, what we
mean by "leftism" will emerge more clearly in the course of our discussion
of leftist psychology (Also, see paragraphs 227-230.)

8. Even so, our conception of leftism will remain a good deal less clear
than we would wish, but there doesn't seem to be any remedy for this. All we
are trying to do is indicate in a rough and approximate way the two
psychological tendencies that we believe are the main driving force of
modern leftism. We by no means claim to be telling the WHOLE truth about
leftist psychology. Also, our discussion is meant to apply to modern leftism
only. We leave open the question of the extent to which our discussion could
be applied to the leftists of the 19th and early 20th century.

9. The two psychological tendencies that underlie modern leftism we call
"feelings of inferiority" and "oversocialization." Feelings of inferiority
are characteristic of modern leftism as a whole, while oversocialization is
characteristic only of a certain segment of modern leftism; but this segment
is highly influential.

leftist hates science and rationality because they classify certain beliefs

still conceive of himself as having the capacity to be strong, and his

leftist is too far gone for that. His feelings of inferiority are so
ingrained that he cannot conceive of himself as individually strong and
valuable. Hence the collectivism of the leftist. He can feel strong only as

fuss

matches.quote:
Psychologists use the term "socialization" to designate the process by
which children are trained to think and act as society demands. A person is
said to be well socialized if he believes in and obeys the moral code of his
society and fits in well as a functioning part of that society. It may seem
senseless to say that many leftists are over-socialized, since the leftist
is perceived as a rebel. Nevertheless, the position can be defended. Many
leftists are not such rebels as they seem

The moral code of our society is so demanding that no one can think,
feel and act in a completely moral way. For example, we are not supposed to
hate anyone, yet almost everyone hates somebody at some time or other,
whether he admits it to himself or not. Some people are so highly socialized
that the attempt to think, feel and act morally imposes a severe burden on
them. In order to avoid feelings of guilt, they continually have to deceive
themselves about their own motives and find moral explanations for feelings
and actions that in reality have a non-moral origin. We use the term
"oversocialized" to describe such people

Oversocialization can lead to low self-esteem, a sense of powerlessness,
defeatism, guilt, etc. One of the most important means by which our society
socializes children is by making them feel ashamed of behavior or speech
that is contrary to society's expectations. If this is overdone, or if a
particular child is especially susceptible to such feelings, he ends by
feeling ashamed of HIMSELF. Moreover the thought and the behavior of the
oversocialized person are more restricted by society's expectations than are
those of the lightly socialized person. The majority of people engage in a
significant amount of naughty behavior. They lie, they commit petty thefts,
they break traffic laws, they goof off at work, they hate someone, they say
spiteful things or they use some underhanded trick to get ahead of the other
guy. The oversocialized person cannot do these things, or if he does do them
he generates in himself a sense of shame and self-hatred. The oversocialized
person cannot even experience, without guilt, thoughts or feelings that are
contrary to the accepted morality; he cannot think "unclean" thoughts. And
socialization is not just a matter of morality; we are socialized to confirm
to many norms of behavior that do not fall under the heading of morality.
Thus the oversocialized person is kept on a psychological leash and spends
his life running on rails that society has laid down for him. In many
oversocialized people this results in a sense of constraint and
powerlessness that can be a severe hardship. We suggest that
oversocialization is among the more serious cruelties that human beings
inflict on one another

We argue that a very important and influential segment of the modern
left is oversocialized and that their oversocialization is of great
importance in determining the direction of modern leftism. Leftists of the
oversocialized type tend to be intellectuals or members of the upper-middle
class. Notice that university intellectuals [3] constitute the most highly
socialized segment of our society and also the most left-wing segment

The leftist of the oversocialized type tries to get off his
psychological leash and assert his autonomy by rebelling. But usually he is
not strong enough to rebel against the most basic values of society.
Generally speaking, the goals of today's leftists are NOT in conflict with
the accepted morality. On the contrary, the left takes an accepted moral
principle, adopts it as its own, and then accuses mainstream society of
violating that principle. Examples: racial equality, equality of the sexes,
helping poor people, peace as opposed to war, nonviolence generally, freedom
of expression, kindness to animals. More fundamentally, the duty of the
individual to serve society and the duty of society to take care of the
individual. All these have been deeply rooted values of our society (or at
least of its middle and upper classes [4] for a long time. These values are
explicitly or implicitly expressed or presupposed in most of the material
presented to us by the mainstream communications media and the educational
system. Leftists, especially those of the oversocialized type, usually do
not rebel against these principles but justify their hostility to society by
claiming (with some degree of truth) that society is not living up to these
principles

Here is an illustration of the way in which the oversocialized leftist
shows his real attachment to the conventional attitudes of our society while
pretending to be in rebellion against it. Many leftists push for affirmative
action, for moving black people into high-prestige jobs, for improved
education in black schools and more money for such schools; the way of life
of the black "underclass" they regard as a social disgrace. They want to
integrate the black man into the system, make him a business executive, a
lawyer, a scientist just like upper-middle-class white people. The leftists
will reply that the last thing they want is to make the black man into a
copy of the white man; instead, they want to preserve African American
culture. But in what does this preservation of African American culture
consist? It can hardly consist in anything more than eating black-style
food, listening to black-style music, wearing black-style clothing and going
to a black-style church or mosque. In other words, it can express itself
only in superficial matters. In all ESSENTIAL respects more leftists of the
oversocialized type want to make the black man conform to white,
middle-class ideals. They want to make him study technical subjects, become
an executive or a scientist, spend his life climbing the status ladder to
prove that black people are as good as white. They want to make black
fathers "responsible." they want black gangs to become nonviolent, etc. But
these are exactly the values of the industrial-technological system. The
system couldn't care less what kind of music a man listens to, what kind of
clothes he wears or what religion he believes in as long as he studies in
school, holds a respectable job, climbs the status ladder, is a
"responsible" parent, is nonviolent and so forth. In effect, however much he
may deny it, the oversocialized leftist wants to integrate the black man
into the system and make him adopt its values

We certainly do not claim that leftists, even of the oversocialized
type, NEVER rebel against the fundamental values of our society. Clearly
they sometimes do. Some oversocialized leftists have gone so far as to rebel
against one of modern society's most important principles by engaging in
physical violence. By their own account, violence is for them a form of
"liberation." In other words, by committing violence they break through the
psychological restraints that have been trained into them. Because they are
oversocialized these restraints have been more confining for them than for
others; hence their need to break free of them. But they usually justify
their rebellion in terms of mainstream values. If they engage in violence
they claim to be fighting against racism or the like

We realize that many objections could be raised to the foregoing
thumb-nail sketch of leftist psychology. The real situation is complex, and
anything like a complete description of it would take several volumes even
if the necessary data were available. We claim only to have indicated very
roughly the two most important tendencies in the psychology of modern
leftism

The problems of the leftist are indicative of the problems of our
society as a whole. Low self-esteem, depressive tendencies and defeatism are
not restricted to the left. Though they are especially noticeable in the
left, they are widespread in our society. And today's society tries to
socialize us to a greater extent than any previous society. We are even told
by experts how to eat, how to exercise, how to make love, how to raise our
kids and so forth

prove that black people are as good as white. They want to make black
fathers "responsible." they want black gangs to become nonviolent, etc. But

kids and so forth.

that ought to have had all sorts of qualifications and reservations attached
to them; and some of our statements may be flatly false. Lack of sufficient
information and the need for brevity made it impossible for us to fomulate
our assertions more precisely or add all the necessary qualifications. And
of course in a discussion of this kind one must rely heavily on intuitive
judgment, and that can sometimes be wrong. So we don't claim that this
article expresses more than a crude approximation to the truth.

232. All the same we are reasonably confident that the general outlines of
the picture we have painted here are roughly correct. We have portrayed
leftism in its modern form as a phenomenon peculiar to our time and as a
symptom of the disruption of the power process. But we might possibly be
wrong about this. Oversocialized types who try to satisfy their drive for
power by imposing their morality on everyone have certainly been around for
a long time. But we THINK that the decisive role played by feelings of
inferiority, low self-esteem, powerlessness, identification with victims by
people who are not themselves victims, is a peculiarity of modern leftism.
Identification with victims by people not themselves victims can be seen to
some extent in 19th century leftism and early Christianity but as far as we
can make out, symptoms of low self-esteem, etc., were not nearly so evident
in these movements, or in any other movements, as they are in modern
leftism. But we are not in a position to assert confidently that no such
movements have existed prior to modern leftism. This is a significant
question to which historians ought to give their attention.

	Yes.  As I recall, on of the things that got Hoffer going was the
success of the Communist secret police in absorbing the operatives of
the Gestapo (and related organs) after World War II.  Ideologically, one
would think this astonishing.  Hoffer thought it meant that the
Communists simply offered the only outlet available for people of a
fanatical mindset.

> would be more relaxed about their own views.  What is natural to humans
> is to associate mostly with friends, whose views we are familiar with and
> who we've found to be congenial to us.  Not to constantly have to deal
> with the opinions of strangers about what we think.
> Also "rigid thinkers" may be rebelling and their views have a psychological
> meaning of rebellion; symbolic, verbal rebellion, so that disagreement
> has a heavy meaning for them.

	Somee of my favorite lines on this come from a bit of contemporary
music.  One is just, "Allies, in a world of too much choice."  The other
is "If faith is blind, through darkness it shall guide us."

	Before it gets lost in all the criticism, I'd point out that the last
line tells one about the virtuous possibilities of zealotry.  There
really are times when confusion and danger overwhelm us, and blind faith
can be the only thing that gives anyone direction.  Fortunately, those
occasions are rare.  Unfortunately, the human capacity to face them
sometimes becomes a need so powerful that, in the words of ISAIF, "If
our society had no social problems at all, the leftists (and here we may
insert, 'any zealot') would have to INVENT problems..."

Scott
